(Surat an-Nur)
It is entirely Madani, and it has sixty-four verses, according to one count (or sixty-two, and it is said four).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear verses, that you may remember.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear verses, that you may remember.﴾

The majority of readers read "sūratun" (سُورَةٌ) with a nominative ending (ḍamma), while Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif read it with an accusative ending (fatḥa). As for those who read it in the nominative, the majority said: beginning a sentence with an indefinite noun (ibtidāʾ bil-nakira) is not permitted, so the estimated meaning is "this is a surah which We have sent down," or we say: "a surah which We have sent down" is a described subject (mubtadaʾ mawṣūf), and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "among what We have revealed to you is a surah which We have sent down." Al-Akhfash said: beginning with an indefinite noun is not far-fetched; so "sūrah" is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and "anzalnāhā" is its predicate. As for the one who read it in the accusative, it is according to the sense of a verb, meaning: "follow a surah," or "recite a surah," or "We have sent down a surah." As for the meaning of "surah" and the meaning of "sending down," these have already been discussed.

If it is said: "Sending down" only occurs from a higher place to a lower place, and this indicates that Exalted Allah is in a direction. We say: the answer is in several respects.

The first: Jibril (peace be upon him) used to memorize it from the Preserved Tablet and then would bring it down upon him (ﷺ), so for this reason it is permissible to say "We sent it down," by way of figurative extension.

The second: Allah, Exalted, sent it down from the Mother of the Book in the lowest heaven all at once, and then afterwards sent it down in installments through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him).

The third: The meaning of "anzalnāhā" is: We gave it to the Messenger, just as a servant, when he speaks to his master, says: "I raised my need to him"; similarly, the sending down can come from the Master to the servant. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fāṭir: 10].

As for His saying: ﴿and made it obligatory﴾, the well-known reading is with the light form (takhfīf), while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the intensive form (tashdīd).

As for the reading with the light form, al-farḍ (obligation) means decisive determination and specification. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿so half of what you have specified﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], meaning: what you determined; ﴿Indeed, He who has imposed upon you the Qur'an﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 85], meaning: He determined. Then, a surah cannot be "made obligatory," because it has already come into existence, and making the already existing come into existence is impossible. Therefore, the intended meaning must be: "and We made obligatory what is explained in it." He said this because most of what is in this surah concerns rulings and prescribed limits, so He followed it with this statement. As for the reading with the intensive form, al-Farrā' said: the intensive form is for emphasis and multiplication. As for emphasis, it is because they are limits and rulings, so there must be emphasis in making them obligatory so that submission to accepting them is achieved. As for multiplication, it is for two reasons.

One of them: Allah, Exalted, explained in it various rulings.

The second: that He, glorified and exalted, made them obligatory upon all the responsible people until the end of time.

As for His saying: ﴿and in which We have sent down clear verses﴾, there are several views on it.

The first: He, glorified, mentioned at the beginning of the surah types of rulings and limits, and at its end proofs of the Oneness of God. So His saying "and made obligatory" refers to the rulings He explained first, and then His saying "and in which We have sent down clear verses" refers to the proofs of Oneness that He explained. What confirms this interpretation is His saying: ﴿that you may remember﴾, for the rulings and laws were not known to them so that they would be commanded to remind themselves of them. As for the proofs of Oneness, they were almost known to them due to their clarity, so they were commanded to remember them.

The second: Abu Muslim said: it is possible that "the clear verses" are what is mentioned in it of limits and laws, like His saying: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights while sound﴾ [Maryam: 10]; he asked his Lord that He would impose upon him an act.

The third: al-Qadi said: just as the surah includes the performance of obligatory acts, it also includes many matters of discussion, which Allah, Exalted, explained. Since His explanation of them was detailed, He described the verses as "clear."

As for the saying of Exalted Allah: ﴿that you may remember﴾, it is read with the doubled dhal and with the single dhal. The meaning of "la'alla" has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. Al-Qadi said: "la'alla" here means "so that" (kay), and this indicates that Allah, glorified, intended for all of them that they remember. The answer: if He had intended that from all, He would not have strengthened their motives toward disobedience; and if that strengthening did not exist, it would necessarily follow that an act occurs without a determining cause; and if that were permissible, it would not be permissible to infer the existence of a determining cause from possibility and origination, and it would necessitate denying the Creator. Since that is so, it is necessary to interpret "la'alla" according to the other meanings mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. Know that He, glorified, mentioned in this surah many rulings:

**The First Ruling: the word of Allah, the Exalted**

﴿The adulterer and the adulteress: flog each one of them with a hundred lashes. Let not compassion for them overtake you in the religion of Allah, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾

Know that the word of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress﴾, is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'). Its predicate (khabar) is omitted according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, in the sense of: "What Allah has enjoined upon you is the adulterer and the adulteress," meaning: "Flog them." The predicate may also be ﴿flog﴾ (fa-jlidu). The fa' (the particle "then") entered the sentence because the alif and lam (of al-ladhi/al-alif wa-l-lam) carry the meaning of "the one who" (alladhi) and include the meaning of a conditional (shart). Its estimated form is: "The woman who committed adultery and the man who committed adultery, flog them," just as you say: "Whoever commits adultery, flog him." It has also been read in the accusative, by supposing a verb that the apparent words explain. It has also been read as ﴿wa-z-zani﴾ without the yā' (ي).

Know that the discussion of this verse is of two kinds: the first concerns the legal matters (shar'iyyat), and the second concerns the rational matters (aqliyyat). We shall address both sections as far as our capacity allows, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.

**The first kind: the legal matters.** Know that fornication (zina') is forbidden and is among the major sins (kaba'ir). Several things indicate this.

First: Allah, the Exalted, linked it with polytheism and the killing of a soul, in His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse—and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and He said: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra': 32].

Second: He made the hundred lashes obligatory in it in full, unlike the punishment for slander (qadhf) and the drinking of wine. He legislated stoning (rajm) in it, forbade the believers from showing compassion, commanded that a group be present for public disgrace (tashhir), and required that that group be of the believers, because the wicked person is more embarrassed before the righteous people of his community.

Third: What Hudhayfah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "O assembly of people, beware of fornication, for in it are six qualities: three in this world and three in the Hereafter. As for those in this world, it removes radiance, brings poverty, and shortens life. As for those in the Hereafter, it brings the wrath of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, a bad reckoning, and the punishment of the Fire." And from Abdullah, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which sin is greatest in the sight of Allah?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour.'" Then Allah revealed, confirming it: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

Know that it is necessary to investigate several matters in this verse:

First: concerning the reality (mahiyyah) of fornication.
Second: concerning the rulings of fornication.
Third: concerning the conditions that must be met for fornication to necessitate those rulings.
Fourth: concerning the means by which the occurrence of fornication is established.
Fifth: who are those addressed by His saying: ﴿flog them﴾?
Sixth: how are the stoning and the flogging commanded in fornication to be carried out?

**The first investigation: the reality of fornication.** Some of our companions said: it is the insertion of a sexual organ into a sexual organ that is naturally desired and absolutely forbidden. On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** They differed over whether the term "fornication" applies to sodomy (liwat). Some said: yes. They argued for it by both text and reason. As for the text, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a man mounts a man, they are both adulterers." As for reason, sodomy is like fornication in form and in meaning. As for form: fornication is the insertion of a sexual organ into a sexual organ that is naturally desired and absolutely forbidden, and the rear passage is also a sexual organ, because the front passage was named a sexual organ (farj) only because of the opening (infiraj) that it has, and this meaning exists in the rear passage. At most, in common usage sodomy is not called fornication, but this does not undermine the linguistic basis, just as one says: "This is a physician," though he is not a scholar, even though medicine is a science. As for meaning: fornication is the satisfaction of desire from a place naturally desired, in an absolutely forbidden way, and this exists in sodomy, because both the front and rear passages are desired, since they share the qualities that are the object of desire: heat, softness, and narrowness of the entrance. For this reason, whoever holds the doctrine of natures does not distinguish between the two places; it is only the Law that distinguishes between them in prohibition and permission. This is the argument of those who said that sodomy falls under the name of fornication.

As for the majority of our companions, they conceded that sodomy does not fall under the name of fornication, and they argued for this with several points:

First: the well-known custom that this is "sodomy" (liwat) and not "fornication," and vice versa, and the default is that there is no change.

Second: if someone swears not to commit fornication and then commits sodomy, he does not break his oath.

Third: the Companions differed over the ruling on sodomy, and they knew the language. Had sodomy been called fornication, the explicit text of the Book concerning the punishment for fornication would have spared them from disagreement and independent reasoning (ijtihad).

As for the hadith, it is to be understood as referring to sin, as shown by his saying (ﷺ): "When a woman mounts a woman, they are both adulteresses," and his saying (ﷺ): "The two hands commit fornication, and the two eyes commit fornication." As for analogy, it is far-fetched, because although the front passage was named "farj" for the opening it has, it does not follow that everything with an opening is called "farj." Otherwise the mouth and the eye would be "farj." Likewise, they named a star "najm" (star) for its visibility, but they did not call every visible thing a "najm." They named the embryo "janin" for its concealment, but they did not call everything concealed a "janin."

Know that al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) had two opinions concerning the act of sodomy. The sounder of them is: the punishment for fornication applies to it; if the offender is married (muhsan), he is stoned, and if he is not married, he is flogged a hundred times and exiled for a year. The second opinion is: both the active and the passive partner are to be killed, whether or not they are married, based on what Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill the one who does it and the one it is done to." Then concerning the manner of killing there are several views:

First: his neck is struck, as with an apostate.
Second: he is stoned with stones; this is the view of Malik, Ahmad, and Ishaq.
Third: a wall is demolished upon him; this is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).
Fourth: he is thrown from the top of a high mountain until he dies; this is reported from Ali (peace be upon him).

They mentioned these views because Allah, the Exalted, punished the people of Lut with all of these, when He said: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74].

According to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), the sodomite is not subject to a prescribed punishment (hadd) but is to be disciplined (yu'azzar). As for the passive partner: if he is sane, adult, and consenting, then if we say the active partner is to be killed, the passive partner is killed in the same manner as the active partner, based on the report; and if we say the active partner receives the punishment for fornication, then the passive partner receives a hundred lashes and exile for a year, whether married or not. It was said: if she is a married woman, she is stoned; but this is not correct, because she does not become muhsan through being penetrated in the rear passage, so the punishment for married women does not apply to her, just as when the passive partner is male.

The argument of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) for the obligation of the prescribed punishment comes from several points:

The first: sodomy either equals fornication in its reality (mahiyyah) or equals it in the necessary consequences of this reality. When that is so, the punishment is obligatory. The proof of the first: his (ﷺ) saying: "When a man mounts a man, they are both adulterers." The wording indicates that the one who sodomizes is an adulterer. A word that indicates a reality by direct meaning (mutabaqah) also indicates by implication (iltizam) the occurrence of all of its necessary consequences, and the indication by direct meaning and by implication both share the basic indication. So the word that indicates the occurrence of fornication indicates the occurrence of all its necessary consequences. Then, after this, if the designation of fornication is realized in sodomy, it enters under His saying: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress: flog﴾; and if the designation of fornication is not realized, then the necessary consequences of the designation of fornication must be realized, since it is established that a word indicating the realization of a reality indicates the realization of all those consequences. Acting on it with respect to the reality has been abandoned, so it must remain in force with respect to indicating all those consequences. But among the necessary consequences of fornication is the obligation of the prescribed punishment, so this must be realized in sodomy. At most, it may be said that acting on this has been abandoned in his (ﷺ) saying: "When a woman mounts a woman, they are both adulteresses," but abandoning action there does not require abandoning it here.

The second: the one who sodomizes must be killed, so he must be killed by stoning. The proof of the first: his (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever does the deed of the people of Lut, kill the one who does it and the one it is done to." The proof of the second: since killing him is obligatory, he must be an adulterer; otherwise it would not be permissible to kill him, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases." Here there is no apostasy after faith, nor killing of a soul without right. So if fornication after marriage (ihsan) did not occur, he should not be killed. Since it is established that fornication after marriage did occur, stoning is obligatory, based on this hadith.

The third: we analogize sodomy to fornication, the common cause being that natural desire inclines toward it because of the pleasure in it, and it is ugly, so it calls for deterrence, and the prescribed punishment is suitable as a deterrent against it. The opponents said: the difference is in two respects.

One: in fornication there are two inducements (dā'iyān), so its occurrence is more corrupting, and so the need for a deterrent is greater.

Two: fornication leads to the corruption of lineages. The answer: their nullification by intercourse with an ugly old woman.

Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) argued with several points:

First: sodomy is not fornication, as previously established, so it should not be punished by death, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases."

Second: sodomy is not equal to fornication in the need for a legal deterrent, nor in the crime, so it is not equal to it in the prescribed punishment. As for the lack of equality in need: although the active partner desires it, the passive partner does not naturally desire it, unlike fornication, where the inducement exists on both sides. As for the lack of equality in crime: fornication involves the loss of lineage, and sodomy does not. Once this is established, it must not be equal to it in punishment, since the evidence negates the legislation of the prescribed punishment because it is harmful. Acting on it has been abandoned in fornication, so it must remain in sodomy according to the original rule.

Third: the prescribed punishment is like a substitute for the dower (mahr). Since the dower is not connected with sodomy, neither is the prescribed punishment.

The answer to the first: although sodomy is not equal to fornication in its reality, it is equal to it in its rulings.

The answer to the second: although the passive partner does not desire it, this is because the active partner's desire is intensified, since a person is eager for what is forbidden.

The answer to the third: a common cause is necessary.

And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** The community (ummah) is unanimous on the prohibition of sexual intercourse with animals (baha'im). Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) had several opinions on its punishment.

The first: the prescribed punishment for fornication applies to it; the married offender is stoned, and the unmarried offender is flogged and exiled.

The second: he is to be killed, whether married or not, based on what is reported from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill him and kill the animal with him." It was said to Ibn Abbas: "What is the matter with the animal?" He said: "I do not think he said that except that he disliked that its meat be eaten, while that act was done with it."

[p. 117]

The third view, which is the most sound, and is the view of Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Thawri and Ahmad, may God have mercy on them, is that the offender deserves *ta'zir* (discretionary punishment, a penalty not fixed by the sacred law). Their reason is that the *hadd* (a fixed punishment prescribed by God) was legislated as a deterrent against what the soul inclines towards, and this act is not something the soul inclines towards. They declared the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, weak because of the weakness of its chain of narration. Even if it is authentic, it is opposed by what is reported, that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade slaughtering an animal except for eating it.

The third issue: sexual relations between women (*sahq*), intercourse with a corpse, and masturbation with the hand. For these, only *ta'zir* is prescribed.

* * *

The second topic: the rulings on fornication (*zina*). Know that at the beginning of Islam, the punishment for an adulterer was confinement until death for the married (*thayyib*), and verbal abuse for the unmarried virgin (*bikr*). God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you. If they testify, then confine them to the houses until death takes them or God makes for them a way.﴾ ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them both. But if they repent and amend, leave them alone.﴾ [al-Nisa' 15–16]. Then this was abrogated (*naskh*, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation), and the *hadd* for fornication was made stoning for the married, and flogging and banishment (*taghrib*) for the unmarried. Let us mention these two issues.

The first issue: the Kharijites (*Khawarij*) denied stoning and argued for it with several points.

The first: God's words, ﴿Upon them is half of the punishment of free women [muhsanat]﴾ [al-Nisa' 25]. So if stoning were obligatory for the married, half of stoning would be obligatory for the slave, but stoning has no half.

The second: God, may He be glorified, mentioned in the Qur'an various types of sins, such as disbelief, murder and theft, and He did not go into detail about their rulings as He did in explaining the rulings on fornication. Do you not see that He forbade fornication by saying ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ [al-Isra' 32], then secondly threatened the Fire for it, as with all sins, then thirdly mentioned flogging, then fourthly specified that flogging must be witnessed by the believers, then fifthly forbade showing pity towards the offenders with His words ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of God, if you believe in God﴾ [al-Nur 2]. Then sixthly He obligated eighty lashes on whoever accuses a Muslim of fornication, and He did not impose that on whoever accuses someone of murder or disbelief, although these are greater than it. Seventhly He said ﴿And do not accept their testimony ever﴾ [al-Nur 4]. Eighthly He mentioned the one who accuses his wife of something that requires mutual cursing (*li'an*) and deserving the wrath of God. Ninthly He mentioned that ﴿the adulteress, none marries her except an adulterer or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur 3]. Tenthly He mentioned that the proof of fornication is restricted to four witnesses. Given this great attention to detail on the rulings of fornication, both minor and major, it is not permissible to neglect the most important of its rulings and its gravest consequences. It is known that if stoning were legislated, it would be the greatest of these consequences. Since God, may He be exalted, did not mention it in His Book, this shows that it is not obligatory.

The third: God's words, ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog each one of them﴾ [al-Nur 2]. This requires the obligation of flogging for all adulterers. To make stoning obligatory for some of them on the basis of a solitary report (*khabar al-wahid*) would be to specify the general wording of the Book by a solitary report, which is not permissible, because the Book is definitive in its text, while a solitary report is not definitive in its text, and what is definitive takes precedence over what is merely probable.

The majority of the jurists argued for the obligation of stoning the married by what is established through *tawatur* (a report transmitted by so many chains that its transmission is certain): that the Prophet, peace be upon him, did this. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: Stoning was narrated by Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Hurayra, Buraydah al-Aslami and Zayd ibn Khalid, along with others among the Companions. Some of these narrators related the account of the stoning of Ma'iz, and others the account of the woman of Lakhm and the woman of Ghamid. 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Were it not that people would say, 'Umar added to the Book of God, I would have written it in the codex."

As for the answer to their first argument: the verse is specified with respect to flogging. If it is said: this would entail specifying the Qur'an by a solitary report. We reply: rather, by a report that is *mutawatir*, since we have explained that stoning is transmitted through *tawatur*. Furthermore, we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) that specifying the Qur'an by a solitary report is permissible.

As for the answer to their second argument: it is not improbable that the sacred rulings are renewed in accordance with the renewal of the public interests (*maslahah*). Perhaps the public interest that requires the obligation of stoning arose after the revelation of those verses.

As for the answer to their third argument: it is reported from 'Ali, peace be upon him, that he used to combine flogging and stoning. This is the view chosen by Ahmad, Ishaq and Dawud, and they argued for it with several points.

The first: the general wording of this verse requires the obligation of flogging, and the *mutawatir* report requires the obligation of stoning. There is no contradiction, so combining them is obligatory.

The second: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The virgin with the virgin: a hundred lashes and a year's banishment. The married with the married: a hundred lashes and stoning with stones."

The third: Abu Bakr al-Razi, in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*, related from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn al-Zubayr, from Jabir: "A man committed fornication with a woman, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, ordered that he be flogged. Then the Prophet was informed that he had been married (*muhsan*), so he ordered that he be stoned."

The fourth: it is related that "'Ali, peace be upon him, flogged Shurahah al-Hamdaniyyah, then stoned her, and said: 'I flogged her by the Book of God, and I stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).'"

Know that most of the jurists agree that the married are stoned and not flogged, and they argued for this by several matters.

The first: the story of the hired labourer (*'asif*). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "O Unays, go to the wife of this man, and if she confesses, stone her." He did not mention flogging. Had flogging been obligatory along with stoning, he would have mentioned it.

The second: the story of Ma'iz was related through different channels, and in none of them is flogging mentioned along with stoning. Had flogging been required along with stoning, the Prophet, peace be upon him, would have flogged him. And if he had flogged him, it would have been transmitted just as stoning was transmitted, since neither of the two is more worthy of transmission than the other. Likewise in the story of the Ghamidiyyah, when she confessed to fornication, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stoned her after she had given birth; if he had flogged her, that would have been transmitted.

The third: what al-Zuhri related from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'I fear that a long time will pass over people until someone says, "We do not find stoning in the Book of God, the Exalted," and so they will go astray by abandoning an obligation God revealed. We used to recite: The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit fornication, then stone them absolutely. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stoned, and we stoned after him.'" So he informed us that what God obligated is stoning. Had flogging been obligatory along with stoning, he would have mentioned it.

As for the answer to their appeal to the verse: it is specified with respect to the married, and specifying the general wording of the Qur'an by a *mutawatir* report is not impermissible. As for his, peace be upon him, saying: "The married with the married: a hundred lashes and stoning with stones," perhaps that was before his saying: "O Unays, go to the wife of this man, and if she confesses, stone her." As for the report that he, peace be upon him, flogged a woman and then stoned her, perhaps he, peace be upon him, did not know she was married, so he flogged her; then when he learned she was married, he stoned her. This is also the answer regarding the act of 'Ali, peace be upon him. This is what is possible of forced reasoning in these answers, and God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: flogging and banishment are combined for the unmarried offender. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: they are flogged, and as for banishment, it is left to the judgment of the ruler (*imam*). Malik said: the man is flogged and banished, and the woman is flogged and not banished.

The proof of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, is the hadith of 'Ubadah, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Take from me, take from me. God has made a way for them: the virgin with the virgin, a hundred lashes and a year's banishment; and the married with the married, a hundred lashes and stoning with stones." It is also indicated by what Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, and Zayd ibn Khalid related: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, my son was a hired labourer for this man, and he committed fornication with his wife. I ransomed myself from him with a slave girl and a hundred sheep. Then the people of knowledge informed me that upon my son is a hundred lashes and a year's banishment, and upon this man's wife is stoning. So judge between us.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will certainly judge between you by the Book of God. As for the sheep and the slave girl, they are returned to you. As for your son, upon him is a hundred lashes and a year's banishment.' Then he said to a man of Aslam: 'Go, O Unays, to this man's wife, and if she confesses, stone her.'"

Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, argued for denying banishment by several points:

The first: the obligation of banishment requires abrogating the verse, and abrogating the Qur'an by a solitary report is not permissible. They established abrogation in three ways.

The first: God, may He be glorified, linked flogging to the act of fornication with the particle *fa* (then), and the particle *fa* marks a consequence. The scholars of language said: an oath by other than God is a mention of a condition and a consequence. They defined the condition as that to which the word *inna* (if) is attached, and the consequence as that to which the particle *fa* is attached. The consequence (*jaza'*) is a term for what fulfills sufficiency, derived from their saying "jazaynahu," meaning "we compensated him," that is, "we repaid him." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "It will suffice you (*tujzika*) and will not suffice anyone after you," meaning it will be enough for you. From this is the saying of the speaker: "I passed the camels by the pasture with the water." Sufficiency is achieved by flogging only if nothing else is obligated along with it, so obligating something else requires abrogating its being sufficient.

The second: since what is mentioned in the verse is flogging, that was the complete *hadd*. If we make banishment considered along with flogging, then flogging becomes only part of the *hadd* and not the whole *hadd*, which leads to abrogating its being the whole *hadd*.

The third: on the assumption that flogging is the complete *hadd*, the rejection of testimony is connected to it. If we make it only part of the *hadd*, that ruling would be removed. Thus it is established that obligating banishment requires abrogating the verse.

The second: Abu Bakr al-Razi said: if banishment were legislated along with flogging, the Prophet, peace be upon him, would have been obliged, when reciting the verse, to inform the Companions of it, so that they would not believe upon hearing the verse that flogging is the complete *hadd*. Had that been the case, its being widely known would have been like the widespread knowledge of the verse. Since the report of banishment was not at this level, but came through solitary transmission, it is known that it is not considered.

The third: what Abu Hurayra related from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said concerning a slave girl: "If she commits fornication, flog her; if she commits fornication, flog her; if she commits fornication, flog her, then sell her, even for a hair rope." In another narration: "Let him apply the *hadd* to her, and there is no reproach upon him." The way of deducing from it is that if banishment were established, he would have mentioned it along with flogging.

The fourth: either banishment is legislated for the slave girl or it is not legislated. It cannot be legislated, because that would entail harm to the master without any wrongdoing on his part, and that is impermissible. Moreover, he, peace be upon him, said: "Sell her, even for a hair rope." If her banishment were obligatory, her sale would not be permissible, because the ability to deliver her to the buyer does not remain after banishment. And it cannot be that it is not legislated, because of God's words: ﴿Upon them is half of the punishment of free women﴾ [al-Nisa' 25].

[p. 118]

And the fifth: If exile (al-taghrib) were prescribed for the man, then it would either be prescribed for the woman as well or not. The second is invalid, because equality in the offence exists in both of them. And if it were prescribed for the woman, then it is either prescribed for her alone or together with a mahram. The first is not permissible, by the text and by reason. As for the text, it is his saying, peace be upon him: "It is not lawful for a woman to travel without a mahram." And as for reason, it is that desire is dominant in women, and restraint by religion occurs only among the select of people; for the usual cause of women's abstaining from fornication is the presence of male guardians and their modesty before their relatives. By exile, a woman leaves the hands of her relatives and guardians, then her modesty diminishes because she is far from those who know her, so the door of fornication opens for her. Perhaps she is poor, and her poverty grows severe during the journey, so the sum of all this becomes a cause for the opening of the door of this great immorality to her. It is not permissible to say: "We exile her together with the husband or the mahram," because punishing one who is not the offender is not permitted, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

And the sixth: what is related from Umar that he exiled Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf for wine to Khaybar, and he joined Heraclius, so Umar said: "I will not exile anyone after him." He did not make an exception for fornication. And it is related from Ali, peace be upon him, that he said concerning the two virgins if they commit fornication: they are flogged and not banished, and that banishing them is part of the trial (fitnah). And from Ibn Umar that a slave-girl of his committed fornication, so he flogged her and did not banish her. Had banishment been required in the hadd for fornication, this would not have remained hidden from the senior Companions.

And the seventh: what is related that "an old man was found upon a slave-girl, having intercourse with her in a ruin, so he was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: Flog him a hundred times. It was said: He is weak for that. He said: Take a palm-spathe containing a hundred shoots and strike him with it once and release him." Had banishment been obligatory, he would have banished him. If it is said: he did not banish him because he was weak and unable to move, we say: a mount should have been hired for him from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) on which he would be banished. If it is said: perhaps he would be too weak to ride, we say: one who was able to commit fornication, how is it that he is not able to hold himself steady?!

And the eighth: banishment is the counterpart of killing, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]. So He placed them in one rank, and when killing is not prescribed for the fornication of a virgin, it is necessary that its counterpart, which is banishment, also not be prescribed. The answer to the first: there is nothing in the speech of God, exalted is He, except the introduction of the letter fa' upon the command to flogging. As for the claim that what the fa' enters upon is called a jaza' (consequent/response), this is not from the speech of God nor from the speech of His Messenger, but is the saying of some men of letters, so it is not a proof. As for his second statement: if banishment were prescribed, flogging would not be the whole of the hadd, we say: there is no dispute that its ruling has been removed, because establishing anything is at least to require the removal of the non-existence that was. However, what is removed here is not a legal ruling; rather, what is removed is merely the original exemption (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah), and such a removal is not impossible to establish by a single report (khabar al-wahid). We said that what is removed is merely the original non-existence, because the imposition of flogging is a shared concept between the imposition of banishment and the imposition of it together with the negation of banishment. The common element between the two divisions does not indicate either of the two divisions. Therefore the imposition of flogging has absolutely no indication either of the imposition of banishment or of the absence of its imposition. Yet the negation of banishment was known by reason, by considering the original exemption. So when a single report comes and indicates the obligation of banishment, it has not removed in the slightest any of the implications of the wording which indicates the obligation of flogging; rather it removed the original exemption. As for flogging alone being sufficient, and flogging alone being the completion of the hadd, and the rejection of testimony being tied to it, all of that follows from the negation of the obligation of the addition. Since that negation is known by reason, it is permissible to accept a single report concerning it, just as if the obligatory acts were five, the discharge of responsibility and the acceptance of testimony would depend upon their performance, and if something else were added, the discharge of responsibility and the acceptance of testimony would depend on performing that addition too; yet it is permissible to establish it by a single report and by analogy, so it is likewise here. As for if God, exalted is He, said: flogging is the completion of the hadd, and we knew that it alone is the object of the rejection of testimony, then a single report is not accepted here to establish the addition, because the negation of the obligation of the addition was established by a definitive, mutawatir legal proof.

The answer to the second: if what he mentioned were correct, then for everything that specifies a general verse, it would be necessary that it reach the same level of fame as that verse; and it is known that this is not so. The answer to the third: his saying "then sell them" does not indicate sequence, so perhaps they are banished and then after banishment they are sold. The answer to the fourth: it is countered by what al-Tirmidhi related in his Jami', that the Prophet, peace be upon him, flogged and banished, and that Abu Bakr flogged and banished. The answer to the fifth: al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, has two opinions concerning the banishment of a slave:

One: he is not banished, because he, peace be upon him, said: "If a slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her the hadd," and did not command banishment; and because banishment is for the sake of disgrace, and there is no disgrace upon the slave in it, since he is transferred from hand to hand; and because his usufruct belongs to the master, so banishing him harms the master. The second, which is the more sound: he is banished, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Upon them is half the punishment of free women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]; and the harm to the master is not considered, just as a slave is killed for apostasy, and flogged for fornication and slander, even if the master is harmed by it. On this view, how much is he banished? There are two opinions:

One: he is banished for half a year, because it accepts halving, just as he is flogged half the hadd of free persons. The second: he is banished for a full year, because the purpose of banishment is estrangement, and that is a matter that relates to temperament, so free and slave are equal in it, like the period of the ila' oath or of impotence.

The answer to the sixth: a woman is not banished alone, but with a mahram. If the mahram does not volunteer to go with her, he is given his wage from the public treasury; and if she has no mahram, she is banished with trustworthy women, just as it is obligatory for her to go out to the Hajj with them. As for his saying that banishment opens for her the door of fornication, we say: we do not concede this, for most fornication arises from familiarity, companionship, and emptiness of heart, and most of these things are nullified by estrangement, for a person falls into loneliness, weariness and hardship, and so is not free for fornication. The answer to the seventh: what is so far-fetched about a person who is unable to ride a mount being able to commit fornication? The answer to the eighth: it is refuted by banishment when it is imposed by way of discretionary punishment (ta'zir). And God knows best.

* * *

The third issue: The community has agreed that the saying of He, glorified and exalted, ﴿The fornicatrix and the fornicator﴾ conveys the ruling for all fornicators, but they differed over the manner of that indication. Some said: the word "fornicator" (al-zani) conveys generality. The preferred view is that it does not, and the following indicates this.

One: if a man says, "I wore the garment" or "I drank the water," it does not convey generality.

Second: it is not permissible to emphasize it with what is used to emphasize the plural, so one does not say, "The man came, all of them."

Third: it is not qualified by plural qualifiers, so one does not say, "The man, the poor came," or "The jurist, the excellent spoke." As for the saying, "The silver dirham and the yellow dinar destroyed people," it is metaphorical, by the evidence that it is not consistently applied. Also, if "the yellow dinar" were literal, then "the yellow dinar" (in the singular with the masculine adjective) would have to be metaphorical, just as when "the yellow dinars" (plural) is literal, "the yellow dinars" (masculine) is metaphorical.

Fourth: the fornicator is a particular of this fornicator, so the imposition of flogging on this fornicator is the imposition of flogging on the fornicator. If the imposition of flogging on the fornicator were an imposition of flogging on every fornicator, then the imposition of flogging on this fornicator would have to be an imposition of flogging on every fornicator; and since it is not so, what they claimed is invalid. If it is said: why is it not permissible to say that an unqualified word only conveys generality on condition of being free from a word of specification, or to say that an unqualified word, though it entails generality, the word of specification entails particularity? We say: as for the first, it is invalid, because absence has no part in influence; as for the second, because it entails contradiction, which contradicts the original principle.

Fifth: it may be said: "Man is the laugher." If the meaning of our saying "man" were "every man," it would descend to the status of saying "every man is the laugher," and that is contradictory, because it entails restricting humanity to each one of the people, and the meaning of restriction is that it is established in it and not in anything else, so it follows that it would be true of every individual person that he alone is the laugher. The opponent argued with two points:

The first: an exception may be made from it, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾ ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Asr: 2, 3]; and an exception removes from speech what would have entered under it had it not been for the exception.

The second: the alif and lam are for definition, and that is not for defining the quiddity (mahiyyah), since that is already achieved by the base of the noun, nor for defining a single specific individual, since there is no indication in the wording of it, nor for defining some degree of specificity, since no degree is preferable to another; so it must be taken as defining the whole. The answer to the first: that exception is metaphorical, by the evidence that it is not valid to say, "I saw man except the believers." The answer to the second: it is problematic with the entry of alif and lam upon the plural form; if you make them there for emphasis, then likewise here. Some people said: although His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The fornicatrix and the fornicator﴾ does not convey generality by the wording, it conveys it by the context, and that is in two respects:

First: the attachment of the ruling to a derived descriptive attribute indicates that this attribute is the cause ('illah) of that ruling, especially when the attribute is appropriate (munasib), and here it is so. This indicates that fornication is the cause for the obligation of flogging, so it must be said: wherever fornication is realized, the obligation of flogging is realized, since the cause is not separated from its effect.

Second: the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿The fornicatrix and the fornicator﴾, is either all fornicators or some of them. If it is the latter, the verse becomes unspecified (mujmal), and that prevents acting upon it; but acting upon it is commanded, and what the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. Therefore it must be taken as general so that it can be acted upon. And God knows best.

* * *

The third section: Concerning the conditions required for fornication to entail stoning on some occasions and flogging on others. We say: They have agreed that for fornication to entail these two rulings is conditional upon reason and puberty, so stoning and the hadd are not obligatory upon a child or a madman; and these two conditions are not peculiar to these two rulings, but rather they are required in all penalties. As for it entailing stoning, then beyond reason and puberty there are other matters required.

The first condition: freedom. They agreed that the enslaved person is not liable to stoning at all.

The second condition: marriage through a valid contract, so ihsan is not attained by intercourse through ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin), nor by a wrongful intercourse (wat' al-shubhah), nor by an invalid marriage.

The third condition: consummation (al-dukhul), which is necessary; for His saying, peace be upon him: "The married (thayyib) for the married (thayyib)," and one only becomes thayyib by intercourse. Here there are two issues:

**The first question: must the sexual intercourse that establishes marriage-based ihsan (ihsan, the status of a married person that makes one liable to stoning) occur after puberty, freedom and sanity?** There are two opinions.

The first: it is not required. So if a slave has intercourse with a female slave within a valid marriage, or while insane or a minor, and then his status is perfected and he commits zina, stoning is obligatory for him. This is because it is an act of intercourse by which the marriage becomes lawful again for the first husband (tahlil), so ihsan is established by it, just as intercourse in a state of full legal capacity establishes it. Also, the marriage contract itself may be valid before full capacity, so intercourse is likewise.

The second, which is the more correct and the apparent meaning of the text, and the view of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him): it is required that the intercourse occur within a marriage after puberty, freedom and sanity. This is because, since the most complete form of intercourse, namely intercourse within a valid marriage, is required, it is required that this intercourse occur in a state of full capacity.

* * *

**The second question: is full capacity required on both sides, or is each party's own full capacity sufficient?** There are two opinions.

The first: it is required on both sides. So if a boy has intercourse with a free, sane, adult woman, she is not made muhsana (a woman of ihsan) by it. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and Muhammad. The second: each party's own full capacity is required on its own. This is the view of Abu Yusuf (may Allah have mercy on him).

The argument for the first view: it is an intercourse that does not confer ihsan on either of the two who engage in it, so it does not confer it on the other either, like intercourse with a female slave.

The argument for the second view: it is not required that they both be in the state of ihsan at the time of the contract, and likewise at the time of consummation.

**The fourth condition: Islam.** Islam is not a condition for zina to make stoning obligatory according to al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) and Abu Yusuf. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) said it is a condition. Al-Shafi'i argued with several points:

First: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If they accept the jizya (the tax paid by non-Muslim subjects), then inform them that they have what the Muslims have, and they have what is upon the Muslims." Among what is upon a Muslim is that he is liable to stoning if he commits zina. So the dhimmi (non-Muslim protected subject) must be like this too, so that equality is achieved.

Second: the hadith of Malik from Nafi' from Ibn Umar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) stoned a Jewish man and a Jewish woman who had committed zina." Either it is said that he (ﷺ) judged by this according to his own law, or according to the law of those before him. If it is the first, the argument from it is clear. If it is the second, it is the same, because it became law for him.

Third: the zina of a disbeliever is like the zina of a Muslim, so what is obligatory upon him must be like what is obligatory upon a Muslim. This is because zina is forbidden and ugly, so it calls for deterrence, and imposing stoning is suitable as a deterrent for it. Nothing remains except the difference of disbelief and belief. Disbelief, though it does not make the offence more grave, does not make it lighter either.

Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) argued with several points:

First: holding to the generality of Allah's words, ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress﴾. This must be applied to the Muslim, and it is not applied to the dhimmi, for a reason absent in the dhimmi. The reason for the distinction is that execution by stones is a very great punishment, so it is obligatory only for a very great offence. The offence grows greater through ingratitude for blessings with regard to the offender, by reason and by law. As for reason: sin is ingratitude for blessing, and the more and greater the blessings, the greater and uglier the ingratitude. As for law: Allah the Exalted said concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a flagrant indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. Since Allah's blessings toward them were greater, the punishment for them was greater. And He said concerning the Messenger: ﴿Indeed, you were close to inclining toward them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾ [al-Isra: 74–75]. His sin was grave only because the blessing toward him was greater, which is the blessing of prophethood. It is known that Allah's blessings toward the Muslim who is muhsan are greater than toward the dhimmi, so the sin of the Muslim is greater, and therefore his punishment must be more severe.

Second: the dhimmi has not committed zina after ihsan, so stoning is not obligatory for him. The explanation of the first: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever associates partners with Allah for the blink of an eye is not muhsan." The explanation of the second: a Muslim who is not muhsan is not liable to execution, by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except for one of three reasons." And if the Muslim is like this, the dhimmi must be like this too, by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If they accept the contract of jizya, inform them that they have what the Muslims have, and upon them is what is upon the Muslims."

Third: we are agreed that for the accusation of zina (qadhf), Islam is considered, so likewise for stoning-ihsan, and the common cause is what we have mentioned of the perfection of blessing.

The answer to the first: it (the stoning) was specific to the Muslim married person, so likewise the dhimmi married person. As for what they cited concerning the increase of blessing upon believers, we say: the blessing of Islam was attained through the servant's own acquisition, so that becomes like additional service. And an increase in service, if it is not a cause for excuse, is at least not a cause for an increase in punishment.

The answer to the second: we do not concede that the dhimmi is a mushrik (polytheist). Even if we concede it, ihsan may be meant as marriage, according to Allah's words: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], and in the exegesis of ﴿And when they become chaste (uhsinna)﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], meaning "when they marry." Having established this, we say: the dhimmi married person is muhsan with this interpretation, so he must be stoned, by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "or zina after ihsan." He arranged the ruling for the Muslim upon this attribute, which shows that the attribute is the cause, and the attribute exists in the case of the dhimmi, so it must necessitate the ruling of stoning.

As for the third: the hadd for qadhf is to remove shame, out of honour for the one falsely accused, and the disbeliever is not a place for honour and preservation of reputation. This differs from what is here.

And Allah knows best.

As for what relates to flogging, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** They agreed that a slave is not stoned, and they agreed that he is flogged. And it is established by the text of the Book that upon female slaves is half the punishment upon free married women. So they agreed unanimously that a female slave is flogged fifty lashes. As for the male slave, the majority agreed that he is also flogged fifty, except the People of the Apparent (Zahiriyya). They said: the generality of Allah's words, ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress﴾, requires a hundred lashes for the male and female slave. But since the text specified halving for the female slave, if we were to analogize the male slave to her, that would be specifying the generality of the Book by analogy, which is not permissible. Among them is one who said: if a female slave marries, she receives fifty lashes; and if she does not marry, she receives a hundred, based on the apparent meaning of Allah's words: ﴿flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾, and they cited that His words, ﴿And when they become chaste (uhsinna)﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], meaning "when they marry," ﴿then upon them is half the punishment of free chaste women﴾ [al-Nisa: 25].

* * *

**The second issue:** Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on them both) said: the dhimmi is flogged. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: he is not flogged. Our arguments are several:

First: the generality of Allah's words, ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress﴾.

Second: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If the female slave of one of you commits zina, let him flog her," and his saying: "Establish the hadd punishments upon what your right hands possess." He did not distinguish between the dhimmi and the Muslim.

Third: the Prophet (ﷺ) stoned the two Jews. If that stoning was from the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), then the aim is achieved. If it was from their law, then when the Messenger (ﷺ) did it, it became part of his law. The real essence of this issue returns to the question of whether disbelievers are addressed with the derivative (furu') rulings of the sacred laws.

* * *

**The fourth investigation: what establishes that zina proceeded from him.** Know that this does not occur except in one of three ways: either the ruler (imam) sees it himself, or he confesses, or witnesses testify against him.

As for the first way, which is when the imam sees it: Imam Muhyi al-Sunna (the Revivalist of the Sunna, al-Baghawi) said in the book al-Tahdhib: there is no disagreement that the judge must refrain from ruling on the basis of his own knowledge, such as when a man claims a right against another and establishes evidence for it, while the judge knows that the other has already discharged him of it; or when he claims that he killed his father at such a time, while the judge has seen the father alive after that; or when he claims the marriage to a woman while the judge heard him divorce her. It is not permissible for him to rule on it, even if he establishes witnesses for it. As for whether it is permissible for the judge to rule on the basis of his own knowledge, such as when someone claims a thousand from another, and the judge saw him lend it, or heard the defendant confess it: there are two opinions. The more correct, and the view of Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and al-Muzani (may Allah have mercy on them), is that it is permissible for him to rule by his knowledge. This is because, since it is permissible for him to rule by the testimony of witnesses, which is based on their supposition, then it is all the more permissible on the basis of what he saw and heard himself, which is knowledge. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said in the book al-Risala: "I rule by my knowledge, which is stronger than two witnesses, or two witnesses and a woman, and it is stronger than a witness and an oath, or a witness and an oath, and it is stronger than refusal (nukul) and the return of the oath."

The second opinion: he does not rule by his own knowledge. This is the view of Ibn Abi Layla, because the absence of suspicion is a condition for judgment, and this is not found in property matters. As for punishments: one looks at whether it concerns rights of people, such as retaliation (qisas) and the hadd for qadhf, whether the judge rules on it by his own knowledge. It is based on property matters: if we say that there he does not rule, then here it is all the more so. Otherwise, there are two opinions. The difference is that the basis of the rights of Allah the Exalted is leniency and tolerance. And there is no difference, according to both opinions, whether the judge acquires knowledge within his province and time of office, or outside it. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) said: if he acquires knowledge within his province or during his term of office, he may rule by his knowledge; otherwise not. We say: knowledge does not differ with the difference of these circumstances, so the ruling must not differ with their difference. And Allah knows best.

The second way: confession. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: confession of zina once makes the hadd obligatory. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) said: rather, confession is necessary four times, in four sessions. Ahmad said: confession four times is necessary, but there is no difference whether it is in four sessions or in one session.

Al-Shafi'i's (may Allah have mercy on him) argument consists of two matters:

The first: the story of al-'Asif, for he (ﷺ) said: "If she confesses, then stone her." This is evidence that confession once is sufficient.

The second: when he confessed to zina, the hadd became obligatory upon him, by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Judge by the apparent." Confession once makes the matter apparent, especially here, because the factor deterring from confessing to zina is strong, since it is a cause of shame in the present and severe pain in the future. The factor deterring from lying is also present, and when the two deterrents combine, the turning away becomes stronger. So it is established that he only made this confession because it was true. When it becomes apparent, it falls under the hadith and under the verse, or we analogize it to confession of murder and apostasy.

Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) argued with several points:

First: the story of Ma'iz. The argument from it is from several aspects. The first: he (ﷺ) turned away from him the first time, and if the hadd had been obligatory upon him, he would not have turned away from him, because turning away from establishing the right of Allah the Exalted after the completion of the proof is not permissible.

The second: he (ﷺ) said: "You testified against yourself four times." If one were equal to four in making the hadd obligatory, this statement would be meaningless.

The third: it is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said to Ma'iz, after he had confessed three times: "If you had confessed a fourth time, the Messenger of Allah would have stoned you."

The fourth: from Buraydah al-Aslami, who said: "We, the company of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), used to say: If Ma'iz had not confessed four times, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not have stoned him."

[Page 125]

Second: they analogized acknowledgment (iqrar) to testimony. Just as zina cannot be established except by four testimonies, so too it cannot be established by confession except four times. The common factor is the effort to conceal this obscenity.

Third: zina is not negated except by four testimonies, or by four oaths in li'an (the mutual oath-swearing between spouses accusing each other). Therefore it is also permissible that it be established only by confession four times. It is distinguished from the other rights (huquq), which are negated by a single oath, so it is permissible that it be established by a single confession.

As for the answer to the first argument: the hadith says only that he (ﷺ) ruled by four testimonies, and that does not negate the permissibility of ruling by a single testimony.

As for the answer to the second: the difference between them is that if the one slandered (maqdhuf) confesses to zina once, the hadd punishment is dropped from the slanderer (qadhif). Had zina not been established, it would not have been dropped, just as when two witnesses testify to zina, the hadd is not dropped from the slanderer, since zina is not established by their testimony. And Allah knows best.

The third method is testimony. They are agreed that four testimonies are necessary. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And call to witness against them four of your men﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:15]. The discussion of this will come, Allah willing, in His words: ﴿Then they do not bring four witnesses﴾ [al-Nur 24:4].

* * *

Fifth investigation: Who is the addressee of the Exalted's words ﴿Flog﴾? The community is agreed that the addressee is the Imam (ruler). Then they argued from this for the obligation of appointing an Imam. They said: since He, glorified is He, commanded the establishment of the hadd, and they are agreed that none undertakes its establishment except the Imam, and that which an obligation cannot be fulfilled without, while it is within the capacity of the responsible person, is itself obligatory, therefore the appointment of the Imam is obligatory. The demonstration of this argument has already passed in His words: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:38]. Remaining here are three issues.

[Page 126]

First issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the master (sayyid) has the right to establish the hadd upon his slave. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Fatima and Aisha. According to Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Zufar, may Allah have mercy on them, he does not have this right. Malik said: the master flogs him for zina, drinking wine and qadhf (false accusation of zina), but does not cut his hand for theft; rather the Imam cuts it. This is also the view of al-Layth. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, argued with several points.

The first: his (ﷺ) saying: "Establish the hudud upon what your right hands possess." And on the authority of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits zina, let him flog her." In another narration: "Let him flog her the hadd." Abu Bakr al-Razi said: there is no proof in these reports, for his saying "Establish the hudud upon what your right hands possess" is like His saying: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterous man, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur 24:2]. It is known that what is meant by it is referring the matter to the Imam to establish the hadd, and the addressees of establishing the hadd are the leaders, while the rest of the people are addressed with referring the matter to them until they establish the hudud upon them. Likewise His saying: "Establish the hudud upon what your right hands possess" is in this sense. As for his saying: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits zina, let him flog her," it is not the case that every flogging is a hadd, since flogging may be by way of ta'zir (discretionary punishment). So when we apply ta'zir, we have fulfilled the content of the hadith.

The response: his saying "Establish the hudud" is a command to establish the hadd, so taking this expression to mean referring the case to the Imam is a departure from the apparent meaning. At most, the apparent meaning has been abandoned in His saying "Flog," but it does not follow that it is abandoned here as well. As for his saying "let him flog her," the meaning being ta'zir is false, since the flogging mentioned right after zina is understood to be nothing other than the hadd.

The second: since the ruler has the right to establish the hadd upon him, his master has it even more so, because the master's connection to the slave is stronger than the ruler's connection to him, since ownership (milk) is stronger than the contract of allegiance (bay'a). The authority of masters over slaves is greater than the authority of the ruler over subjects. Indeed, if a slave-girl has both a master and a father, the right of marriage guardianship belongs to the master rather than the father, and then the father takes precedence over the ruler in the right of marriage guardianship. So the master takes precedence over the ruler by several degrees, and therefore he is more entitled. Also, the master has in this domain powers of disposal that the Imam does not have. Thus it is established that the master is more entitled.

The third: we are agreed that the master has the right to ta'zir, so likewise the hadd, since each is a counterpart of the other, even if one of them is prescribed and the other is not prescribed. Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for the position of Abu Hanifa with several points.

The first: he said: the saying of the Exalted ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterous man, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ is undoubtedly addressed to the leaders rather than to the common people. So the meaning is: "Flog, O leaders and rulers, each one of them a hundred lashes." This verse does not distinguish between free persons and slaves who are subject to the hadd, so the leaders must be the ones addressed with establishing the hudud upon free persons and slaves alike, not the masters.

The second: if it were permissible for the master to hear the testimony of witnesses against his slave for theft and then cut off his hand, then if the witnesses retracted their testimony, it would follow that he could hold them liable for compensation, since the liability of witnesses depends on the judge's ruling on the basis of testimony. For if he did not rule on their testimony, they would not be liable for anything. Thus he would become a judge in his own case by imposing liability upon them, and that is invalid, since no one among people may rule in his own favour. So we know that the master does not have the right to hear evidence against his slave for this, nor to cut him off.

The third: the owner may not carry out the hadd in full because of his compassion for his property, and when he is subject to suspicion, he must not be entrusted with it.

As for the answer to the first: his saying ﴿Flog﴾ is not, in its plain wording, addressed to the Imam. But through an indirect route: since consensus was reached that anyone other than the Imam does not undertake it, we took that address to be directed at the Imam. Here, however, consensus has not been reached that the Imam does not undertake it, since this is precisely the point of dispute.

As for the answer to the second: Muhyi al-Sunna said in his book "al-Tahdhib": Is it permissible for the master to cut off the hand of his slave for theft or for highway robbery? There are two opinions. The more correct of them is that it is permissible; al-Shafi'i stated this in the narration of al-Buwayti, based on what is reported from Ibn Umar, that he cut off the hand of a slave of his who had stolen. Just as he flogs him for zina and drinking wine.

The second opinion: no, rather the amputation goes to the Imam, unlike flogging, because the master possesses the genus of flogging, which is ta'zir, but does not possess the genus of amputation. Then he said: every hadd that the master establishes upon his slave, he establishes only when it has been proven by the slave's confession. But if there is evidence against him, does the master hear the testimony? There are two opinions. One of them: he hears it, since he has the right to establish it upon confession, so he has it upon evidence too, like the Imam. The second: he does not hear it; rather that is for the judges.

As for the answer to the third: it is refuted by ta'zir.

* * *

Second issue: if the Imam is absent, individual people do not have the right to establish these hudud; rather it is better that they appoint one of the righteous to undertake it.

Third issue: Does the Kharijite who has seized power have the right to establish the hudud? Some said: he has that right. Others said: he does not, because establishing the hadd on the authority of one whose authority we are obliged to remove is further away than delegating it to one of the righteous men.

* * *

Sixth investigation: On the manner of establishing the hadd. As for flogging: know that what is mentioned in the verse is flogging, and this is common to both severe flogging and light flogging, and flogging on all the limbs or on some of the limbs. So in the verse there is no indication of any of these restrictions; rather the verse requires that whoever carries out the flogging, however it is done, is discharged of the obligation, since he has done what he was commanded, so he must be discharged. The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: in the word "jald" (flogging) there is an indication that the pain should not extend to the flesh. Also, "jald" means striking the skin; one says "jaladahu," like your saying "zahrahu" (struck his back) with a fatha on the ha', and "batanahu" (struck his belly) and "ra'asahu" (struck his head). However, since we know that its purpose is deterrence, and deterrence is achieved only by light flogging, scholars have therefore discussed the manner of flogging by way of analogy. Next, there are issues here:

First issue: the muhsan (married person) is flogged while wearing his clothes and is not stripped, but it should be such that the pain reaches him, and the padding and the fur are removed from his clothing. Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah narrated that a man was brought to him for a hadd, and the man began to take off his shirt, saying: it is not proper for the body of this sinner to be struck while he is wearing a shirt. Abu Ubayda said: do not let him take off his shirt, and he struck him over it. As for a woman, there is no disagreement that she must not be stripped; rather her garments are tied on her so that she is not uncovered, and a woman carries out the flogging on her.

Second issue: he is not stretched out nor tied, but is left so that he can protect himself with his hands. A man is flogged standing, and a woman is flogged seated. Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Ibn Abi Layla flogged a woman who had committed qadhf while she was standing, and Abu Hanifa considered that a mistake.

Third issue: he is flogged with a medium whip, neither new (which would wound) nor worn-out (which would not cause pain), and he is flogged with a stroke between two strokes, neither severe nor weak. Abu Uthman al-Nahdi narrated: Umar was brought a man for a hadd, then a whip with strength in it was brought, and he said: I want something softer than this. So a whip with softness was brought, and he said: I want something harder than this. So a whip between the two whips was brought, and he was satisfied with it.

Fourth issue: the lashes are spread over his limbs and not gathered in one place. They agreed that he protects the vital areas, such as the face, the belly and the private parts. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that one strikes the head. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: one does not strike the head. [Page 128] This is also the position for which al-Shafi'i has an argument. Abu Bakr said: I strike the head, for the devil is in it. And it is reported from Umar that he struck Sabigh ibn Usayl on his head when he asked about the Dhariyat in a spirit of obstinacy. The argument of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him: we are agreed that one does not strike the face, so likewise the head, and the common factor is the ruling and the reason. As for the ruling: the disfigurement that affects the head by the effect of the blow is like that which affects the face, as evidenced by the fact that the wound to the skull (al-muwaddiha) and the rest of the head injuries have the same ruling for the head and the face, whereas they differ from the rest of the body, since for a muwaddiha outside the head and face only an assessed compensation (hukumah) is due, and the full compensation for a muwaddiha on the head and face is not due. So the head and face must be equal in the obligation to protect them from striking.

As for the reason: he was prohibited from striking the face because of the harm it would do to the eye, and this is present in the head, since striking the head darkens the sight, and sometimes water forms in the eye, and sometimes it causes confusion of the mind. Our companions answered this by saying: the difference between the face and the head is established, since when a blow lands on the face, the bone of the forehead is thin and may break, unlike the bone of the nape, which is extremely hard. Also, the eye is extremely delicate, so striking it causes blindness. Also, striking the face breaks the nose, since it is made of delicate cartilage, and breaks the teeth, since they are delicate bones, and it falls on the cheeks, which are two flesh-masses close to the brain, and a blow to them is extremely dangerous because that effect reaches the substance of the brain quickly. None of this occurs when striking the head.

Fifth issue: if he spreads the lashes of the hadd so that no deterrence is achieved by it, such as striking one or two lashes each day which are not counted, and if he strikes twenty or more each day they are counted. The better course is not to spread them out.

* * *

**Question 6:** If the hadd is due on a pregnant woman, it is not carried out until she has given birth. ʿImran ibn al-Husayn narrated that a woman from Juhayna came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while she was pregnant from fornication and said: "O Prophet of Allah, I have committed a hadd offence, so establish it upon me." The Prophet (ﷺ) summoned her guardian and said: "Treat her well, and when she has given birth, bring her to me." He did so, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that her garments be tied around her, then ordered that she be stoned, and then he prayed over her. Moreover, the purpose is discipline (ta'dib, correction) and not destruction.

* * *

**Question 7:** If the lashing is due on a sick person, it is examined. If he has an illness whose cure is expected, such as a headache, weakness or postnatal condition, the punishment is delayed until he recovers, just as when one hadd has been applied and another hadd is not applied until he has recovered from the first. If he has an illness whose cure is not expected, such as consumption (sull) or chronic paralysis (zamanah), then it is not delayed and he is not struck with whips, since he would die and the aim is not his death. This ruling is the same whether his fornication occurred while he was healthy and then he became ill, or while he was already ill. Rather, he is struck with a bundle (ʿithkal) bearing one hundred stalks (shimrakh), which counts as one hundred lashes. As Allah the Exalted said in the story of Ayyub (peace be upon him): ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [of rods] and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ (Sad 38:44). According to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), he is struck with whips. Our evidence is what is reported: "A paralysed man committed fornication with a woman, so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to take one hundred stalks and strike him with them in a single blow." Also, if prayer varies according to his condition, then the hadd is more deserving of this.

* * *

**Question 8:** The hadd is applied in moderate weather. If it is in extreme heat or cold, then: if the punishment is stoning, it is carried out as it is carried out during illness, because the aim is his death. It has been said: if stoning was established against him by his own confession, then it is delayed until the weather is moderate and the illness whose cure is expected has gone, because he may retract his confession during the stoning, and the stoning will have affected his body, so the intensity of heat, cold and illness would help to destroy him.
