This is unlike the case where it was established by evidence (bayyina), because it is not dropped. If the punishment is lashing, it is not permissible to carry it out in extreme heat or cold, just as it is not carried out during illness.

* * *

As for stoning (rajm), there are several issues:

**First issue:** Al-Shafiʿi (may Allah have mercy on him) and Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: it is permissible for the imam to attend the stoning or not to attend it, and likewise the witnesses are not obliged to attend. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) said: if fornication was established by evidence, the witnesses must begin the stoning, then the imam, then the people; if it was established by confession, the imam begins, then the people. The proof of al-Shafiʿi (may Allah have mercy on him): "The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the stoning of Maʿiz and the Ghamidiyya, and he did not attend their stoning."

**Second issue:** If fornication was established by his confession, then whenever he retracts, he is released, whether or not some of the punishment had been applied to him. This was the view of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), al-Thawri, Ahmad and Ishaq. al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla and Dawud said his retraction is not accepted. There are two reports from Malik (may Allah have mercy on him). The evidence of the first view: "When the stones struck Maʿiz and he fled, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Why did you not leave him alone?'"

**Third issue:** A pit is dug for the woman up to her chest so that she is not exposed, and stones are thrown at her; no pit is dug for a man. This is based on what Abu Saʿid al-Khudri reported: "Maʿiz came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have committed an immoral act, so establish the hadd upon me.' The Prophet (peace be upon him) turned him away several times. Then he asked his people, and they said: 'We know of no wrong in him.' So he ordered us to stone him. We took him to the cemetery of Baqiʿ al-Gharqad, and we did not tie him up nor dig a pit for him. He said: We threw at him bones, clods and potsherds. He ran off and we ran after him until he reached the edge of al-Harra and stood before us, and we pelted him with the rocks of al-Harra until he was still." The basis of the argument is that he said: "We did not tie him up nor dig a pit for him," and because he fled, and had he been in a pit he would not have been able to do so.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** If he dies during the hadd, he is washed, shrouded, prayed over, and buried in the graveyards of the Muslims. This is what we wished to mention concerning the explanation of the legal rulings connected with this verse.

As for the rational discussions: know that some people said: There is no doubt that the body is composed of many parts. Either each part has its own life, knowledge and power, or all the parts have one life, one knowledge and one power. The second is impossible, because it is impossible for one accident to subsist in many loci. Therefore the first is established. If that is so, then each part of the body is alive separately, knowing separately and powerful separately. If this is established, we say: the fornicator is the genitals, not the back. How, then, is it fitting for the Wise (al-Hakim) to command the striking of the back? Also, a person may be thin and emaciated at the time of committing fornication and then become fat afterwards; how is it permissible to inflict pain on those additional parts, when they were innocent of the act of fornication? If someone says this is refuted in two ways:

The first: It is not the case that each part of the body acts separately and lives separately, and that is impossible. Rather, life, knowledge and power subsist in one part and then make the judgment of being alive, knowing and powerful apply to the whole collection of parts, so the whole becomes one living, one knowing and one powerful thing. On this assumption the question disappears.

The second: It is said that what acts, moves and perceives is a thing that is neither a body nor corporeal; it is only the manager (mudabbir) of this body. On this assumption too the question disappears.

The answer: As for the first, it is weak, because if knowledge subsists in one part, then either a single knowing-state arises from the whole collection of parts, which requires one attribute to subsist in many loci, which is impossible, or each part has its own knowing-state, which brings back the same problem. As for the second, it is extremely far-fetched, because if the doer of the wrong is that separate entity, why is this body struck? Know that the aim of the legal rulings of the Sharia is to safeguard the interests (maslaha), and we know that the legislation of the hadd serves deterrence, so the aim is achieved. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And let not compassion for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah﴾, there are two issues:

**First issue:** Ra'fa means tenderness and mercy. The reading of the majority is with a sukun on the hamza. It has also been read ra'fa with a fatha on the hamza, and ra'aafa on the pattern fa'aala.

**Second issue:** It may be that the meaning is: let not compassion take hold of you so that the hadd is suspended or reduced. The meaning is: do not suspend the limits of Allah, and do not abandon establishing them out of pity and mercy. This is the view of Mujahid, ʿIkrima and Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and the preference of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It may also be that compassion should not take hold of you so that the lashing is lightened. This is the view of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan and Qatada. It is possible that both meanings are intended, but the first is better, because what was mentioned earlier was the command to lash itself, without its manner being mentioned, so what follows it must be understood as referring to it. And the Messenger of Allah is sufficient as an example in this, when he said: "If Fatima the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand." By His saying "in the religion of Allah" He points out that when the religion has made something obligatory, it is not valid to use compassion to oppose it.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿If you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, this is a means of stirring up and inflaming zeal for Allah the Exalted and His religion. Al-Jubba'i said: the implied meaning of the verse is: if you are believers, then do not abandon establishing the hadd. This indicates that engaging in performing obligations is part of faith, contrary to what the Murji'a say. The answer: compassion takes hold only when a person judges by his nature that it is better not to establish those limits, and then he would be rejecting the religion and would be outside faith. In a hadith: "A ruler will be brought who had reduced the hadd by one lash, and he will be asked: 'Why did you do that?' He will say: 'Out of mercy for Your servants.' He will be told: 'You are more merciful to them than I am!' He will be commanded to the Fire. Another will be brought who had added one lash, and he will be asked: 'Why did you do that?' He will say: 'So that they would refrain from Your disobedience.' He will be told: 'You are more wise in that than I am!' He will be commanded to the Fire."

* * *

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** His saying the Exalted: ﴿let a group witness﴾ is a command, and its apparent meaning is obligation. However, the jurists said that the presence of a gathering is recommended, and the aim is to announce the establishment of the hadd, because it adds greater deterrence, and because it removes suspicion from the one who carries out the lashing. It has also been said that by "group" is meant the witnesses, because their presence is required so that it is known that they still stand by their testimony.

**Second issue:** Scholars disagreed about the minimum size of the group, with several opinions. One: it is a single man; this is the view of al-Nakha'i and Mujahid, who argued from His saying the Exalted: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ (al-Hujurat 49:9). Second: it is two; this is the view of ʿIkrima and ʿAta', who argued from His saying the Exalted: ﴿Why does not a party from every division of them go forth, that they may gain understanding in the religion﴾ (al-Tawba 9:122). Every three is a division, and the one who departs from the three is one or two, and caution requires taking the larger number. Third: it is three; this is the view of al-Zuhri and Qatada. They said: the group is the company that can form a circle, as if it were the gathering surrounding a thing, and the least that must be present for that form is three. Fourth: it is four, according to the number of witnesses to fornication; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Shafiʿi (may Allah be pleased with them). Fifth: it is ten; this is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, because ten is the complete number.

**Third issue:** Calling it "punishment" (ʿadhab) indicates that it is a penalty. It is permissible to call it ʿadhab because it prevents repetition, just as it is called nakal (deterrent example) for that reason. By His saying "of the believers," the Exalted points out that those who witness must have this description, because when they are such, the value of their presence in deterrence is greater, and the value of their reporting what they witnessed is greater, so the one lashed fears the disgrace of their presence, and that is more powerful in restraint. And Allah knows best.

**The second ruling:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The fornicating man does not marry except a fornicating woman or an idolatress, and the fornicating woman is not married except by a fornicating man or an idolater, and that has been forbidden to the believers.﴾

It was recited as "لا يَنْكِحْ" (*lā yankiḥ*) with a jazm (the apocopate ending), as a prohibition, and as "وحَرَّمَ" (*wa-ḥarrama*) with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ. There are several questions about the verse:

**The first question:** His saying, ﴿The fornicating man does not marry except a fornicating woman or an idolatress﴾, is apparently a statement of fact. But the matter is not as this apparent meaning suggests, because we see that a fornicator may marry a believing chaste woman, and a fornicatress may be married by a chaste believing man.

**The second question:** He said, ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾, but this is not so, for it is permissible for a believer to marry a fornicating woman. The answer: Know that the exegetes (*mufassirūn*), because of these two questions, mentioned several opinions.

The first, which is the best of them, is what al-Qaffāl said: the wording, though general, is intended to mean the majority of cases (*al-aʿamm al-aghlab*). This is because the wicked debauchee whose nature is fornication and immorality does not desire to marry virtuous women; he desires only a wicked fornicating woman like himself, or an idolatress. And the wicked fornicating woman is not desired in marriage by righteous men, who shun her; rather, she is desired only by those of her kind among the fornicators and idolaters. So this is according to the majority of cases, just as one says, "Only the pious man does good," though one who is not pious may do some good. So it is likewise here.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾, the answer is given from two aspects:

The first: the marriage of a believer who is praised in the sight of God to a fornicating woman, and his desire for her, and his entering by that into the rank of the fornicators characterized by fornication, is forbidden to him, because it involves imitating the fornicators, being present in places of suspicion, and causing bad talk about him and backbiting. How much exposure to the commission of sins is there in keeping company with sinners, so how much more in marrying fornicatresses and debauchees?

The second: that directing one's desire entirely toward fornicatresses and abandoning desire for righteous women is forbidden to the believers, because His saying, ﴿The fornicating man does not marry except a fornicating woman﴾, means that the fornicator does not desire except a fornicatress. This restriction is forbidden to the believers, but the prohibition of this restriction does not entail the prohibition of marrying a fornicatress. This is the reliable view in the interpretation of the verse.

The second aspect: the definite article in His saying ﴿the fornicating man﴾ and in His saying ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾, although apparently general, is here specific to the particular people about whom this verse was revealed. Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Qatādah said: the emigrants (*muhājirūn*) came to Madīnah, and among them were poor people who had no wealth and no tribal kin. In Madīnah there were prostitute women (*bagāyā*) who hired out themselves, and they were at that time the most prosperous people of Madīnah. Each of them had a sign at her door like the sign of a veterinarian, so that it would be known that she was a fornicatress, and no one entered upon her except a fornicator or an idolater. Some poor Muslims desired their earnings and said, "We will marry them until God enriches us from them." They asked permission of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. The meaning of the verse, then, is: "Those fornicators do not marry except those fornicatresses, and those fornicatresses are not married except by those fornicators, and marrying them is forbidden to the believers."

[p. 132]

The third aspect in the answer: that His saying, ﴿The fornicating man does not marry except a fornicating woman﴾, although apparently a statement of fact, is intended as a prohibition. The meaning is that whoever is a fornicator should not marry except a fornicatress, and "that has been forbidden to the believers." This was the ruling at the beginning of Islam. On this aspect, they mentioned two views:

The first: that this ruling remains in force until now, so that it is forbidden for the fornicator and the fornicatress to marry a chaste person, and vice versa. This is said to be the view of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd and ʿĀʾishah. Among these, some equate the initial contract with continuation: they say, just as it is not permissible for a believer to marry a fornicatress, so too it is not permissible for him, if she commits fornication while she is his wife, to remain with her. Others distinguish, because among the things that prevent marriage are some that do not prevent the continuation of a marriage, such as the state of ihrām and the waiting period (*ʿiddah*).

The second view: that this ruling has been abrogated (*mansūkh*), and they differed about its abrogating text (*nāsikh*). According to al-Jubbāʾī, its abrogating text is the consensus (*ijmāʿ*). And according to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, it was abrogated by the general sense of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So marry what is lawful to you of women﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 3] and ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ [al-Nūr: 32]. The scholars who investigated the matter said: these two views are weak. As for the first: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*) that consensus is neither abrogated nor abrogates. Moreover, a consensus that arises after a disagreement is not a proof, and the consensus on this question is preceded by the opposition of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAlī, so how can it be valid?

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So marry what is lawful to you﴾, it cannot be valid as an abrogating text, because it must be stipulated that there is no impediment to marriage by reason of kinship, affinity, or something else. One may say that the marriage of a believer to a fornicatress is not included in it, just as her marriage to a brother or a nephew is not included in it. We say that fornication has an effect on separation that other things do not have. Do you not see that if he accuses her of fornication, separation follows in some respects, and this is not required for the other things that entail the prescribed punishment (*ḥadd*)? Moreover, fornication, by its nature, brings shame and affects the marriage bed, so it differs from other matters.

Then those who claim this abrogation argued that Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, was asked about a man who committed fornication with a woman: may he marry her? Ibn ʿAbbās permitted it, and likened it to one who stole the fruit of a tree and then bought it. And it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he was asked about this and said: "Its beginning is illicit intercourse, and its end is marriage," and the unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful.

The fourth aspect: that "marriage" (*nikāḥ*) be understood as sexual intercourse (*waṭʾ*), so that the meaning is that the fornicator, at the time he commits fornication, has intercourse only with a fornicatress or an idolatress, and likewise the fornicatress; ﴿and that has been forbidden to the believers﴾, that is, fornication has been forbidden to the believers. This is the interpretation of Abū Muslim. Al-Zajjāj said: this interpretation is corrupt in two respects:

The first: the word *nikāḥ* in the Book of God occurs only with the meaning of marriage (*tazwīj*), and it never occurs with the meaning of intercourse.

The second: that this removes the speech from its benefit. For if we say the meaning is that the fornicator does not have intercourse except with a fornicatress, the difficulty returns, because we see that the fornicator may have intercourse with a chaste woman when he marries her. And if we say the meaning is that the fornicator does not have intercourse except with a fornicatress at the time his intercourse is fornication, then this speech has no benefit. This is the end of the discussion on this point.

**The third question:** What is the difference between His saying, ﴿The fornicating man does not marry except a fornicating woman﴾, and His saying, ﴿and the fornicating woman is not married except by a fornicating man﴾?
The answer: The first statement indicates that the fornicator desires only to marry a fornicatress. This does not prevent a non-fornicator from desiring to marry a fornicatress. Therefore the second statement clarifies this.

**The fourth question:** Why is the fornicating woman mentioned before the fornicating man in the previous verse, but here the reverse?
The answer: That verse was sent down concerning her punishment for her crime, and the woman is the source (*māddah*) of fornication. As for this second verse, it is concerned with mentioning marriage, and the man is the principal in it, because he is the one who desires and seeks.

**Ruling Three: Slander (qadhf).** The words of God Most High: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses — lash them eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after. And those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that the apparent meaning of the verse does not indicate the thing by which they accuse the chaste women, and mention of "accusation" (ramy) does not indicate adultery (zina), since one may accuse her of theft, drinking wine, or disbelief. Rather, there must be a clear indication specifying it. The scholars have agreed that what is meant is accusation of adultery. In the verse there are statements that indicate this:

First: the prior mention of adultery.

Second: God mentioned "muhsanat" (chaste women), who are the chaste ones, which indicates that what is meant by "accusation" is accusing them of the opposite of chastity.

Third: His saying ﴿then they do not produce four witnesses﴾, meaning to confirm what they accused them of, and it is known that this number of witnesses is not required except in the case of adultery.

Fourth: there is consensus that flogging is not obligatory for accusing someone of something other than adultery, so it must be that what is meant is accusation of adultery. Having understood this, the discussion of this verse concerns the accusation, the accuser, and the one accused.

* * *

**The First Section: On the Accusation.** It contains several issues.

**First issue:** The wording of slander is divided into explicit (sarih), allusive (kinayah), and indirect (ta'rid). The explicit is to say "O adulteress," or "you committed adultery," or "your front or your back committed adultery." If he said "your body committed adultery," there are two views:

One: it is allusive, like saying "your hand committed adultery," because the reality of adultery is from the private part, so from the rest of the body there is only assistance.

The second, and the more correct, is that it is explicit, because the act proceeds from the whole body, and the private part is only an instrument in the act. As for allusive expressions, such as saying "O immoral woman," "O sinful woman," "O wicked woman," "O hired woman," "O daughter of the forbidden," or "my wife does not turn away the hand of one who touches her," and the reverse of these, this is not slander unless he intends it. Likewise, if he says to an Arab "O Nabati" (a derogatory term), this is not slander unless he intends it. If he intended slander, it is slander against the mother of the one addressed; otherwise, it is not. If he says, "I meant by it the Nabati of residence and language," and the mother of the one addressed claims he intended slander, then the word of the speaker is accepted with his oath.

As for indirect allusion (ta'rid), it is not slander even if he intended it, such as saying, "O son of the lawful, as for me, I have not committed adultery, and my mother is not an adulteress." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih, may Allah have mercy on them all.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the hadd is obligatory for it. Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is slander in a state of anger but not in a state of contentment.

Our evidence: indirect allusion to slander is open to being slander or to something else, so the hadd must not be obligatory, because the original state is the innocence of the obligation, and one does not depart from it on doubt. Also, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: «Avert the hudud by doubts.» And because the hudud were legislated contrary to the text that negates harm. The harm resulting from explicit speech is greater than that resulting from indirect speech.

The opponent argued with what al-Awza'i related from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from Ibn Umar, who said: "Umar used to apply the hadd for indirect allusion." It is also related that two men quarreled during the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and one of them said to the other: "By Allah, I am not an adulterer, nor is my mother an adulteress." Umar consulted the people about it. One said: "He praised his father and mother." Others said: "His father and mother had praise other than this." So Umar flogged him eighty lashes.

The answer: that Umar's consulting the Companions about the ruling on indirect allusion indicates that there was no explicit textual instruction (tawqif) among them on it, and that they gave an opinion by way of ijtihad.

* * *

**Second issue: On multiple slanders.** One may either slander one person repeatedly or slander a group. If he slanders one person repeatedly, consider: if he intended by all of them one adulteress, such as saying "you committed adultery with 'Amr," repeated several times, only one hadd is obligatory. If he initiated the second after being flogged for the first, he is disciplined (ta'zir) for the second. If he slandered her with different acts of adultery, such as saying "you committed adultery with Zayd," then "you committed adultery with 'Amr," is the hadd multiplied or not? There are two views:

One: it multiplies, considering the wording, and because it is a right of the servants, so overlap does not occur in it, like debts.

The second, and the more correct: it overlaps, so only one hadd is obligatory, because they are two hudud of one kind for one entitled party, so they should overlap like the hudud of adultery. If he slandered his wife repeatedly, the more correct view is that one li'an suffices, whether we say the hadd multiplies or not.

As for when he slanders a number of persons: consider. If he slandered each one with a separate word, a full hadd is obligatory for each one. According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, only one hadd is obligatory. Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for Abu Hanifah's view from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and analogy.

From the Qur'an: God's saying ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾. The meaning is that whoever accuses chaste women is obligated to the flogging, and this implies that one who accuses a group of chaste women is not flogged more than eighty. So whoever obligates more than one hadd on the one who slanders a group of chaste women has contradicted the verse.

From the Sunnah: what 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, that Hilal ibn Umayyah slandered his wife before the Prophet, peace be upon him, accusing her with Sharik ibn Sahma'. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "No; either evidence or a hadd on your back." So the Prophet did not obligate on Hilal except one hadd, despite his slandering his wife and Sharik ibn Sahma', until the verse of li'an was revealed, and li'an was established for wives in place of the hadd for non-wives.

From analogy: every act that makes the hadd obligatory, if it occurs from him repeatedly, only one hadd is obligatory, such as one who commits adultery repeatedly, drinks repeatedly, or steals repeatedly. So here too. The common cause is averting greater harm.

The answer to the first: God's saying ﴿alladhina﴾ is a plural form, and ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ is a plural form, and when plural is matched with plural, singular is matched with singular, so the meaning becomes: whoever accuses one chaste woman is obligated to the hadd. At this point the way al-Shafi'i relied on the verse becomes clear. Also, God's saying ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses — lash them﴾ [al-Nur: 4] indicates that the flogging is ordered upon accusing chaste women, and the ordering of the ruling upon the attribute, especially when it is appropriate, signals causation. So the verse indicates that accusing a chaste woman, insofar as she bears this description, makes the flogging obligatory. Having established this, we say: if he slanders one person, that slander becomes a cause of the hadd; if he slanders a second, the second slander must also be a cause of the hadd. The cause of the second slander cannot be the first hadd itself, because that was already obligated by the first slander, and making the obligated obligatory again is impossible. So he must be flogged a second hadd for the second slander. At most, what can be raised against this inference is the hudud of adultery. But we say: the application of this proof was set aside there, because the hadd of adultery is more severe than the hadd of slander, and when a difference is evident, combining them becomes impossible.

As for the Sunnah, there is no indication in it regarding this issue, because the slander of both was with one word. We have a detailed discussion on this issue that will come, God willing.

As for analogy, it is flawed, because the hadd of slander is a right of the human being, as evidenced by the fact that it is not imposed except upon the demand of the one slandered, and rights of human beings do not overlap, unlike the hadd of adultery, which is a right of God Most High. All of this applies when he slandered a group, each one with a separate word. As for when he slandered them with one word, saying "You are adulterers" or "You have committed adultery," there are two views. The more correct of them, and his view in the "New" (al-Jadid) opinion, is that a full hadd is obligatory for each one, because it is a right of the servants and therefore does not overlap, and because he brought disgrace upon each of them, so it is as if he had slandered them with separate words. In the "Old" (al-Qadim) opinion, only one hadd is obligatory for all, considering the wording, since the wording is one. But the first is more correct, because it better fits the understanding of the verse. Accordingly, if he said to a man, "O son of the two adulterers," which is slander against his two parents with one word, then he is liable to two hudud.

* * *

**Third issue: What permits slander.** Slander is divided into forbidden, permitted, and obligatory. The summary is that if there is no child whom he wishes to disown, it is not obligatory. As for whether it is permitted or not: if he sees her committing adultery with his own eyes, or she confesses herself, and he believes her, or he hears it from one he trusts, or he has not heard it but it has spread among the people that so-and-so commits adultery with so-and-so, and the husband has seen him leaving her house or seen him with her in a house, then slander is permitted for him, because the suspicion is confirmed, and he may keep her and conceal it for her.

This is based on what is related: "A man said, O Messenger of Allah, I have a wife who does not turn away the hand of one who touches her. He said: Divorce her. He said: I love her. He said: Then keep her."

But if he heard it from one who is not trusted, or it spread among the people, yet the husband did not see him with her, or the reverse, it is not lawful for him to slander her, because one who is not trustworthy may mention it, and it spreads, and he enters her house out of fear of an aggressor, or for theft, or seeking immorality, and the woman refuses. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander are a band among you﴾ [al-Nur: 11].

If there is a child whom he wishes to disown, consider: if he is certain that it is not his, by not having had intercourse with her, or having had intercourse but she bore the child less than six months from the time of intercourse, or more than four years, then he is obligated to disown it by li'an, because he is prohibited from attributing to himself the lineage of another just as he is prohibited from denying his own lineage. This is based on what is related from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: «Any woman who introduces into a people one who is not of them, has nothing to do with Allah, and Allah will not admit her into His Paradise.» Since it is forbidden for a woman to introduce into a people one who is not of them, the man is likewise. But if it is possible that the child is his, by her bearing it more than six months from the time of intercourse and less than four years, then consider: if he has not cleansed her with a menstrual cycle (istibra'), or he cleansed her and she bore the child less than six months from the time of the cleansing, it is not lawful for him to slander or disown, even if he suspects her of adultery.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: «Any man who denies his child while looking at it, Allah will veil Himself from him on the Day of Resurrection and will disgrace him before the heads of the first and the last.» If he cleansed her and she bore the child more than six months from the time of cleansing, then he is permitted to slander and disown. But it is better that he not do so, because she may see blood during pregnancy. And if his wife bears a child who does not resemble him, for example if they were both white and she bore a black one, consider: if he does not suspect her of adultery, he has no right to disown it, based on what Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related: "A man said to the Prophet, peace be upon him, 'My wife has given birth to a black boy.' He said, 'Do you have camels?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'What color are they?' He said, 'Red.' He said, 'Is there any grey among them?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'How is that?' He said, 'A vein pulled it.' He said, 'Perhaps this one was pulled by a vein.'"

If he suspects her of adultery, or suspects her with a particular man, and she bears a child resembling him, is it permitted for him to disown it? There are two views:

One: no, because hereditary traits pull.

The second: he may do so, because the suspicion has been confirmed by the resemblance.

* * *

**The Second Section: On the One Who Accuses.**

**First issue:** If a boy or a madman accuses his wife or a stranger, then neither a hadd nor li'an is obligatory for either of them, not at the present time

Surah 24, verses 4–5 (part 2 of 4)

And (the rule is) not after puberty, because of the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "The pen is lifted from three (categories)." However, both (the child and the insane) are disciplined with a discretionary punishment (ta'zir) for correction, if they have discernment (tamyiz). So if the imposition of the discretionary punishment upon the child was not carried out until he reached puberty, al-Qaffal said: the discretionary punishment lapses, because it was for deterrence from misconduct, and a stronger deterrent has occurred, which is puberty.
* * *
Second issue: A mute person who has an understandable sign, or known writing, and who commits qadhf (slander) by means of the sign or by allusion, is liable to the hadd penalty. Likewise his li'an (mutual oath of condemnation) is valid by sign and by allusion. According to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, the qadhf of a mute person is not valid, nor is his li'an.

The view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse, because whoever writes or gestures an accusation of zina has indeed slandered a chaste woman and attached disgrace to her, so it is necessary that it falls under the apparent wording. Also, we analogize his qadhf and his li'an to all other rulings.
* * *
Third issue: They differed concerning a slave who commits qadhf against a free person. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Malik, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar and Uthman (said): the bondsman (qinn) is liable to forty lashes. Al-Thawri narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, that Ali, peace be upon him, said: "The slave is flogged forty times for qadhf." And from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "I met Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and those after them among the caliphs, and they all used to flog the slave forty times for qadhf." Al-Awza'i said he is flogged eighty, and this is related from Ibn Mas'ud. It is also related that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz flogged a slave eighty times for slander. The root of the matter rests on one point: this verse is explicit in requiring eighty. Whoever reduces this penalty to forty must follow the path that God the Exalted said: ﴿And if they are married and then commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free chaste women﴾ [an-Nisa: 25], so He explicitly stated that the penalty of a slave-woman for zina is half that of a free woman. Then they analogized the male slave to the female slave in halving the penalty for zina, then they analogized halving the penalty for a slave's qadhf to halving the penalty for his zina. Thus the outcome comes down to specifying the general wording of the Book by this analogy.
* * *
Fourth issue: They agreed that the disbeliever enters under the general wording of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾, because the term covers him and there is no impediment. So if a Jew slanders a Muslim, he is flogged eighty times. And God knows best.
* * *
Third inquiry: Concerning the one accused, who is the chaste woman (muhsanah). Abu Muslim said: the term ihsan applies to a married woman and to a chaste woman even if she has not married, based on His saying concerning Mary: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Anbiya: 91]. It derives from preventing the private part; when a woman marries she guards it except from her husband, and an unmarried woman guards it from everyone. Several issues branch from this:

First issue: The apparent wording of the verse encompasses all chaste women, whether Muslim or disbeliever, and whether free or enslaved. However, the jurists said: the conditions of ihsan are five: Islam, sanity, puberty, freedom, and chastity from zina. We regarded Islam as a condition because of his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever associates partners with God is not muhsan." We regarded sanity and puberty as conditions because of his saying (peace be upon him): "The pen is lifted from three." We regarded freedom as a condition because the slave is of lesser rank, so the reproach of zina does not weigh heavily upon him. We regarded chastity from zina as a condition because the hadd is prescribed to refute the slanderer; so if the one accused is a zani, the slanderer is truthful in the accusation.

Likewise, if the one accused had intercourse with a woman under a doubtful claim (shubha) or an invalid marriage, because in it there is the doubt of zina just as there is the doubt of licitness. Just as one of the two doubts removes the hadd from the one who had intercourse, so the other removes it from his slanderer as well. Then we say: whoever slanders a disbeliever, a madman, a child, or a slave, or someone who has committed zina with a woman, there is no hadd upon him, but he is disciplined with ta'zir for the harm caused. Even if he committed zina once in the height of his youth, then repented, his condition became good and he grew old in righteousness, his slanderer is not subjected to the hadd. Likewise, if a disbeliever or a slave committed zina, then embraced Islam, was freed, and his condition became good, and then a slanderer slandered him, there is no hadd upon the slanderer. This is unlike the case where he committed zina while a child or insane, and then reached puberty or regained sanity, and then a slanderer slandered him: the slanderer is liable to the hadd, because the act of a child or a madman is not zina.

If someone slanders a muhsan, and before the slanderer is subjected to the hadd, the one accused commits zina, the hadd is dropped from his slanderer; because the occurrence of zina creates doubt about his past condition, since God the Generous does not expose the concealment of His servant at the very first time he commits sin, so by its manifestation it is known that he had been characterized by it before. It is related that a man committed zina in the time of Umar, and said: "By God, I have not committed zina except with this one (woman)." Umar said: "You lie, for God does not expose His servant at the first time." Al-Muzani and Abu Thawr said: a zina that occurs later does not remove the hadd from the slanderer.
* * *
Second issue: Al-Hasan al-Basri said that His saying ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ applies to men and women. All the other scholars rejected this, because the word muhsanat is the plural of a feminine form, so it does not encompass men; rather, consensus indicates there is no difference in this matter between muhsanun and muhsanat.

Third issue: Accusing those who are not chaste does not entail the hadd, but entails only ta'zir, unless the one accused is known for what he was accused of, in which case there is neither hadd nor ta'zir there. This is the summary of the discussion in explaining His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾.
* * *
As for His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿Then they do not produce four witnesses﴾, there are two discussions:

First discussion: Know that God the Exalted has decreed three rulings regarding the slanderer who does not produce four witnesses: first, eighty lashes; second, the invalidity of his testimony; third, a judgment of his being a wrongdoer (fasiq) until he repents. The scholars differed over how these rulings are established, after agreeing that the hadd is obligatory upon him by the act of slander itself when he is unable to establish proof of zina.

Some said: his testimony has been invalidated and the mark of wrongdoing is attached to him before the hadd is carried out upon him; this is the view of al-Shafi'i and al-Layth ibn Sa'd. Abu Hanifa, Malik, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Zufar said: his testimony is accepted as long as he has not been flogged. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: this is the implication of their view, that he is not marked with the mark of wrongdoing until the hadd has been applied to him, because if the mark of wrongdoing attached to him, his testimony would not be valid, since the mark of wrongdoing invalidates the testimony of one so marked. Then Abu Bakr argued for the soundness of Abu Hanifa's view with several points:

First: His saying, the Glorified: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses, flog them eighty lashes﴾. The apparent wording of the verse requires that the obligation of the hadd is consequent upon the combination of the slander and the inability to produce testimony. So if we attached this ruling to the slander alone, that would undermine its being conditioned on both matters, and that is contrary to the verse. Also, the obligation of flogging is a ruling consequent upon two matters combined, so it must not be realized by the mere occurrence of one of them, just as if he said to his wife: "If you enter the house and speak to so-and-so, then you are divorced," and she did one of the two things without the other, the condition is not fulfilled. Likewise here.

Second: The slanderer is not judged a liar merely by his slander, and if that is so, his testimony must not be rejected merely by the slander. The proof of the first point is in three aspects:

The first: If the mere slander made him a liar, it would necessarily follow that his subsequent proof of zina would not be accepted, since he has been judged a liar; and the judgment that he is a liar in his slander is a judgment invalidating the testimony of one who testified to the truth of the accusation that the one accused was a zani. Since they agreed that his proof is accepted, it is established that he was not judged a liar merely by his slander.

The second: The one who slanders his wife with zina is not judged a liar by the mere act of slander; otherwise, li'an between him and his wife would not be permissible, and he would not be commanded to swear by God that he is truthful regarding what he accused her of, along with a judgment of her being a liar. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) said after conducting li'an between the spouses: "God knows that one of you is a liar; is there any among you who repents?", he informed that one of them, without specification, was the liar, and he did not judge the slanderer to be a liar. This is evidence that the slander itself does not make him a liar.

The third: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses? Since they did not bring the witnesses, they are the liars in the sight of God﴾ [an-Nur: 13]. He did not judge them to be liars by the slander alone. Through these aspects it is established that the slanderer is not judged a liar merely by the slander. And if that is so, his testimony must not be invalidated merely by the slander, because he was a just and trustworthy person, and what proceeded from him is not contradicted; and since he must remain upon his uprightness, it follows that his testimony is accepted.

Third: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Muslims are upright toward one another, except one who has been subjected to the hadd for slander." He informed that the uprightness of the slanderer remains as long as he has not been flogged.

Fourth: What Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, in the story of Hilal ibn Umayya, when he slandered his wife before the Messenger of God (peace be upon him). The Messenger of God said: "Hilal shall be flogged, and his testimony among the Muslims shall be invalidated." So he informed that the invalidation of his testimony is connected to the infliction of the flogging upon him, and that indicates that the mere slander does not invalidate testimony.

Fifth: Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, held that if the witnesses to slander come separately, their testimony is accepted. If the slander had invalidated his testimony, it would necessarily follow that it should not be accepted after that, and if three others testify with him, because he has become a wrongdoer by his slander and his lie must be judged; and in accepting their testimony when they come separately is what necessitates that their testimony is not invalidated by the slander itself. As for the basis of al-Shafi'i's view, it is that God the Exalted attached to the slander, together with the failure to produce four witnesses, three matters joined to one another by the conjunction "wa" (and), and the conjunction "wa" does not require sequence. So it follows that none of them is necessarily consequent upon another, and so the rejection of testimony is not necessarily consequent upon the carrying out of the hadd; rather, the rejection of testimony must be established whether or not the hadd is carried out upon him. And God knows best.
* * *
Second discussion: Concerning the manner of testimony for zina. God the Exalted said: ﴿And those of your women who commit immorality, call four witnesses against them from among you﴾ [an-Nisa: 15], and He said: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses﴾. Sa'd ibn Ubada said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think if I find a man with my wife, shall I leave him until I bring four witnesses?" He said: "Yes." Here there are some issues:

First issue: Does confession of zina establish proof by the testimony of two men? There are two opinions.

One of them: It is not established except by four, like the act of zina itself.

The second: It is established, unlike the act of zina, because the act is something whose witnessing is difficult to observe, so it was made stringent by requiring four; whereas confession is an apparent matter, so witnessing it is not difficult.

Second issue: If they testify to the act of zina, they must state the zani and the one with whom he committed it, because he may see him with a slave-girl of his own and assume she is a stranger. They must also testify: "We saw his member enter her private part like the kohl-stick entering the kohl-pot." If they testify only generally that he committed zina, it is not established, because they may regard mutual thigh-rubbing as zina. This is unlike the case where someone slanders a person and says "You committed zina," where the hadd is obligatory and it is not required to inquire further. If someone confesses against himself to zina, is it required to inquire? There are two views.

One of them: Yes, like the witnesses.

The second: It is not obligatory, as in slander.

[p. 139]

The third issue: al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said there is no difference whether the witnesses come separately or together. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said that if they testify separately, the testimony is not established and they incur the hadd (fixed penalty) for slander (qadhf). Al-Shafi'i's proof, may God have mercy on him, is in several respects:

The first: bringing four witnesses is a common element whether they are brought together or separately. A word that indicates what is common does not indicate what distinguishes. So the one who brings them separately is acting upon the text and must be released from the obligation.

The second: every ruling that is established by the testimony of witnesses when they come together is also established when they come separately, like all other rulings. Indeed, this is more appropriate, because when they come separately they are further from suspicion and from one of them being coached by another. Therefore we say: if the judge has doubts about the testimony of the witnesses, he separates them so that any flaw in their testimony may become apparent.

The third: it is not required that they testify at the same moment. Rather, if they gather before the judge and each one is brought in and testifies after another, their testimony is accepted. Likewise if they gather at his door and then each enters one after another. Abu Hanifa's proof, may God have mercy on him, is in two respects:

The first: when a single witness testifies, he has thereby slandered the person, and he has not brought four witnesses. Therefore the hadd is obligatory upon him, based on the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses﴾. At most, they have expressed that slander with the word "testimony," but that carries no weight, because it would lead to the complete cancellation of the hadd for slander. Every slanderer would be unhindered by the word "testimony," and would make that a means of removing the hadd from himself while still achieving his aim from the slander.

The second: what is related, that al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba was testified against for fornication before Umar ibn al-Khattab by four men: Abu Bakra, Nafi', Nufay', and Ziyad, who was the fourth. Ziyad said: "I saw a buttock rising and down, a breath panting, and her legs on his shoulders like the ears of a donkey, and I do not know what is beyond that." So Umar flogged the three and did not ask whether they had another witness with them. If the testimony of others were accepted after that, he would have hesitated, because the hudud are among matters in which one must hold back and take precaution.

The fourth issue: if fewer than four witnesses testify to fornication, the fornication is not established. Is the hadd for slander obligatory upon the witnesses? There are two opinions.

One of them: it is not obligatory, because they came in the manner of witnesses. Also, if we imposed the hadd, the door of testimony regarding fornication would be closed, since each witness would not be secure from his companion failing to agree with him, and so he would incur the hadd.

The second opinion, which is the more correct one, and which Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, also held: the hadd is obligatory upon them. The evidence for it is the two proofs we mentioned in the third issue.

The fifth issue: if a man slanders another man and then brings four unrighteous (fasiq) persons, who testify against the one slandered with fornication, Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: the hadd falls from the slanderer, and the hadd is not obligatory upon the witnesses. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said in one of his two opinions: they are to be subjected to the hadd. The basis of Abu Hanifa's view is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses﴾, and this man has produced four witnesses, so the hadd is not incumbent upon him.

Also, the unrighteous person is among those eligible to testify, and the conditions for testimony regarding fornication have been met in them, by their gathering before the judge. However, their testimony was not accepted because of suspicion. Just as we considered suspicion in removing the hadd from the one testified against, so also it is required to consider it in removing the hadd from them. The basis of al-Shafi'i's view, may God have mercy on him, is that they do not have the attributes required for acceptance of testimony, so they have gone outside being witnesses, and so they remain purely slanderers.

Here ends the discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿then they do not produce four witnesses﴾.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So flog them eighty lashes﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: the addressee of His saying ﴿flog them﴾ is the ruler (imam), as we explained in the verse on fornication, or the owner (of the slave), according to al-Shafi'i's school, or a righteous man whom the people appoint when the ruler is absent.

The second issue: some cases have been excepted from the general application of this verse.

One of them: a father who slanders his child or any of his descendants. He is not subject to the hadd, just as he is not subject to qisas (retaliation) for killing him.

The second: if the slanderer is a slave, the obligation is to flog him forty lashes. Likewise the mukatab (slave contracted to purchase his freedom) and the umm walad (slave woman who has borne her master's child). Whoever is partly free and partly slave, his punishment is that of slaves.

The third: whoever slanders a female slave who is chaste, or a woman who had committed fornication in earlier times and then repented, she is, by the meaning of the language, a muhsana (chaste woman), yet despite that the hadd for slandering her is not obligatory.

The third issue: they said: the most severe of the beatings among the hudud is the beating for fornication, then the beating for drinking wine, then the beating for the slanderer. This is because the cause of his punishment is something that may be true or false, yet he is punished in order to protect honour and to deter people from violating it.

The fourth issue: Malik and al-Shafi'i said: the hadd for slander is inheritable. If the one slandered dies before the hadd is carried out and before pardon is granted, the right to the hadd for slander passes to his heir. Likewise, if the obligation due from his slander was a ta'zir (discretionary punishment), it is inherited from him. And similarly, if he initiated the slander after the death of the one slandered, the right to demand the hadd passes to his heir. But according to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, the hadd for slander is not inheritable and it lapses upon death. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, is that the hadd for slander is a right of a human being, because it is dropped by his pardon, and it is not carried out except by his demand, and the defendant swears an oath concerning it if he denies it. And since it is a right of a human being, it must be inheritable, based on the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever leaves a right, it belongs to his heirs." The proof of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, is that if it were inheritable, the husband or wife would have a share in it. Also, it is a right that does not have the meaning of property or security, so it is not inheritable, like agency (wakala) or profit-sharing (mudaraba).

As for the answer to the first: the more correct view among the Shafi'is is that all the heirs inherit it, just as they inherit property. There is a second view in their school that all of them inherit it except the husband and wife, because the marital relationship ends with death. Also, the purpose of the hadd is to remove disgrace from the lineage, and that does not attach to the husband and wife.

The fifth issue: if a person slanders another person in front of the judge, or slanders his wife with a specific man while that man is absent, then the judge must send to the one slandered and inform him that so-and-so has slandered you, and the hadd for slander has become established for you against him. This is like when a right to property is established for someone against another, and he does not know it; it is obligatory to inform him. In this sense, the Prophet, peace be upon him, sent Unays to inform her that so-and-so had slandered her with his son, and he did not send him to investigate her fornication. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: the ruler does not have the right, when a man accuses someone of fornication, to send to him and ask him about it, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not spy﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. He meant by this the case where the slanderer is not specified, such as if a man says before the judge: "People say that so-and-so committed fornication." In that case the judge does not send to him to question him.

As for His saying: ﴿and do not accept their testimony ever﴾, the jurists differed concerning it. Most of the Companions and the Successors said that if he repents, his testimony is accepted, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him. Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih, may God have mercy on them, said: the testimony of one punished with the hadd for slander is not accepted even if he repents. This question is based on whether His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾ returns to all the rulings mentioned, or is restricted to the last clause. According to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, the exception mentioned after many clauses is restricted to the last clause. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, it returns to all of them. We have summarized this question in the study of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), and here we mention what is appropriate to this place, God willing. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, argued that his testimony is accepted, with several proofs:

The first: His saying, peace be upon him: "The one who repents of sin is like one who has no sin." And one who has no sin has accepted testimony, so the one who repents must also have accepted testimony.

The second: a disbeliever who slanders and then repents of disbelief has his testimony accepted by consensus. So a Muslim slanderer who repents of slander must also have his testimony accepted, because slander with Islam is less grave than slander with disbelief. If it is said that Muslims are not hurt by the insulting of disbelievers, since they are known for their hostility toward them and for speaking against them falsely, so the one slandered by a disbeliever does not suffer the same disgrace and reproach as one slandered by a Muslim like himself, therefore the hadd is made more severe for a Muslim slanderer to deter him from bringing shame and reproach. Also, one who repents of disbelief is not subject to the hadd, whereas one who repents of slander is not relieved of the hadd. We reply that this distinction is nullified by His saying, peace be upon him: "Inform them that they have what the Muslims have, and they are subject to what the Muslims are subject to."

The third: we agree that one who repents of disbelief, murder, or fornication has accepted testimony, so likewise one who repents of slander, because this sin is no greater than fornication itself.

The fourth: Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, accepts his testimony if he repents before the hadd, even though the hadd is the right of the one slandered and so is not removed by repentance. Therefore, if his testimony is accepted when he repents after the hadd is carried out, when his condition has improved and the name of wickedness has been removed from him, that is more appropriate.

The fifth: His saying, ﴿except those who repent﴾, is an exception mentioned after a series of clauses, so it must return to all of them. This is indicated by several matters:

The first: we agree that if someone says, "My slave is free and my wife is divorced, God willing," the exception returns to everything. Likewise in the case under discussion. If it is said that the difference is that "God willing" enters to cancel the ruling of the whole speech, so that nothing is established in it, whereas an exception introduced by the particle of exception cannot enter to cancel the ruling of the speech entirely. Do you not see that one may say, "You are divorced, God willing," and nothing takes effect; but if one says, "You are divorced, except a divorce," the divorce takes effect and the exception is void, because it is impossible for it to cancel the ruling of the speech completely. Thus it is established that the return of "God willing" to everything preceding does not necessitate the return of an exception with its particle to everything preceding. We reply: this is a difference outside the point of the comparison, because "God willing" may enter to cancel the ruling of the speech entirely, so it is permissible for it to return to all the clauses mentioned. Otherwise, if it could enter only to cancel part of the speech, it would be necessary to permit its return to all the clauses on this view, so that it would entail that some part is excluded from each of the clauses mentioned.

The second: the "and" (waw) indicates unrestricted joining. So His saying, ﴿So flog them eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever, and those are the wicked ones﴾, the joining becomes as if it were mentioned all together, with no precedence of some over others.

[end of part 3]

When the exception came after it, returning it to one of the clauses was no more appropriate than returning it to the rest, since none of the clauses has any precedence over another in meaning. So it must return to all of them. A parallel to this, on the view of Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him), is His saying: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 6]. The particle *fa* (indicating sequence, *fa' al-ta'qib*) does not attach to washing the face alone, but to the whole group of these acts, because the *wa* (and) does not indicate order. In the same way here, the word *illa* (except) is not attached to one specific item, because the particle *wa* does not indicate order, and it attaches to the whole group.

If it is objected that *wa* may indicate conjunction, as you have said, but it may also indicate resumption, and it is so in His saying: ﴿And it is those who are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾, because it indicates conjunction only in what does not differ in meaning and whose arrangement is a single sentence. Thus all of it becomes like what is mentioned together, like the verse of ablution, for all of it is one command, as if He had said: "Wash these limbs," since the word of command includes all of it.

As for the verse of slander, its beginning is a command and its end is a statement, so they cannot be arranged as one sentence, and the *wa* must be for resumption, so the exception is specific to it. We reply: why is it not permissible for us to make the three sentences together the response to the condition, as if it were said: "Those who slander chaste women, flog them, reject their testimony, and declare them defiant," meaning: gather for them the flogging, the rejection and the declaring of defiance, except those who repent of the slander and make amends, for God forgives them, so they return neither flogged, nor rejected, nor declared defiant.

Third: His saying ﴿And do not accept their testimony ever﴾ is followed by His saying ﴿And it is those who are the defiantly disobedient﴾, which indicates that the reason for not accepting that testimony is that he is defiant, because linking a ruling to an attribute implies causation, especially when the attribute is appropriate. That he is defiant is an appropriate reason for his testimony not being accepted. Since it is established that the reason for rejecting the testimony is nothing but his being defiant, and the exception indicates the removal of defiance, the reason has been removed, so the ruling must be removed with the removal of the reason.

Fourth: such an exception exists in the Qur'an. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿The penalty of those who wage war against God and His Messenger is only that...﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 33], up to His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾. There is no disagreement that this exception refers to what preceded from the beginning of the verse, and that repentance is attainable by all of them. Likewise His saying: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], up to His saying: ﴿and you find no water, so perform tayammum﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. Tayammum becomes for one who is obliged to perform ghusl, just as it is prescribed for one who is obliged to perform wudu'. This argument was mentioned by Abu 'Ubayd in establishing the school of al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him).

The companions of Abu Hanifa argued that the ruling of the exception is specific to the final sentence, with several arguments:

First: the exception from an exception is specific to the final sentence, so likewise in all cases, by analogy.

Second: the cause for the generality of the preceding sentences is present, and the counter-factor, which is the exception, is satisfied by attaching it to one sentence, because by this amount the exception ceases to be meaningless, so it must be attached to the single sentence only.

Third: if the exception returned to all the preceding sentences, it would follow that if he repents he should not be flogged, and this is invalid by consensus (ijma'), so the exception must be specific to the final sentence.

The answer to the first: the exception from a negation is an affirmation, and from an affirmation is a negation. So if a second exception follows an exception and returns to the first exception and to the excepted item, then to the extent that it negates one of them it affirms in the other, so the deficient is compensated by the excess, and the second exception becomes without benefit. For this reason we said that an exception from an exception is specific to the final sentence.

The answer to the second: we have shown that the conjunctive *wa* does not imply order, so some sentences are not later in conception than others, and attaching it to some is no more appropriate than attaching it to the rest, so it must be attached to all.

The answer to the third: the ruling was abandoned with respect to some of them, but was not abandoned with respect to the rest.

The companions of Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) argued on this question with several reports:

First: what Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) related concerning the case of Hilal ibn Umayya, when he slandered his wife with Shurayk ibn Sahma'. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Hilal shall be flogged, and his testimony shall be voided among the Muslims." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed that the infliction of the flogging on him voids his testimony, without the condition of repentance for its acceptance.

Second: the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "Muslims are upright (*'udul*), some over others, except one who has been punished with the legal penalty (*mahdud*) for slander," and he did not stipulate the existence of repentance from it.

Third: what 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb related from his father, from his grandfather, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "The testimony of one who has received the legal penalty is not permitted in Islam." The Shafi'is said: this is opposed by several arguments:

First: the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "When you know something as clear as the sun, then testify." The command implies obligation, so when the one who received the penalty knows, testimony becomes obligatory upon him. If it were not acceptable, it would not be obligatory, for it would be pointless.

Second: the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "We judge by the apparent." Here the apparent has been established, for his religion, his intellect and his chastity, which are attained through repentance, produce the presumption that he is truthful.

Third: what is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he flogged those who testified against al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, namely Abu Bakra, Nafi' and Nufay', then said to them: "Whoever retracts himself, his testimony is accepted, and whoever does not, I will not permit his testimony." Nafi' and Nufay' retracted themselves and repented, and he accepted their testimony. As for Abu Bakra, he did not accept his testimony. And none of the Companions objected to him in this. This is the full discussion of this question.

As for His saying ﴿And it is those who are the defiantly disobedient﴾, know that it indicates two matters:

The first: that slander is among the major sins, because the name *fisq* (defiant disobedience) applies only to one who has committed a major sin.

The second: that it is a name for one who deserves punishment, because if it were derived from his act, repentance would not prevent its continuation, just as it does not prevent describing him as one who "strikes" or "shoots" and so on.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾, know that they differ over how repentance from slander is to be done. Al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) said: repentance from it is to retract oneself (*ikdhab nafsahu*). His companions differed over its meaning. Al-Istakhri said: he says, "I lied in what I said, and I will not return to its like." Abu Ishaq said: he should not say "I lied," because perhaps he is truthful, and then his saying "I lied" would be a lie, and lying is a sin, and committing a sin is not repentance from another sin. Rather, the slanderer says: "I regret what I said, I retract it, and I will not return to it."

As for His saying: ﴿and make amends﴾, our companions said: after repentance, a period must pass in which his conduct is good, until his testimony is accepted and his authority restored. Then they determined that period to be one year, so that the four seasons, in which conditions and temperaments change, pass over him, just as a term of one year is set for the impotent man. The Law has attached rulings to the year, such as zakat, the jizya and others.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, the meaning is that because He is Forgiving and Merciful, He accepts repentance. This indicates that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason. For if it were obligatory, His acceptance of it would not show Him to be Forgiving and Merciful, since if it were obligatory, He would accept it out of compulsion and force, knowing that if He did not accept it He would be foolish and would have gone beyond the bounds of divinity. But when it is not obligatory and He accepts it, then mercy and benevolence are truly realized. And success is from God.

**Ruling Three: Slander (qadhf).** The words of God Most High: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses — lash them eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after. And those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that the apparent meaning of the verse does not indicate the thing by which they accuse the chaste women, and mention of "accusation" (ramy) does not indicate adultery (zina), since one may accuse her of theft, drinking wine, or disbelief. Rather, there must be a clear indication specifying it. The scholars have agreed that what is meant is accusation of adultery. In the verse there are statements that indicate this:

First: the prior mention of adultery.

Second: God mentioned "muhsanat" (chaste women), who are the chaste ones, which indicates that what is meant by "accusation" is accusing them of the opposite of chastity.

Third: His saying ﴿then they do not produce four witnesses﴾, meaning to confirm what they accused them of, and it is known that this number of witnesses is not required except in the case of adultery.

Fourth: there is consensus that flogging is not obligatory for accusing someone of something other than adultery, so it must be that what is meant is accusation of adultery. Having understood this, the discussion of this verse concerns the accusation, the accuser, and the one accused.

* * *

**The First Section: On the Accusation.** It contains several issues.

**First issue:** The wording of slander is divided into explicit (sarih), allusive (kinayah), and indirect (ta'rid). The explicit is to say "O adulteress," or "you committed adultery," or "your front or your back committed adultery." If he said "your body committed adultery," there are two views:

One: it is allusive, like saying "your hand committed adultery," because the reality of adultery is from the private part, so from the rest of the body there is only assistance.

The second, and the more correct, is that it is explicit, because the act proceeds from the whole body, and the private part is only an instrument in the act. As for allusive expressions, such as saying "O immoral woman," "O sinful woman," "O wicked woman," "O hired woman," "O daughter of the forbidden," or "my wife does not turn away the hand of one who touches her," and the reverse of these, this is not slander unless he intends it. Likewise, if he says to an Arab "O Nabati" (a derogatory term), this is not slander unless he intends it. If he intended slander, it is slander against the mother of the one addressed; otherwise, it is not. If he says, "I meant by it the Nabati of residence and language," and the mother of the one addressed claims he intended slander, then the word of the speaker is accepted with his oath.

As for indirect allusion (ta'rid), it is not slander even if he intended it, such as saying, "O son of the lawful, as for me, I have not committed adultery, and my mother is not an adulteress." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih, may Allah have mercy on them all.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the hadd is obligatory for it. Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is slander in a state of anger but not in a state of contentment.

Our evidence: indirect allusion to slander is open to being slander or to something else, so the hadd must not be obligatory, because the original state is the innocence of the obligation, and one does not depart from it on doubt. Also, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: «Avert the hudud by doubts.» And because the hudud were legislated contrary to the text that negates harm. The harm resulting from explicit speech is greater than that resulting from indirect speech.

The opponent argued with what al-Awza'i related from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from Ibn Umar, who said: "Umar used to apply the hadd for indirect allusion." It is also related that two men quarreled during the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and one of them said to the other: "By Allah, I am not an adulterer, nor is my mother an adulteress." Umar consulted the people about it. One said: "He praised his father and mother." Others said: "His father and mother had praise other than this." So Umar flogged him eighty lashes.

The answer: that Umar's consulting the Companions about the ruling on indirect allusion indicates that there was no explicit textual instruction (tawqif) among them on it, and that they gave an opinion by way of ijtihad.

* * *

**Second issue: On multiple slanders.** One may either slander one person repeatedly or slander a group. If he slanders one person repeatedly, consider: if he intended by all of them one adulteress, such as saying "you committed adultery with 'Amr," repeated several times, only one hadd is obligatory. If he initiated the second after being flogged for the first, he is disciplined (ta'zir) for the second. If he slandered her with different acts of adultery, such as saying "you committed adultery with Zayd," then "you committed adultery with 'Amr," is the hadd multiplied or not? There are two views:

One: it multiplies, considering the wording, and because it is a right of the servants, so overlap does not occur in it, like debts.

The second, and the more correct: it overlaps, so only one hadd is obligatory, because they are two hudud of one kind for one entitled party, so they should overlap like the hudud of adultery. If he slandered his wife repeatedly, the more correct view is that one li'an suffices, whether we say the hadd multiplies or not.

As for when he slanders a number of persons: consider. If he slandered each one with a separate word, a full hadd is obligatory for each one. According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, only one hadd is obligatory. Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for Abu Hanifah's view from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and analogy.

From the Qur'an: God's saying ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾. The meaning is that whoever accuses chaste women is obligated to the flogging, and this implies that one who accuses a group of chaste women is not flogged more than eighty. So whoever obligates more than one hadd on the one who slanders a group of chaste women has contradicted the verse.

From the Sunnah: what 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, that Hilal ibn Umayyah slandered his wife before the Prophet, peace be upon him, accusing her with Sharik ibn Sahma'. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "No; either evidence or a hadd on your back." So the Prophet did not obligate on Hilal except one hadd, despite his slandering his wife and Sharik ibn Sahma', until the verse of li'an was revealed, and li'an was established for wives in place of the hadd for non-wives.

From analogy: every act that makes the hadd obligatory, if it occurs from him repeatedly, only one hadd is obligatory, such as one who commits adultery repeatedly, drinks repeatedly, or steals repeatedly. So here too. The common cause is averting greater harm.

The answer to the first: God's saying ﴿alladhina﴾ is a plural form, and ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ is a plural form, and when plural is matched with plural, singular is matched with singular, so the meaning becomes: whoever accuses one chaste woman is obligated to the hadd. At this point the way al-Shafi'i relied on the verse becomes clear. Also, God's saying ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses — lash them﴾ [al-Nur: 4] indicates that the flogging is ordered upon accusing chaste women, and the ordering of the ruling upon the attribute, especially when it is appropriate, signals causation. So the verse indicates that accusing a chaste woman, insofar as she bears this description, makes the flogging obligatory. Having established this, we say: if he slanders one person, that slander becomes a cause of the hadd; if he slanders a second, the second slander must also be a cause of the hadd. The cause of the second slander cannot be the first hadd itself, because that was already obligated by the first slander, and making the obligated obligatory again is impossible. So he must be flogged a second hadd for the second slander. At most, what can be raised against this inference is the hudud of adultery. But we say: the application of this proof was set aside there, because the hadd of adultery is more severe than the hadd of slander, and when a difference is evident, combining them becomes impossible.

As for the Sunnah, there is no indication in it regarding this issue, because the slander of both was with one word. We have a detailed discussion on this issue that will come, God willing.

As for analogy, it is flawed, because the hadd of slander is a right of the human being, as evidenced by the fact that it is not imposed except upon the demand of the one slandered, and rights of human beings do not overlap, unlike the hadd of adultery, which is a right of God Most High. All of this applies when he slandered a group, each one with a separate word. As for when he slandered them with one word, saying "You are adulterers" or "You have committed adultery," there are two views. The more correct of them, and his view in the "New" (al-Jadid) opinion, is that a full hadd is obligatory for each one, because it is a right of the servants and therefore does not overlap, and because he brought disgrace upon each of them, so it is as if he had slandered them with separate words. In the "Old" (al-Qadim) opinion, only one hadd is obligatory for all, considering the wording, since the wording is one. But the first is more correct, because it better fits the understanding of the verse. Accordingly, if he said to a man, "O son of the two adulterers," which is slander against his two parents with one word, then he is liable to two hudud.

* * *
