Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 26:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wicked words are for wicked men, and wicked men for wicked words; and good words are for good men, and good men for good words. Those are declared innocent of what they say; for them is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾

Know that "al-khabithat" (wicked things, i.e., wicked words or wicked women) applies to the words that are the slander uttered by the people of the lie (ahl al-ifk), and it also applies to speech that is like blame and cursing. The intended meaning of this is not the very word that comes from Allah, exalted is He, but rather the content of the word. It also applies to adulterous women. In this verse, all of these aspects are possible. If we take it to mean the slander uttered by the people of the lie, the meaning is: wicked words from the speech of the people of the lie are for the wicked men, and vice versa; and good words from the speech of those who denied the lie are for the good men, and vice versa. If we take it to mean speech that is like blame and cursing, the meaning is that blame and cursing are prepared for wicked men, and wicked men are exposed to cursing and blame.

The same applies to "al-tayyibat" (good things). "Those" (ulaika) refers to the good men, and that they are declared innocent of the wicked words that wicked men say. If we take it to mean adulterous women, the meaning is: wicked women are for wicked men and vice versa, in accordance with the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress﴾ [al-Nur: 3], and good women are for good men. The meaning is that such slander as was uttered by the hypocrites is only fitting for wicked women and wicked men, not for good women and good men such as the Messenger (ﷺ) and his wives. If it is said: according to this interpretation, it would follow that a chaste man may not marry an adulteress. The answer is what has preceded in His saying: ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress﴾, and His saying: ﴿Those are declared innocent﴾, meaning the good women and good men from what the people of the lie say. Apart from the view of one who takes it to mean words, it is as if He said: the good men are declared innocent of what the wicked men say. And when "ulaika" is taken in this sense, its wording is like its meaning in that it is plural. If you take it to refer to Aisha and Safwan, who are two, how is it expressed with a plural form? Its answer is in two respects:

First: that slander was directed at the Prophet (ﷺ), at Aisha and at Safwan, so Allah, exalted is He, declared each one of them free from the accusation appropriate to him.

Second: that what is meant by it is all the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), as if Allah, exalted is He, declared them innocent of this lie. Yet no one may cast doubt on them as they dared to do with Aisha, and He exonerated the Messenger (ﷺ) through this from such matters. This is clearer. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, made clear that good women are for good men, and there is no one better or purer than the Messenger, so his wives may not be other than good women. Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾, meaning acquittal from Allah and His Messenger, ﴿and a noble provision﴾ in the Hereafter. It may be that this is a definite report, so it is known from this that the wives of the Messenger, peace be upon him, are with him in Paradise, and reports have come to this effect. It may also be that what is meant is on condition of avoiding major sins and repentance. The first is more appropriate, because we only need the condition if the verse cannot be taken in that sense; but if it is possible, there is no reason to seek a condition.

This indicates that Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, will enter Paradise, unlike the doctrine of the Rafidah, who declare her a disbeliever because of the battle of the Camel, for they thereby reject the explicit text of the Qur'an. If it is said: certainty that she is among the people of Paradise is an incitement to wrongdoing for her. We say: Did not Allah, exalted is He, inform the Messenger (ﷺ) that he was among the people of Paradise, and that was not an incitement to wrongdoing for him? Likewise the ten who were given the good news of Paradise; so it is the same here. And Allah knows best. The story of the people of the lie is complete.

**[Page 170]**

The sixth ruling concerns seeking permission (*istiʼdhān*, asking leave to enter). His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants. That is best for you, that you may remember.﴾

﴿And if you find no one in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Return," then return; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

Know that He, Exalted, turned away from what relates to the accusation of adultery (*ramy*) and slander (*qadhf*), and the ruling pertaining to them, to what is fitting for this matter. This is because the people of the slander (*ahl al-ifk*) found their way to their calumny only through the opportunity of being alone together, so it became like a path of suspicion. Therefore Allah, Exalted, made it obligatory that a person not enter another's house except after seeking permission and greeting, because entering in a manner other than this leads to the occurrence of suspicion, and there is harm in that which is not hidden. So He said: ﴿That is because those who disbelieved...﴾ and so on. There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** *Istiʼnās* (familiarity) is an expression for the intimacy that arises from sitting together. He, Exalted, said: ﴿nor lingering for conversation﴾. This intimacy occurs only after entering and greeting, so it would have been better to place the greeting before the seeking of familiarity. Why, then, does the verse come in the reverse order? The answer to this has several aspects:

First: what is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is that it is actually *ḥattā tastaʾdhinū* ("until you seek permission"), and the scribe erred.

In the recitation of Ubayy: *ḥattā tastaʾdhinū lakum* ("until you seek permission for yourselves"). "And the greeting is better for you than the greeting of the Jāhiliyyah and the *dumūr*," which is entering without permission. Its derivation is from *ad-damār*, which is destruction, as if its doer is ruined (*dāmir*) because of the greatness of what he committed. In a hadith: "Whoever his eye precedes his seeking permission has been ruined (*damar*)." Know that this statement from Ibn ʿAbbās is open to scrutiny, because it implies criticism of the Qur'an which was transmitted by continuous transmission (*tawātur*), and it implies the authenticity of a Qur'an that was not transmitted by continuous transmission. Opening these two doors leads doubt to the whole Qur'an, and that it is false.

Second: what is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, that he said: there is an inversion (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*) in the speech, and the meaning is: "until you greet its occupants and seek familiarity," because the greeting precedes the familiarity. In the recitation of ʿAbd Allāh: *ḥattā tusallimū ʿalā ahlihā wa-tastaʾdhinū* ("until you greet its occupants and seek permission"). This also is weak, because it contradicts the apparent meaning.

Third: to let the speech stand on its apparent meaning. Then, regarding the explanation of *istiʼnās*, there are several views:

The first: "until you seek familiarity through permission," because when they seek permission and greet, the people of the house become at ease; but if they entered without permission, they would be startled and it would be distressing for them.

The second: explaining *istiʼnās* as seeking information and discovering: it is an *istifʻāl* form from *ānasa al-shayʾ*, when one sees a thing clearly and openly. The meaning is: "until you seek information and discover the situation, whether your entry is wanted." From this is their saying: *istaʾnis, hal tarā aḥadan* ("seek familiarity, do you see anyone?"), and *istaʾnastu fa-lam ara aḥadan* ("I sought familiarity and did not see anyone"), meaning I sought knowledge and information. If someone says: when it is understood as familiarity, the greeting should precede it, as it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" We say: the one seeking permission may not know whether anyone is in the house, so there is no sense in his greeting in this state.

The closer view is that by seeking permission he finds out whether there is anyone who will grant permission; when permission is granted and he enters, he becomes face to face with them, and then he greets them.

The third: that the derivation of *istiʼnās* is from *ins* (humankind), meaning that one ascertains whether there is a human being there. There is no doubt that this precedes the greeting.

The fourth: even if we concede that familiarity occurs only after the greeting, the *wāw* (and) does not necessarily imply sequence. Thus placing the familiarity before the greeting in the wording does not necessarily require placing it before in action.

* * *

**The second question:** What is the ruling on making the seeking of permission obligatory before entry? The answer: that wisdom is what Allah, Exalted, drew attention to in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses.﴾ By this it is indicated that the reason for which entry is prohibited except under this condition is that the houses are inhabited, because whoever rushes into them without seeking permission cannot be sure that he will not come upon what it is not lawful for him to look at of the private parts (*ʿawrah*), or upon what the people do not wish others to know of their circumstances. This is among the "causes" (*ʿilal*) indicated by the text. Also, it is a disposal over another's property, so it must be with his consent, otherwise it resembles usurpation (*ghaṣb*).

* * *

**The third question:** How is seeking permission to be done? The answer: "A man sought permission from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: *Aʾalij?* (May I enter?). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a woman called Rawḍah: 'Get up, go to this man and teach him, for he does not know how to seek permission properly. Say to him: Peace be upon you, may I enter?' The man heard it and said it. He said: 'Enter.' He entered and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about several things, and he answered. The man said: 'Is there in knowledge what you do not know?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'He has given me much good, and indeed there is in knowledge what no one knows except Allah,' and he recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ to the end."

The people of the Jāhiliyyah used to say, when a man entered a house other than his own: "Good morning to you, good evening to you," then he would enter, and it might happen that the man found himself with his wife under one covering. So Allah, Exalted, turned away from that and taught what is better and more beautiful. It is related from Mujāhid that *ḥattā tastaʾnisū* ("until you seek familiarity") means clearing the throat (*tanaḥnuh*). ʿIkrimah said it means glorifying Allah (*tasbīḥ*) and magnifying Him (*takbīr*), or the like.

* * *

**The fourth question:** How many times is permission to be sought? The answer: Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seeking permission is three times: at the first, they are to be silent; at the second, they are to prepare; at the third, they grant permission or refuse." And from Jundub, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "If one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted permission, let him return." And from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, he said: "I was sitting in one of the gatherings of the Anṣār when Abū Mūsā came in, frightened. We said to him: 'What has frightened you?' He said: 'ʿUmar commanded me to come to him, so I came to him and sought permission three times, but I was not granted permission, so I returned.' He (ʿUmar) said: 'What prevented you from coming to me?' I said: 'I came and sought permission three times, but I was not granted permission, and the Prophet (ﷺ) has said: "If one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted permission, let him return."' He said: 'You must bring me evidence for this, or I will punish you.' Ubayy said: 'None will stand with you except the youngest of the people.' Abū Saʿīd stood up and bore witness for him." In some reports, ʿUmar said to Abū Mūsā: "I did not suspect you, but I feared that people might attribute false things to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

And from Qatādah: seeking permission is three times: the first, so that the living hears; the second, so that they may prepare; the third, if they wish they grant permission, and if they wish they refuse. Know that this is among the excellent manners, because at the first time, some occupations may prevent them from granting permission; at the second time, there may be something that prevents or requires refusal or equality; when he is not answered at the third time, he infers from the absence of permission that there is a firm barrier, and that may create dislike of his being near the door, so for this reason it is recommended for him to return.

For this reason they say: it is obligatory in seeking permission three times that it not be continuous; rather there must be an interval of time between each and the next. As for knocking on the door violently and shouting at the owner of the house, that is forbidden, because it involves harm and causing unease. The story of the Banū Asad is sufficient as a deterrent, and what was revealed concerning it, the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers—most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 4].

* * *

**The fifth question:** How is one to stand at the door? The answer: It is related that "Abū Saʿīd sought permission from the Messenger (ﷺ) while he was facing the door, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do not seek permission while you are facing the door.'"

And it is related that "when he (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left side, and he would say: 'Peace be upon you.'" This was because the houses at that time did not have curtains (*sutūr*).

* * *

**The sixth question:** The word *ḥattā* ("until") indicates a limit (*ghāyah*), and the ruling after the limit is different from what precedes it. So His saying: ﴿do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity﴾ implies the permissibility of entering after seeking permission, even if the owner of the house has not given permission. What do you say about this? The answer has several aspects:

First: Allah, Exalted, made the limit *istiʼnās* (familiarity), not *istiʼdhān* (seeking permission), and familiarity does not occur except when permission is granted after seeking it.

Second: since we know from the text that the wisdom behind seeking permission is that a person should not enter upon another without his permission, for that is something that displeases him, and we know that this purpose is not achieved except after permission is granted, we know that seeking permission that is not followed by permission must not be sufficient.

Third: the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And if you find no one in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾ prohibits entry except with permission. This indicates that permission is conditional upon the permissibility of entry in the first verse. If it is said: once it is established that permission is necessary, can something else take its place or not? We say: Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man's messenger to a man is his permission." And from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "If one of you is invited and comes with the messenger, that is permission for him." This report indicates two meanings:

**[Page 173]**

One of them: that permission is implied in His saying: ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾, and this is what is meant by it.

The second: that the invitation is permission when one comes with the messenger, and that he does not need a second seeking of permission. Some of them said: whoever has the customary permission to enter does not need to seek permission.

* * *

**The seventh question:** What is the ruling on one who looks into another's house without his permission? The answer: Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: if his eye is gouged out, it is wasted (*hadar*, unrecompensed), and he relied on what Sahl ibn Saʿd narrated, he said: "A man looked into one of the rooms of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he had a comb with which he was scratching his head. He (ﷺ) said: 'If I had known you were looking at me, I would have stabbed you in the eye with it. Permission is only required before looking.'" And Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever looks into the house of a people without their permission, and they gouge out his eye, his eye is wasted (*hadarat*)."

Abū Bakr al-Rāzī said: this report is rejected because it contradicts the established principles of analogy, for there is no disagreement that if someone enters another's house without permission and the owner gouges out his eye, the owner is liable, and there is retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) if he did it intentionally, and compensation (*arsh*) if he did it by mistake. It is well known that the one who entered looked and exceeded looking, so the apparent meaning of the hadith contradicts what there is consensus upon. If it is authentic, its meaning is: whoever looks into the house of a people and looks at their sacred space (*ḥaram*) and their women, and is prevented but does not desist, and his eye is lost during the resistance, then it is wasted.

But if there was only looking, and there was no resistance or prohibition in it, and then someone came and gouged out his eye, this person is a wrongdoer and is bound by the ruling of his offence, based on the apparent meaning of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45], to His saying: ﴿and wounds in retaliation﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45]. Know that relying on the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ in this matter is weak, because we have agreed that this text is conditional upon the eye not being forfeit; for if the eye were forfeit, retaliation would not be due. So why do you say that whoever looks into a person's house, his eye is not forfeit? And this is the beginning of the question.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 27–29 (part 2 of 2):

As for his saying: if he entered, it would not be permissible to gouge out his eye; so likewise if he looked. We say: the difference between the two matters is clear, because if he enters, the people know of his entrance upon them, so they guard against him and conceal themselves. But if he looks, they may not know of it, and so he gains knowledge of what it is not permissible to witness. Therefore, it is not far-fetched in the ruling of the Shari'ah to be emphatic in the prohibition here, to close the door to this harm. In sum, rejecting the Hadith (a report of the Prophet's sayings and actions) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding this amount of speech is not permissible.

* * *

The eighth question: Since you have explained that permission is necessary, does any permission suffice, whatever its form, or must it be a specific permission? The answer: the apparent meaning of the verse requires accepting permission in general, whether the one giving permission is a child, a woman, a slave, or a non-Muslim dhimmi. For this permission, the qualifications of testimony are not required. Likewise is the acceptance of the reports of these people regarding gifts and similar matters.

* * *

The ninth question: Is seeking permission required when entering upon mahram relatives? The answer: Yes. It is related from Ata ibn Yasar: "A man asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying: 'Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister?' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Yes. Would you like to see her naked?'" A man asked Hudhayfa: "Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister?" He said: "If you do not seek permission to enter upon her, you will see what will distress you." Ata said: I asked Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister, and upon one whom I spend on?" He said: "Yes. Indeed Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission as those before them sought permission﴾ [al-Nur: 59]." He did not distinguish between one who is a stranger and one who is a mahram relative.

Know that abandoning seeking permission from mahram relatives, although it is not permissible, is lighter, because looking at her hair, chest, leg, and similar parts of the body is permissible. The verification in this matter is that if the prohibition against entering upon others is because those others may be uncovered, then this includes everyone except wives and those whom the right hand possesses. If it is because they may be occupied with a matter they dislike others seeing, then it must apply to all, so that one may not enter upon a wife or a female slave except with permission.

* * *

The tenth question: If a matter arises in a house, such as a fire, the intrusion of a thief, or the appearance of something reprehensible, is seeking permission obligatory? The answer: All of that is excepted by evidence. This is the sum of the discussion on seeking permission. As for greeting (salam), it is from the Sunnah of the Muslims, which they were commanded to follow. It is a safety for the people, it is the greeting of the people of Paradise, it brings about affection, and it removes resentment and rancor. It is related from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah the Exalted created Adam, peace be upon him, and breathed the spirit into him, he sneezed, and said: 'All praise is for Allah.' So he praised Allah with Allah's permission. His Lord said to him: 'May your Lord have mercy upon you, O Adam. Go to those angels, who are a group sitting there, and say: Peace be upon you.' When he did that, they replied, and he returned to his Lord, who said: 'This is your greeting and the greeting of your offspring.'"

And it is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The rights of a Muslim over a Muslim are six: he greets him when he meets him, he answers him when he invites him, he advises him sincerely in his absence, he blesses him when he sneezes, he visits him when he is ill, and he attends his funeral when he dies."

And it is related from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If it pleases you that the rancor be removed from your hearts, then spread the greeting of peace among you."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is better for you﴾, its meaning is clear: it means that doing this is better and more fitting for you than entering without permission. ﴿So that you may remember﴾, i.e., so that you may remember this discipline and hold fast to it. Then He said: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾, i.e., in the houses, ﴿then do not enter them﴾, because the reason in both cases is one: the possibility that there are hidden circumstances that the one entering would dislike to see. Then He said: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾. That is because just as entering may be disliked by the owner of the house, so too standing at the door may be disliked by him. Therefore it is more proper and purer for the visitor to return, to remove discomfort and harm. When Allah the Exalted mentioned the ruling on inhabited houses, He afterwards mentioned the ruling on houses that are not inhabited, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is [some] use for you﴾. That is because the barrier to entering without permission is removed from them. The exegetes differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿uninhabited houses﴾, according to several opinions:

The first, which is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, is that they are inns, lodging houses, shops of merchants, and places of benefit, such as shelter from heat and cold, lodging for travelers, goods, and buying and selling. It is narrated that Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has sent down to you a verse about seeking permission, and we travel for our trade and stay in these inns. Should we not enter them except with permission?" So this verse was revealed.

The second: that they are ruined houses in which one relieves oneself, and the benefit is relieving oneself.

The third: markets.

The fourth: bathhouses.

The better view is that it may be said that there is no impediment to all of these entering under the verse, so it is taken to cover all of them. The reason for this is that when they are as described, they are permitted for entry by custom. Similarly, we say that if they were uninhabited but were usurped property, then it would not be permissible for the one entering to enter them. But the apparent state of inns is that they are established for the entry of those who enter.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾, it is a warning to those who enter ruined houses and uninhabited houses of people of suspicion.

**[Page 170]**

The sixth ruling concerns seeking permission (*istiʼdhān*, asking leave to enter). His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants. That is best for you, that you may remember.﴾

﴿And if you find no one in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Return," then return; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

Know that He, Exalted, turned away from what relates to the accusation of adultery (*ramy*) and slander (*qadhf*), and the ruling pertaining to them, to what is fitting for this matter. This is because the people of the slander (*ahl al-ifk*) found their way to their calumny only through the opportunity of being alone together, so it became like a path of suspicion. Therefore Allah, Exalted, made it obligatory that a person not enter another's house except after seeking permission and greeting, because entering in a manner other than this leads to the occurrence of suspicion, and there is harm in that which is not hidden. So He said: ﴿That is because those who disbelieved...﴾ and so on. There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** *Istiʼnās* (familiarity) is an expression for the intimacy that arises from sitting together. He, Exalted, said: ﴿nor lingering for conversation﴾. This intimacy occurs only after entering and greeting, so it would have been better to place the greeting before the seeking of familiarity. Why, then, does the verse come in the reverse order? The answer to this has several aspects:

First: what is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is that it is actually *ḥattā tastaʾdhinū* ("until you seek permission"), and the scribe erred.

In the recitation of Ubayy: *ḥattā tastaʾdhinū lakum* ("until you seek permission for yourselves"). "And the greeting is better for you than the greeting of the Jāhiliyyah and the *dumūr*," which is entering without permission. Its derivation is from *ad-damār*, which is destruction, as if its doer is ruined (*dāmir*) because of the greatness of what he committed. In a hadith: "Whoever his eye precedes his seeking permission has been ruined (*damar*)." Know that this statement from Ibn ʿAbbās is open to scrutiny, because it implies criticism of the Qur'an which was transmitted by continuous transmission (*tawātur*), and it implies the authenticity of a Qur'an that was not transmitted by continuous transmission. Opening these two doors leads doubt to the whole Qur'an, and that it is false.

Second: what is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, that he said: there is an inversion (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*) in the speech, and the meaning is: "until you greet its occupants and seek familiarity," because the greeting precedes the familiarity. In the recitation of ʿAbd Allāh: *ḥattā tusallimū ʿalā ahlihā wa-tastaʾdhinū* ("until you greet its occupants and seek permission"). This also is weak, because it contradicts the apparent meaning.

Third: to let the speech stand on its apparent meaning. Then, regarding the explanation of *istiʼnās*, there are several views:

The first: "until you seek familiarity through permission," because when they seek permission and greet, the people of the house become at ease; but if they entered without permission, they would be startled and it would be distressing for them.

The second: explaining *istiʼnās* as seeking information and discovering: it is an *istifʻāl* form from *ānasa al-shayʾ*, when one sees a thing clearly and openly. The meaning is: "until you seek information and discover the situation, whether your entry is wanted." From this is their saying: *istaʾnis, hal tarā aḥadan* ("seek familiarity, do you see anyone?"), and *istaʾnastu fa-lam ara aḥadan* ("I sought familiarity and did not see anyone"), meaning I sought knowledge and information. If someone says: when it is understood as familiarity, the greeting should precede it, as it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" We say: the one seeking permission may not know whether anyone is in the house, so there is no sense in his greeting in this state.

The closer view is that by seeking permission he finds out whether there is anyone who will grant permission; when permission is granted and he enters, he becomes face to face with them, and then he greets them.

The third: that the derivation of *istiʼnās* is from *ins* (humankind), meaning that one ascertains whether there is a human being there. There is no doubt that this precedes the greeting.

The fourth: even if we concede that familiarity occurs only after the greeting, the *wāw* (and) does not necessarily imply sequence. Thus placing the familiarity before the greeting in the wording does not necessarily require placing it before in action.

* * *

**The second question:** What is the ruling on making the seeking of permission obligatory before entry? The answer: that wisdom is what Allah, Exalted, drew attention to in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses.﴾ By this it is indicated that the reason for which entry is prohibited except under this condition is that the houses are inhabited, because whoever rushes into them without seeking permission cannot be sure that he will not come upon what it is not lawful for him to look at of the private parts (*ʿawrah*), or upon what the people do not wish others to know of their circumstances. This is among the "causes" (*ʿilal*) indicated by the text. Also, it is a disposal over another's property, so it must be with his consent, otherwise it resembles usurpation (*ghaṣb*).

* * *

**The third question:** How is seeking permission to be done? The answer: "A man sought permission from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: *Aʾalij?* (May I enter?). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a woman called Rawḍah: 'Get up, go to this man and teach him, for he does not know how to seek permission properly. Say to him: Peace be upon you, may I enter?' The man heard it and said it. He said: 'Enter.' He entered and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about several things, and he answered. The man said: 'Is there in knowledge what you do not know?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'He has given me much good, and indeed there is in knowledge what no one knows except Allah,' and he recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ to the end."

The people of the Jāhiliyyah used to say, when a man entered a house other than his own: "Good morning to you, good evening to you," then he would enter, and it might happen that the man found himself with his wife under one covering. So Allah, Exalted, turned away from that and taught what is better and more beautiful. It is related from Mujāhid that *ḥattā tastaʾnisū* ("until you seek familiarity") means clearing the throat (*tanaḥnuh*). ʿIkrimah said it means glorifying Allah (*tasbīḥ*) and magnifying Him (*takbīr*), or the like.

* * *

**The fourth question:** How many times is permission to be sought? The answer: Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seeking permission is three times: at the first, they are to be silent; at the second, they are to prepare; at the third, they grant permission or refuse." And from Jundub, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "If one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted permission, let him return." And from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, he said: "I was sitting in one of the gatherings of the Anṣār when Abū Mūsā came in, frightened. We said to him: 'What has frightened you?' He said: 'ʿUmar commanded me to come to him, so I came to him and sought permission three times, but I was not granted permission, so I returned.' He (ʿUmar) said: 'What prevented you from coming to me?' I said: 'I came and sought permission three times, but I was not granted permission, and the Prophet (ﷺ) has said: "If one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted permission, let him return."' He said: 'You must bring me evidence for this, or I will punish you.' Ubayy said: 'None will stand with you except the youngest of the people.' Abū Saʿīd stood up and bore witness for him." In some reports, ʿUmar said to Abū Mūsā: "I did not suspect you, but I feared that people might attribute false things to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

And from Qatādah: seeking permission is three times: the first, so that the living hears; the second, so that they may prepare; the third, if they wish they grant permission, and if they wish they refuse. Know that this is among the excellent manners, because at the first time, some occupations may prevent them from granting permission; at the second time, there may be something that prevents or requires refusal or equality; when he is not answered at the third time, he infers from the absence of permission that there is a firm barrier, and that may create dislike of his being near the door, so for this reason it is recommended for him to return.

For this reason they say: it is obligatory in seeking permission three times that it not be continuous; rather there must be an interval of time between each and the next. As for knocking on the door violently and shouting at the owner of the house, that is forbidden, because it involves harm and causing unease. The story of the Banū Asad is sufficient as a deterrent, and what was revealed concerning it, the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers—most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 4].

* * *

**The fifth question:** How is one to stand at the door? The answer: It is related that "Abū Saʿīd sought permission from the Messenger (ﷺ) while he was facing the door, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do not seek permission while you are facing the door.'"

And it is related that "when he (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left side, and he would say: 'Peace be upon you.'" This was because the houses at that time did not have curtains (*sutūr*).

* * *

**The sixth question:** The word *ḥattā* ("until") indicates a limit (*ghāyah*), and the ruling after the limit is different from what precedes it. So His saying: ﴿do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity﴾ implies the permissibility of entering after seeking permission, even if the owner of the house has not given permission. What do you say about this? The answer has several aspects:

First: Allah, Exalted, made the limit *istiʼnās* (familiarity), not *istiʼdhān* (seeking permission), and familiarity does not occur except when permission is granted after seeking it.

Second: since we know from the text that the wisdom behind seeking permission is that a person should not enter upon another without his permission, for that is something that displeases him, and we know that this purpose is not achieved except after permission is granted, we know that seeking permission that is not followed by permission must not be sufficient.

This report indicates two meanings:

The third: markets.

The fourth: bathhouses.

The better view is that it may be said that there is no impediment to all of these entering under the verse, so it is taken to cover all of them. The reason for this is that when they are as described, they are permitted for entry by custom. Similarly, we say that if they were uninhabited but were usurped property, then it would not be permissible for the one entering to enter them. But the apparent state of inns is that they are established for the entry of those who enter.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾, it is a warning to those who enter ruined houses and uninhabited houses of people of suspicion.

**[Page 170]**

The sixth ruling concerns seeking permission (*istiʼdhān*, asking leave to enter). His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants. That is best for you, that you may remember.﴾

﴿And if you find no one in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, "Return," then return; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

Know that He, Exalted, turned away from what relates to the accusation of adultery (*ramy*) and slander (*qadhf*), and the ruling pertaining to them, to what is fitting for this matter. This is because the people of the slander (*ahl al-ifk*) found their way to their calumny only through the opportunity of being alone together, so it became like a path of suspicion. Therefore Allah, Exalted, made it obligatory that a person not enter another's house except after seeking permission and greeting, because entering in a manner other than this leads to the occurrence of suspicion, and there is harm in that which is not hidden. So He said: ﴿That is because those who disbelieved...﴾ and so on. There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** *Istiʼnās* (familiarity) is an expression for the intimacy that arises from sitting together. He, Exalted, said: ﴿nor lingering for conversation﴾. This intimacy occurs only after entering and greeting, so it would have been better to place the greeting before the seeking of familiarity. Why, then, does the verse come in the reverse order? The answer to this has several aspects:

First: what is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is that it is actually *ḥattā tastaʾdhinū* ("until you seek permission"), and the scribe erred.

In the recitation of Ubayy: *ḥattā tastaʾdhinū lakum* ("until you seek permission for yourselves"). "And the greeting is better for you than the greeting of the Jāhiliyyah and the *dumūr*," which is entering without permission. Its derivation is from *ad-damār*, which is destruction, as if its doer is ruined (*dāmir*) because of the greatness of what he committed. In a hadith: "Whoever his eye precedes his seeking permission has been ruined (*damar*)." Know that this statement from Ibn ʿAbbās is open to scrutiny, because it implies criticism of the Qur'an which was transmitted by continuous transmission (*tawātur*), and it implies the authenticity of a Qur'an that was not transmitted by continuous transmission. Opening these two doors leads doubt to the whole Qur'an, and that it is false.

Second: what is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, that he said: there is an inversion (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*) in the speech, and the meaning is: "until you greet its occupants and seek familiarity," because the greeting precedes the familiarity. In the recitation of ʿAbd Allāh: *ḥattā tusallimū ʿalā ahlihā wa-tastaʾdhinū* ("until you greet its occupants and seek permission"). This also is weak, because it contradicts the apparent meaning.

Third: to let the speech stand on its apparent meaning. Then, regarding the explanation of *istiʼnās*, there are several views:

The first: "until you seek familiarity through permission," because when they seek permission and greet, the people of the house become at ease; but if they entered without permission, they would be startled and it would be distressing for them.

The second: explaining *istiʼnās* as seeking information and discovering: it is an *istifʻāl* form from *ānasa al-shayʾ*, when one sees a thing clearly and openly. The meaning is: "until you seek information and discover the situation, whether your entry is wanted." From this is their saying: *istaʾnis, hal tarā aḥadan* ("seek familiarity, do you see anyone?"), and *istaʾnastu fa-lam ara aḥadan* ("I sought familiarity and did not see anyone"), meaning I sought knowledge and information. If someone says: when it is understood as familiarity, the greeting should precede it, as it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" We say: the one seeking permission may not know whether anyone is in the house, so there is no sense in his greeting in this state.

The closer view is that by seeking permission he finds out whether there is anyone who will grant permission; when permission is granted and he enters, he becomes face to face with them, and then he greets them.

The third: that the derivation of *istiʼnās* is from *ins* (humankind), meaning that one ascertains whether there is a human being there. There is no doubt that this precedes the greeting.

The fourth: even if we concede that familiarity occurs only after the greeting, the *wāw* (and) does not necessarily imply sequence. Thus placing the familiarity before the greeting in the wording does not necessarily require placing it before in action.

* * *

**The second question:** What is the ruling on making the seeking of permission obligatory before entry? The answer: that wisdom is what Allah, Exalted, drew attention to in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses.﴾ By this it is indicated that the reason for which entry is prohibited except under this condition is that the houses are inhabited, because whoever rushes into them without seeking permission cannot be sure that he will not come upon what it is not lawful for him to look at of the private parts (*ʿawrah*), or upon what the people do not wish others to know of their circumstances. This is among the "causes" (*ʿilal*) indicated by the text. Also, it is a disposal over another's property, so it must be with his consent, otherwise it resembles usurpation (*ghaṣb*).

* * *

**The third question:** How is seeking permission to be done? The answer: "A man sought permission from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: *Aʾalij?* (May I enter?). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a woman called Rawḍah: 'Get up, go to this man and teach him, for he does not know how to seek permission properly. Say to him: Peace be upon you, may I enter?' The man heard it and said it. He said: 'Enter.' He entered and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about several things, and he answered. The man said: 'Is there in knowledge what you do not know?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'He has given me much good, and indeed there is in knowledge what no one knows except Allah,' and he recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ to the end."

The people of the Jāhiliyyah used to say, when a man entered a house other than his own: "Good morning to you, good evening to you," then he would enter, and it might happen that the man found himself with his wife under one covering. So Allah, Exalted, turned away from that and taught what is better and more beautiful. It is related from Mujāhid that *ḥattā tastaʾnisū* ("until you seek familiarity") means clearing the throat (*tanaḥnuh*). ʿIkrimah said it means glorifying Allah (*tasbīḥ*) and magnifying Him (*takbīr*), or the like.

* * *

**The fourth question:** How many times is permission to be sought? The answer: Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seeking permission is three times: at the first, they are to be silent; at the second, they are to prepare; at the third, they grant permission or refuse." And from Jundub, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "If one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted permission, let him return." And from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, he said: "I was sitting in one of the gatherings of the Anṣār when Abū Mūsā came in, frightened. We said to him: 'What has frightened you?' He said: 'ʿUmar commanded me to come to him, so I came to him and sought permission three times, but I was not granted permission, so I returned.' He (ʿUmar) said: 'What prevented you from coming to me?' I said: 'I came and sought permission three times, but I was not granted permission, and the Prophet (ﷺ) has said: "If one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted permission, let him return."' He said: 'You must bring me evidence for this, or I will punish you.' Ubayy said: 'None will stand with you except the youngest of the people.' Abū Saʿīd stood up and bore witness for him." In some reports, ʿUmar said to Abū Mūsā: "I did not suspect you, but I feared that people might attribute false things to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

And from Qatādah: seeking permission is three times: the first, so that the living hears; the second, so that they may prepare; the third, if they wish they grant permission, and if they wish they refuse. Know that this is among the excellent manners, because at the first time, some occupations may prevent them from granting permission; at the second time, there may be something that prevents or requires refusal or equality; when he is not answered at the third time, he infers from the absence of permission that there is a firm barrier, and that may create dislike of his being near the door, so for this reason it is recommended for him to return.

For this reason they say: it is obligatory in seeking permission three times that it not be continuous; rather there must be an interval of time between each and the next. As for knocking on the door violently and shouting at the owner of the house, that is forbidden, because it involves harm and causing unease. The story of the Banū Asad is sufficient as a deterrent, and what was revealed concerning it, the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers—most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 4].

* * *

**The fifth question:** How is one to stand at the door? The answer: It is related that "Abū Saʿīd sought permission from the Messenger (ﷺ) while he was facing the door, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do not seek permission while you are facing the door.'"

And it is related that "when he (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left side, and he would say: 'Peace be upon you.'" This was because the houses at that time did not have curtains (*sutūr*).

* * *

**The sixth question:** The word *ḥattā* ("until") indicates a limit (*ghāyah*), and the ruling after the limit is different from what precedes it. So His saying: ﴿do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity﴾ implies the permissibility of entering after seeking permission, even if the owner of the house has not given permission. What do you say about this? The answer has several aspects:

First: Allah, Exalted, made the limit *istiʼnās* (familiarity), not *istiʼdhān* (seeking permission), and familiarity does not occur except when permission is granted after seeking it.

Second: since we know from the text that the wisdom behind seeking permission is that a person should not enter upon another without his permission, for that is something that displeases him, and we know that this purpose is not achieved except after permission is granted, we know that seeking permission that is not followed by permission must not be sufficient.

Third: the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And if you find no one in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾ prohibits entry except with permission. This indicates that permission is conditional upon the permissibility of entry in the first verse. If it is said: once it is established that permission is necessary, can something else take its place or not? We say: Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man's messenger to a man is his permission." And from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "If one of you is invited and comes with the messenger, that is permission for him." This report indicates two meanings:

**[Page 173]**

One of them: that permission is implied in His saying: ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾, and this is what is meant by it.

The second: that the invitation is permission when one comes with the messenger, and that he does not need a second seeking of permission. Some of them said: whoever has the customary permission to enter does not need to seek permission.

* * *

**The seventh question:** What is the ruling on one who looks into another's house without his permission? The answer: Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: if his eye is gouged out, it is wasted (*hadar*, unrecompensed), and he relied on what Sahl ibn Saʿd narrated, he said: "A man looked into one of the rooms of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he had a comb with which he was scratching his head. He (ﷺ) said: 'If I had known you were looking at me, I would have stabbed you in the eye with it. Permission is only required before looking.'" And Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever looks into the house of a people without their permission, and they gouge out his eye, his eye is wasted (*hadarat*)."

Abū Bakr al-Rāzī said: this report is rejected because it contradicts the established principles of analogy, for there is no disagreement that if someone enters another's house without permission and the owner gouges out his eye, the owner is liable, and there is retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) if he did it intentionally, and compensation (*arsh*) if he did it by mistake. It is well known that the one who entered looked and exceeded looking, so the apparent meaning of the hadith contradicts what there is consensus upon. If it is authentic, its meaning is: whoever looks into the house of a people and looks at their sacred space (*ḥaram*) and their women, and is prevented but does not desist, and his eye is lost during the resistance, then it is wasted.

But if there was only looking, and there was no resistance or prohibition in it, and then someone came and gouged out his eye, this person is a wrongdoer and is bound by the ruling of his offence, based on the apparent meaning of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45], to His saying: ﴿and wounds in retaliation﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 45]. Know that relying on the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ in this matter is weak, because we have agreed that this text is conditional upon the eye not being forfeit; for if the eye were forfeit, retaliation would not be due. So why do you say that whoever looks into a person's house, his eye is not forfeit? And this is the beginning of the question.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 27–29 (part 2 of 2):

As for his saying: if he entered, it would not be permissible to gouge out his eye; so likewise if he looked. We say: the difference between the two matters is clear, because if he enters, the people know of his entrance upon them, so they guard against him and conceal themselves. But if he looks, they may not know of it, and so he gains knowledge of what it is not permissible to witness. Therefore, it is not far-fetched in the ruling of the Shari'ah to be emphatic in the prohibition here, to close the door to this harm. In sum, rejecting the Hadith (a report of the Prophet's sayings and actions) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding this amount of speech is not permissible.

* * *

The eighth question: Since you have explained that permission is necessary, does any permission suffice, whatever its form, or must it be a specific permission? The answer: the apparent meaning of the verse requires accepting permission in general, whether the one giving permission is a child, a woman, a slave, or a non-Muslim dhimmi. For this permission, the qualifications of testimony are not required. Likewise is the acceptance of the reports of these people regarding gifts and similar matters.

* * *

The ninth question: Is seeking permission required when entering upon mahram relatives? The answer: Yes. It is related from Ata ibn Yasar: "A man asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying: 'Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister?' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Yes. Would you like to see her naked?'" A man asked Hudhayfa: "Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister?" He said: "If you do not seek permission to enter upon her, you will see what will distress you." Ata said: I asked Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister, and upon one whom I spend on?" He said: "Yes. Indeed Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission as those before them sought permission﴾ [al-Nur: 59]." He did not distinguish between one who is a stranger and one who is a mahram relative.

Know that abandoning seeking permission from mahram relatives, although it is not permissible, is lighter, because looking at her hair, chest, leg, and similar parts of the body is permissible. The verification in this matter is that if the prohibition against entering upon others is because those others may be uncovered, then this includes everyone except wives and those whom the right hand possesses. If it is because they may be occupied with a matter they dislike others seeing, then it must apply to all, so that one may not enter upon a wife or a female slave except with permission.

* * *

The tenth question: If a matter arises in a house, such as a fire, the intrusion of a thief, or the appearance of something reprehensible, is seeking permission obligatory? The answer: All of that is excepted by evidence. This is the sum of the discussion on seeking permission. As for greeting (salam), it is from the Sunnah of the Muslims, which they were commanded to follow. It is a safety for the people, it is the greeting of the people of Paradise, it brings about affection, and it removes resentment and rancor. It is related from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah the Exalted created Adam, peace be upon him, and breathed the spirit into him, he sneezed, and said: 'All praise is for Allah.' So he praised Allah with Allah's permission. His Lord said to him: 'May your Lord have mercy upon you, O Adam. Go to those angels, who are a group sitting there, and say: Peace be upon you.' When he did that, they replied, and he returned to his Lord, who said: 'This is your greeting and the greeting of your offspring.'"

And it is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The rights of a Muslim over a Muslim are six: he greets him when he meets him, he answers him when he invites him, he advises him sincerely in his absence, he blesses him when he sneezes, he visits him when he is ill, and he attends his funeral when he dies."

And it is related from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If it pleases you that the rancor be removed from your hearts, then spread the greeting of peace among you."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is better for you﴾, its meaning is clear: it means that doing this is better and more fitting for you than entering without permission. ﴿So that you may remember﴾, i.e., so that you may remember this discipline and hold fast to it. Then He said: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾, i.e., in the houses, ﴿then do not enter them﴾, because the reason in both cases is one: the possibility that there are hidden circumstances that the one entering would dislike to see. Then He said: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾. That is because just as entering may be disliked by the owner of the house, so too standing at the door may be disliked by him. Therefore it is more proper and purer for the visitor to return, to remove discomfort and harm. When Allah the Exalted mentioned the ruling on inhabited houses, He afterwards mentioned the ruling on houses that are not inhabited, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is [some] use for you﴾. That is because the barrier to entering without permission is removed from them. The exegetes differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿uninhabited houses﴾, according to several opinions:

The first, which is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, is that they are inns, lodging houses, shops of merchants, and places of benefit, such as shelter from heat and cold, lodging for travelers, goods, and buying and selling. It is narrated that Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has sent down to you a verse about seeking permission, and we travel for our trade and stay in these inns. Should we not enter them except with permission?" So this verse was revealed.

The second: that they are ruined houses in which one relieves oneself, and the benefit is relieving oneself.

The third: markets.

The fourth: bathhouses.

The better view is that it may be said that there is no impediment to all of these entering under the verse, so it is taken to cover all of them. The reason for this is that when they are as described, they are permitted for entry by custom. Similarly, we say that if they were uninhabited but were usurped property, then it would not be permissible for the one entering to enter them. But the apparent state of inns is that they are established for the entry of those who enter.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾, it is a warning to those who enter ruined houses and uninhabited houses of people of suspicion.

[Page 176]

**The seventh ruling (ḥukm): the ruling on looking (al-naẓar).** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do.﴾ ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what appears of it, and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, what their right hands possess, male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private matters. And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they hide of their adornment. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you may be successful.﴾

Know that He said: ﴿Say to the believing men﴾. He singled them out for this because others are not obliged to lower their gaze from what is not lawful for them, nor to guard their private parts from what is not lawful for them. These rulings are like branches (furūʿ) of Islam, and the believers are commanded to observe them from the outset, whereas the disbelievers are first commanded to accept that upon which these rulings depend. Although their situation is like that of the believers in deserving punishment for abandoning them, the believer is able to perform this obedience without a preliminary step, while the disbeliever is not able to do so except by first taking the preliminary step of those who came before him. This does not prevent the obligations (takālīf) from applying to him.

Know that He, glorified is He, commanded men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and He commanded women with the same as He commanded men, and added for them that they should not display their adornment except to specific groups of people.

As for His saying ﴿they should lower their gaze﴾, there are issues (masāʾil) concerning it:

**The first issue:** Most scholars said that the particle *min* (from) here is partitive (lit-tabʿīḍ), and that the meaning is lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and limiting oneself to what is permitted. Al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) permitted that it be superfluous (zāʾida), and its parallel is His saying: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 85], and ﴿Among you there is none who could hold him back from it﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 47]. Sībawayh rejected this. If it is asked: why was it included with lowering the gaze but not with guarding the private parts? We say: it indicates that the matter of looking is broader. Do you not see that there is no harm in looking at the hair and chests of mahram women, and likewise at slave-girls who are being displayed?

As for the matter of the private parts, it is restricted. It suffices as a distinction that looking is permitted except for what is excluded from it, while sexual intercourse is prohibited except for what is excluded from it. Some said: ﴿they should lower their gaze from their sight﴾ means they should reduce their looking. So when the eye is not enabled to perform its function, it is lowered and prevented from it. On this view, *min* is neither superfluous nor partitive, but belongs to the verb *ghaḍḍ* (lowering). It is said: "I lowered [my regard] from so-and-so," when I diminished his worth.

[Page 177 — continued in the margin]

**The second issue:** Know that the parts of the body that must be covered (ʿawrāt) fall into four categories: the ʿawra of a man with a man, the ʿawra of a woman with a woman, the ʿawra of a woman with a man, and the ʿawra of a man with a woman.

As for a man with a man: he may look at the whole of another man's body except his ʿawra, and the ʿawra is what lies between the navel and the knee. The navel and the knee are not ʿawra. According to Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah have mercy on him), the knee is ʿawra. Mālik said the thigh is not ʿawra. The evidence that it is ʿawra is what is narrated from Ḥudhayfa: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him in the mosque while he had his thigh uncovered, and he (peace be upon him) said: 'Cover your thigh, for it is part of the ʿawra.'" And he said to ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): "Do not expose your thigh, and do not look at the thigh of a living or dead person."

If his looking at the face or the rest of the body is with desire, or with fear of temptation (fitna), such as when the person is a beardless youth (amrad), then looking at him is not permitted. A man may not lie beside a man, even if each of them is on a separate side of the bed, because of what Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narrated: that he (peace be upon him) said: "A man should not lie with a man under one garment, and a woman should not lie with a woman under one garment."

Embracing and kissing the face are disliked, except that a father may kiss his child out of affection. Shaking hands is recommended, because of what Anas narrated: a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, when one of us meets his brother or friend, should he bow to him?" He said, "No." He asked, "Should he embrace him and kiss him?" He said, "No." He asked, "Should he take his hand and shake it?" He said, "Yes."

As for the ʿawra of a woman with a woman, it is like the ʿawra of a man with a man. She may look at the whole of another woman's body except what lies between the navel and the knee. If there is fear of temptation, it is not permitted. Lying together is also not permitted.

As for whether a dhimmī woman may look at the body of a Muslim woman: it has been said that she may, like a Muslim woman with a Muslim woman. The more correct view is that she may not, because she is a stranger in religion, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿or their women﴾, and a dhimmī woman is not of "our women."

As for the ʿawra of a woman with a man: the woman is either a stranger (ajnabiyya), or a woman related by blood who is forbidden to marry (dhāt raḥim maḥram), or a woman he may enjoy (mustamtaʿa, i.e. his wife or concubine). If she is a stranger, she is either free or a slave-girl (amma). If she is free, her whole body is ʿawra, and he may not look at any part of her except the face and the two palms. This is because she needs to reveal her face in buying and selling, and to extend her palm for giving and receiving. By "palm" we mean its back and front up to the wrists (al-kūʿayn). It has been said that the back of the palm is ʿawra.

Know that we have mentioned that looking at any part of her body is not permitted, and looking at her face and palm is permitted, and each of these two statements contains an exception. As for the statement that looking at her face and palm is permitted, know that it falls into three categories: either there is neither purpose nor temptation in it, or there is temptation without purpose, or there is both temptation and purpose.

As for the first category: know that it is not permitted to deliberately look at the face of a stranger without a purpose. If his gaze falls on her unexpectedly, he should lower his gaze, because of His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾. It has been said that it is permitted once, if it is not a place of temptation, and Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah have mercy on him) said this. It is not permitted to repeat the look at her, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of these will be questioned﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 36], and because of His saying (peace be upon him): "O ʿAlī, do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours, but the second is not yours." And from Jābir, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away." Also, because it is generally not possible to avoid the first glance, so it is excused whether one intended it or not.

[Page 178 — no, continuing at page 177]

As for the second category, where there is a purpose but no temptation, there are several cases:

First: a man wishing to marry a woman may look at her face and palms. Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: "A man wished to marry a woman from the Anṣār, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Look at her, for there is something in the eyes of the Anṣār.'" He (peace be upon him) also said: "When one of you proposes to a woman, there is no blame on him for looking at her, provided that he looks at her only for the proposal." Al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba said: "I proposed to a woman, and he (peace be upon him) said: 'Did you look at her?' I said, 'No.' He said: 'Look at her, for it is more likely to make lasting harmony between you two.'"

All of this indicates the permissibility of looking at her face and palms, even out of desire, when he intends to marry her. This is also indicated by His saying: ﴿Women are no longer lawful to you, nor is it lawful for you to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 52]. Their beauty would not please him except after seeing their faces.

Second: when he wishes to buy a slave-girl, he may look at what is not ʿawra in her.

Third: at the time of a transaction, he may look at her face attentively, until he can recognize her when he needs to.

Fourth: he may look at her when bearing witness, and he should not look at anything other than the face, because recognition is achieved through it.

As for the third category, where he looks at her out of desire, this is forbidden. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The two eyes commit adultery." And from Jābir, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away."

It has been said: it is written in the Torah, "A glance plants desire in the heart, and many a desire has bequeathed long sorrow."

As for the second statement, that it is not permitted for a stranger man to look at the body of a stranger woman, jurists have made exceptions to it, in several cases:

First: it is permitted for a trustworthy physician to look at her for treatment, just as it is permitted for a circumciser to look at the private part of the one being circumcised, because it is a place of necessity.

Second: it is permitted to deliberately look at the private parts of adulterers in order to bear witness to adultery. Likewise, one may look at a woman's private part in order to bear witness to a birth, and at a nursing woman's breast in order to bear witness to a suckling. Abū Saʿīd al-Iṣṭakhrī said: it is not permitted for a man to intend to look in these places, because concealing adultery is recommended, and in matters of birth and suckling, the testimony of women is accepted, so there is no need for men to look for the sake of testimony.

Third: if she falls into drowning or fire, he may look at her body in order to rescue her.

As for when the stranger woman is a slave-girl: some said her ʿawra is what lies between the navel and the knee. Others said her ʿawra is what is not revealed during work (al-mihna). From this it follows that her head, forearms, shins, neck, and chest are not ʿawra. The disagreement mentioned applies to her back, belly, and what is above her forearms. It is not permitted to touch her, nor for her to touch him, in any circumstance, not for cupping, nor for applying kohl, nor for anything else, because touching is stronger than looking, as evidenced by the fact that ejaculation caused by touch breaks the fast of a fasting person, whereas looking does not break it.

Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah have mercy on him) said: it is permitted to touch from a slave-girl whatever it is permitted to look at. As for a woman who is a mahram to him by blood, fostering, or marriage affinity (ṣihr), her ʿawra with him is what lies between the navel and the knee, like the ʿawra of a man. Others said: rather, her ʿawra is what is not exposed during work, and this is also the view of Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah have mercy on him). As for the remaining details, they will come, if Allah wills, in the explanation of the verse.

As for when the woman is one he may enjoy, such as a wife or a slave-girl with whom he is permitted to have intercourse, then he may look at her whole body, even at her private part. However, it is disliked for him to look at her private part, and likewise at his own private part, because it is related that it causes the erasure (ṭamas) of the memory. It has been said that it is not permitted to look at her private part. There is no difference whether the slave-girl is a pure slave (qinna), or a mudabbara (one whose master has promised freedom upon his death), or an umm walad (one who has borne her master's child), or a pledged slave (marhūna).

If she is a Magian, an apostate, an idolatress, or jointly owned between him and another, or married, or a mukātaba (one who has contracted to purchase her freedom), then she is like a stranger. ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When one of you marries off his slave-girl to his slave or his hired man, then he should not look at what lies below the navel and above the knee."

As for the ʿawra of a man with a woman: if she is a stranger to him, then his ʿawra with her is what lies between the navel and the knee. It has been said that his whole body except the face and the two palms is ʿawra with her, as hers is with him. The first view is more correct, unlike the woman's position with respect to a man, because the woman's body is itself ʿawra, as evidenced by the fact that her prayer is not valid if her body is uncovered, whereas a man's body is not like this. It is not permitted for her to deliberately look (at a man) where there is fear of temptation, nor to repeat the look at his face, because of what is narrated from Umm Salama: "She was with the Prophet (ﷺ) and Maymūna when Ibn Umm Maktūm came and entered upon them. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Veil yourselves from him.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is he not blind, so he cannot see us?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Are you two blind? Do you not see him?'"

If he is a mahram of hers, then her nakedness in front of him is from the navel to the knee. If he is her husband or her master, the one whose intercourse with her is lawful, then she may look at his whole body, except that looking at his private part is disliked, as is the case with her looking at her own (the husband's) private part. A man may not sit naked in an empty house when he has something with which to cover his nakedness, because it has been narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was asked about this and said: "Allah has more right that one should be shy before Him." It is also narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Beware of going naked, for with you are those who never leave you except at the time of relieving oneself and when a man is with his spouse." And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Al-Shibli was asked about His saying: ﴿They should lower their gaze﴾, and he said: the gaze of the heads is lowered from what is forbidden, and the gaze of the hearts is lowered from everything other than Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and guard their private parts﴾, what is meant is guarding them from what is not lawful. Abu al-'Aliyah said: Everything in the Qur'an of the form "﴿and guard their private parts﴾" or "and let them guard their private parts" refers to fornication, except the one in Surat al-Nur: ﴿from their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, which means that no one should look at them. This is weak, because it is a specification without evidence.

What the apparent meaning requires is that the sense is guarding them from everything Allah has forbidden regarding them: fornication, touching, and looking. Moreover, if the intended meaning were the prohibition of looking, then touching and intercourse are also intended by the verse, since they are more severe than looking. So if Allah had explicitly mentioned looking, the implication of the discourse would still require the prohibition of intercourse and touching, just as His saying: ﴿So do not say to them "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra' 23] requires the prohibition of what is beyond that, such as insulting and striking.

As for His saying: ﴿That is purer for them﴾ [al-Nur: 30], meaning that their adherence to this is purer and more pure for them, because it is among the things by which they are purified and deserve praise and commendation. It may be said that He, exalted is He, specified the believers in the address because of His wish to purify them by it, and this does not befit the disbeliever.

As for His saying: ﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, the discussion of it is as previously mentioned. If it is asked, why was lowering the gaze mentioned before guarding the private parts? We say: because looking is the messenger of fornication and the lure of debauchery, and the trial in it is more severe and more frequent, and one can hardly guard against it.

As for His saying: ﴿And they should not display their adornment except what appears of it﴾, this is among the rulings that pertain mostly to women. We said "mostly" because it is forbidden for a man to display his adornment, whether jewelry, clothing, or otherwise, to non-marriageable women, because of the temptation in it. Here are some issues:

Page 179

The first issue: They differed about what is meant by ﴿their adornment﴾. Know that "adornment" (zinah) is a term that applies both to the beauties of creation which Allah created and to everything a person adorns himself with, such as fine clothing, jewelry, and other things. Some denied that the term "adornment" applies to natural creation, because one hardly says of natural creation that it is part of a woman's adornment; rather, that is said of what she acquires, such as kohl, dye, and the like. The closer view is that natural creation is included in adornment, and two things indicate this:

The first: that many women are distinguished by their natural form from everything else that is considered adornment; so if we take it to mean natural creation, we give the generality its due, and the inclusion of other things in it is not thereby excluded.

The second: His saying: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾ indicates that what is meant by adornment is what covers both natural form and other things; it is as if He, exalted is He, forbade them from displaying the beauties of their natural form by requiring that they be covered with a veil. As for those who said that adornment means what is other than natural creation, they restricted it to three things:

One: cosmetics, such as kohl, dye with wasma on her eyebrows, ghamra on her cheeks, and henna on her palms and feet.

Second: jewelry, such as rings, bracelets, anklets, armlets, necklaces, crowns, sashes, and earrings.

Third: garments. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], and He meant garments.

* * *

The second issue: They differed about what is meant by His saying: ﴿except what appears of it﴾. As for those who understood adornment as natural creation, al-Qaffal said the meaning of the verse is: except what a person customarily displays. For women, this is the face and the palms; for men, it is the extremities of the face, the hands, and the feet. So they were commanded to cover what necessity does not require to be uncovered, and were permitted to uncover what is customarily uncovered and what necessity requires to be shown, since the laws of Islam are upright, easy, and tolerant. Since the appearance of the face and the palms is almost necessary, they agreed that these are not 'awrah. As for the foot, its display is not necessary, so they differed over whether it is part of the 'awrah or not, and there are two views:

The more correct view is that it is 'awrah, like the top of the foot. As for her voice, there are two views, the more correct of which is that it is not 'awrah, because the wives of the Prophet ﷺ used to narrate hadiths to men.
