So humanity, insofar as it is humanity, is something different from these individualized particulars. Thus we have intellected the universal quiddity. As for perception of universals being more noble: perception of universals cannot change, while perception of particulars must change; and because perception of the universal includes perception of the particulars under it, since what is established for the quiddity is established for all its instances, though not conversely. Thus it is established that intellectual perception is more noble.

The third: sensory perception is not productive, while intellectual perception is productive, so the intellect must be more noble. As for sensory perception not being productive: whoever senses something, that sensing is not a cause for another sensing of his. Rather, if he uses the sense again, he will sense it again, but that is not the producing of one sensation by another. As for intellectual perception being productive: when we intellect things and then combine them in our minds, through their combination we attain the acquisition of other sciences, and so on with every intellection obtained, for it is possible to use it to attain another intellection, ad infinitum. Thus it is established that intellectual perception is more noble.

The fourth: sensory perception does not contain many things, while intellectual perception does contain them, so intellectual perception must be more noble. As for sensory perception not containing many things: when many colors succeed one another upon the eye, it is unable to distinguish them, and it perceives a color as if it resulted from the mixture of those colors; and when many words succeed one another upon the hearing, those words become confused and no distinction is achieved. As for intellectual perception containing many things: whoever has acquired more sciences is more able to acquire new ones with ease, and conversely; and this entails the judgment that intellectual perception is more noble.

The fifth: when the sensory faculty perceives strong sensibles, at that time it is unable to perceive weak ones, for whoever hears a loud sound cannot, in that state, hear a faint sound. But the intellectual faculty is not occupied by one intelligible from another intelligible.

[Page 197]

The sixth: the sensory faculties weaken after forty, and weaken with the abundance of thoughts which necessitate the soul's domination over the body, which necessitates the ruin of the body. The intellectual faculties grow stronger after forty and grow stronger with the abundance of thoughts that necessitate the ruin of the body. This indicates the independence of the intellectual faculty from these instruments, and the dependence of the sensory faculties upon them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 2 of 5):**

Seventh: The visual faculty (al-quwwa al-basira) does not perceive the seen object when it is very near, nor when it is very far. The intellective faculty (al-quwwa al-'aqliyya), by contrast, is not affected in its condition by nearness or distance. It ascends above the Throne and descends beneath the earth in less than a single moment. Indeed, it perceives the Essence of God and His attributes, although He is exalted above nearness, distance, and direction. Therefore the intellective faculty is more noble.

Eighth: The sensory faculty (al-quwwa al-hissiyya) perceives of things only their outward aspects. When it perceives a human being, in reality it has perceived only the outer surface of his body and the color present on that surface. By agreement, a human being is not merely a surface and a color. The visual faculty is therefore incapable of penetrating the interior. The intellective faculty, however, relates to the inner and outer aspects of things equally. It perceives the inner and outer aspects and penetrates into them and into their parts. Thus the intellective faculty is a light in relation to both the inner and the outer. The visual faculty is light in relation to the outer, but darkness in relation to the inner. Therefore the intellective faculty is more noble than the visual faculty.

Ninth: The object perceived by the intellective faculty is God Most High and all of its acts, whereas the object perceived by the visual faculty is colors and shapes. Therefore the ratio of the nobility of the intellective faculty to the nobility of the visual faculty must be like the ratio of the nobility of the Essence of God Most High to the nobility of colors and shapes.

Tenth: The intellective faculty perceives all existents, non-existents, and quiddities, which are the accidents of existents and non-existents. For this reason, the first of its wisdoms is that existence and non-existence cannot be combined nor can they be removed, and this is necessarily preceded by the conception of the meaning of existence and the meaning of non-existence. Thus, through these two conceptions, it has encompassed all matters in some respects. As for the visual faculty, it perceives only lights and colors, and these are among the basest accidents of bodies. Bodies are baser than the spiritual substances. Thus the object of the visual faculty is among the basest of existents. As for the object of the intellective faculty, it is all existents and non-existents. Therefore the intellective faculty is more noble.

* * *

Eleventh: The intellective faculty is able to unify the many and to multiply the one, whereas the visual faculty is not able to do so. As for the intellective faculty's ability to unify the many, this is because it joins the genus to the differentia, and from the two there arises one specific nature. As for its ability to multiply the one, this is because it takes the human being, who is one quiddity, and divides it into its concepts and its necessary accidents and its separable accidents. Then it divides its constituents into genus and genus of genus, differentia and differentia of differentia, genus of differentia and differentia of genus, and into the rest of the constituent parts which are not counted among genera or differentiae. Then it continues to carry out this division within each one of these categories until, from those compounds, it reaches the true simples. Then it considers, regarding the necessary accidents, whether those accidents are simple or compound and necessary through intermediaries or through an intermediary or without any intermediary. Thus the intellective faculty seems to have penetrated into the depths of quiddities, permeated them, distinguished each of their parts from its companion, and placed each of them in its suitable place. As for the visual faculty, it does not gain knowledge of the states of quiddities, but rather sees only one matter, and does not know what it is or how it is. Thus it became clear that the intellective faculty is more noble.

Twelfth: The intellective faculty is able to attain infinite perceptions, whereas the sensory faculty is not able to do so.

The demonstration of the first point is through several aspects:

The first: The intellective faculty can use present knowledge as a means to deduce unknown matters. Then it makes those conclusions premises for other conclusions without end. You have already learned that the sensory faculty is not capable of deduction at all.

The second: The intellective faculty is able to conceive the levels of numbers, and they have no end.

The third: The intellective faculty can conceive itself, and it can conceive that it has conceived, and so on without end.

The fourth: Relations and relatives are infinite, and they are intelligible, not sensible. Thus it became clear that the intellective faculty is more noble.

Thirteenth: By his intellective faculty, the human being shares with God Most High in the perception of realities, and by his sensory faculty he shares with the beasts. The ratio is significant, so the intellective faculty is more noble.

Fourteenth: The intellective faculty is independent, in its intellectual perception, of the existence of the intelligible object outside the mind. The sensory faculty, in its sensory perception, depends on the existence of the sensible object outside. The independent is more noble than the dependent.

Fifteenth: These external existents are contingent in their essences, and they are in need of an agent. The agent cannot bring them into being in the manner of perfection except after the prior occurrence of knowledge. Therefore, the existence of these things outside is subsequent to intellectual perception. As for sensing them, there is no doubt that it is subsequent to their existence outside. Therefore the sensing faculty is a follower of the follower of the intellective faculty.

Sixteenth: The intellective faculty does not need instruments in order to understand. The proof is that if a person's five senses were impaired, he would still understand that one is half of two, and that things equal to one and the same thing are equal to each other. The sensory faculty, however, needs many instruments, and the independent is more excellent than the dependent.

Seventeenth: Visual perception occurs only for a thing that is in directions. Furthermore, it does not move freely in all directions; rather, it reaches only what is opposite it or what is in the position of the opposite. By our saying "in the position of the opposite," we exclude four matters:

The first: An accident. It is not opposite, because it is not in a place, but it is in the position of the opposite by virtue of its subsisting in the body that is opposite.

The second: Seeing a face in a mirror. The ray emerges from the eye to the mirror, then returns from it to the face, so the face becomes visible. From this perspective, it is like being opposite to itself.

The third: A person seeing his own back when he places one of two mirrors facing his face and the other facing his back.

The fourth: Seeing what is not opposite because of the bending of the ray in moist bodies, as explained in the book of Optics (al-Manazir).

As for the intellective faculty, it is free of directions. It conceives direction, and direction is not in direction. For this reason it conceives that a thing is either in a direction or not in a direction. This division is not valid except after conceiving the meaning of our statement "it is not in a direction."

Eighteenth: The visual faculty is powerless when there is a barrier, whereas the intellective faculty is not blocked by anything at all. Therefore it is more noble.

[Page 199]

Nineteenth: The intellective faculty is like the ruler, and the sensory faculty is like the servant. The ruler is more noble than the servant, and the distinction between rulership and service is well known.

Twentieth: The visual faculty often errs greatly, for it may perceive a moving object as still and vice versa, as with someone sitting in a ship, who may perceive the moving ship as still and the still shore as moving. Were it not for the intellect, the error of sight could not be distinguished from its correctness. The intellect is the judge, and the senses are the judged. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that intellectual perception is more noble than visual perception. Each of the two perceptions entails manifestation, which is the most noble property of light. Therefore intellectual perception is more deserving of being called light than visual perception.

Once this is established, we say: These intellectual lights are of two kinds. The first is what necessarily occurs when conditions are sound, and these are the innate intellections (al-ta'aqqulat al-fitriyya). The second is what is acquired, and these are the speculative intellections (al-ta'aqqulat al-nazariyya).

As for the innate ones, they are not among the necessary properties of the human essence, because in childhood he was not knowing at all. These innate lights came into being after they were not, so they must have a cause. As for the speculative ones, it is known that the human innate disposition is often subject to deviation. Since this is the case, there must be a guiding guide, and there is no guide above the speech of God Most High or above the guidance of the prophets. Thus the status of the verses of the Qur'an for the eye of the intellect is like the status of the sunlight for the visual eye, since through it sight is completed. It is therefore fitting that the Qur'an be called light, just as sunlight is called light. The light of the Qur'an resembles the light of the sun, and the light of the intellect resembles the light of the eye. By this the meaning of His saying becomes clear: ﴿So believe in God and His Messenger and the light which We have sent down﴾ [al-Taghabun: 8], and His saying: ﴿There has come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾ [al-Nisa': 174] and ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174].

Once it is established that the explanation of the Messenger is stronger than the light of the sun, it follows that his holy soul must be greater in luminosity than the sun. Just as the sun in the world of bodies gives light to others and does not receive light from others, so the soul of the Prophet (ﷺ) gives intellectual lights to all human souls, and does not receive intellectual lights from any human soul. For this reason God Most High described the sun as a lamp, when He said: ﴿And He placed in it a lamp and a moon giving light﴾ [al-Furqan: 61], and He described Muhammad (ﷺ) as a radiant lamp.

Once you know this, we say: It has been established by rational and transmitted evidences that the lights present in the spirits of the prophets are borrowed from the lights present in the spirits of the angels. God Most High said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Nahl: 2], and He said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has descended with it, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193-194]. Revelation does not occur except through the intermediary of the angels. So, if we make the spirits of the prophets greater in illumination than the sun, then the spirits of the angels, which are like the mines for the lights of the intellects of the prophets, must necessarily be greater than the lights of the spirits of the prophets, because the cause must necessarily be stronger than the effect.

Then we say: It has also been established by rational and transmitted evidences that the heavenly spirits differ, so some of them receive and some of them give. God Most High said, describing Jibril (peace be upon him): ﴿Obeyed, and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir: 21]. Since he is obeyed by the angels, those who obey must necessarily be under his command. And He said: ﴿And there is not among us anyone but that he has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164]. Once this is established, the one who gives is more deserving of being a light than the one who receives, for the reason mentioned, and because of the degrees of lights in the world of spirits.

An example: When the light of the sun reaches the moon, then enters through a window of a house and falls upon a mirror set on a wall, then is reflected from it to another wall on which another mirror is set, then is reflected from it to a basin full of water placed on the ground, and is reflected from it to the ceiling of the house, then the greatest light is in the sun, which is the source; secondly, in the moon; thirdly, what reached the first mirror; fourthly, what reached the second mirror; fifthly, what reached the water; and sixthly, what reached the ceiling. Every light that is nearer to the first source is stronger than what is farther from it. Likewise, the heavenly lights, since they are arranged

[Page 200]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 3 of 5):

Thus the light of the one who gives light (al-mufid) is more intense in radiance than the light of the one who receives it (al-mustafid). Then these lights continue to ascend until they reach the greatest Light and the Spirit (al-Ruh), which is the greatest of the spirits in rank with God, and which is what He, glorified is He, means by His saying: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks﴾ [al-Naba' 78:38].

Then we say: there is no doubt that these sensible lights, if they are lower (suflIyyah), are like the lights of fires, or if they are higher ('ulwiyyah), are like the lights of the sun, the moon and the stars. Likewise the intellectual lights, if they are lower, are like the lower spirits that belong to the prophets and the saints (awliya'), or if they are higher, are like the higher spirits, which are the angels. All of them are, in their entirety, possible in their essence (mumkinah li-dhatiha), and the possible in its essence deserves non-existence from its own essence and existence from another. Non-existence is the darkness that results, and existence is light. Therefore everything other than God is dark in its essence, illuminated by the command of God, exalted is He. Likewise, all their knowledge after their existence is derived from the existence of God, exalted is He. So the Truth, glorified is He, is the One who made them manifest through existence after they had been in the darkness of non-existence, and who poured upon them the lights of knowledge after they had been in the darkness of ignorance. Thus nothing among things becomes manifest except by His manifesting it. The essential property of light is giving manifestation, disclosure and unveiling. At this point it becomes clear that the absolute Light is God, glorified is He, and that the application of the term "light" to other than Him is metaphorical (majaz), since everything other than God, considered in itself, is darkness, because in itself it is pure non-existence. Rather, when we look at lights in themselves, they are darkness, because in themselves they are possibilities (mumkinat), and the possible in itself is non-existent, and the non-existent is dark. So light, when considered in itself, is darkness; but when it is regarded from the standpoint that the Truth, glorified is He, has poured upon it the light of existence, then by this consideration it becomes lights. Thus it is established that He, glorified is He, is the Light, and that everything else is not light except in a metaphorical sense.

Then he (may God have mercy on him) spoke after this on two matters:

The first: why did He, glorified is He, attribute the light to the heavens and the earth? He answered, saying: You have known that the heavens and the earth are filled with intellectual lights and sensible lights. As for the sensible ones, these are what is observed in the heavens of the stars, the sun and the moon, and what is observed on the earth of the rays spread over the surfaces of bodies, so that the various colors become apparent through them; and were it not for them, colors would have no manifestation, rather no existence. As for the intellectual lights, the higher world is filled with them, and they are the substances of the angels; and the lower world is filled with them, and they are the vegetative, animal and human faculties. Through the lower human light the order of the lower world became manifest, just as through the angelic light the order of the higher world became manifest. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ [al-Nur 24:55], and He said: ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾ [al-Naml 27:62]. When you know this, you know that the whole world is filled with outward visible lights and inward intellectual lights. Then you know that the lower ones overflow, some from others, like the overflow of light from a lamp, for the lamp is the prophetic spirit (al-Ruh al-Nabawi). Then the prophetic and holy lights are borrowed from the higher spirits in the manner that a lamp is kindled from light; and the higher beings borrow from one another, and among them there is an ordering of stations. Then their totality ascends to the Light of lights, its mine and its primal source, and that is God alone, with no partner. Therefore, all is His light, and for this reason He said: ﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾.

The second question: if God is the Light, why was proof needed to establish it? He answered: The meaning of His being the light of the heavens and the earth is known with reference to visible outward light. When you see the greenness of spring in the brightness of day, you do not doubt that you see the colors. You may perhaps think that you see nothing with the colors other than the colors; you say, "I see with the greenness nothing but the greenness." But when the sun sets, you perceive a necessary distinction between the color at the time the light falls upon it and its state when the light does not fall upon it. Therefore you certainly know that light is a meaning other than color, which is perceived along with colors, except that because of its intense union with them it is not perceived, and because of its intense manifestation it becomes hidden; and manifestation may be the cause of concealment.

When you know this, know that just as everything became visible to the sight through outward light, so everything has become visible to the inner insight through God; and His light is present with every thing and does not leave it. But there remains here a difference, namely that outward light can be conceived of as departing and being veiled by the setting of the sun; then it becomes evident that it is other than color. But the divine Light, through which everything becomes manifest, cannot be conceived of as absent; rather its change is impossible, so it remains with things perpetually. Thus the path of inference by means of distinction is cut off. Were its absence conceivable, the heavens and the earth would be destroyed, and there would be perceived in its absence such distinction as would produce necessary knowledge. But since all things are equal in one pattern in testifying to the existence of their Creator, and since everything glorifies Him with His praise, not just some things, and at all times, not just some times, the distinction is lifted and the path is hidden. For the outward path is knowing things through their opposites, and what has no opposite and no change, due to the similarity of its states, is not far from being hidden, and its hiddenness is due to the intensity of its manifestation and clarity. Glory be to Him who is hidden from creation because of the intensity of His manifestation, and who is veiled from them by the radiance of His light.

Know that this discourse that we have related from Shaykh al-Ghazali (may God have mercy on him) is an agreeable discourse. But its essential meaning, after verification, returns to this: that the meaning of His being light, glorified is He, is that He is the Creator of the world and the Creator of the faculties of perception; and this is the meaning of our statement that the meaning of His being the light of the heavens and the earth is that He is the Guide of the people of the heavens and the earth. So there is no discrepancy between what he (al-Ghazali) said and what we have transmitted from the exegetes (mufassirun) regarding the meaning. And God knows best.

* * *

The second section: on the explanation of His (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed God has seventy veils of light and darkness; were He to remove them, the glories of His face would burn up whatever His sight reaches." In some narrations it is seven hundred, and in some it is seventy thousand.

I say: Since it has been established that God, glorified and exalted is He, is manifest in His essence through His essence, the veil must necessarily be relative to the one veiled, and the one veiled must be veiled either by a veil composed of light and darkness, or by a veil composed of light alone, or by a veil composed of darkness alone. As for those veiled by pure darkness, they are the ones who have gone so far in preoccupation with bodily attachments that their minds do not turn to whether it is possible to infer the existence of the Necessary Existent from the existence of these sensible things or not. This is because you have known that everything other than God, exalted is He, considered in itself, is dark, and it is illuminated only insofar as it derives light from the presence (hadrah) of God, exalted is He. So whoever occupies himself with corporeal things in themselves, and that occupation becomes a barrier preventing him from turning toward the side of light, his veil is pure darkness. And since the kinds of preoccupation with bodily attachments are beyond limit and enumeration, likewise the kinds of dark veils are beyond limit and enumeration.

The second kind: those veiled by veils mixed of light and darkness.
Know that whoever looks at these sensible things either believes that they are independent of an Agent (mu'aththir), or believes that they are in need. If he believes that they are independent, this is a veil mixed of light and darkness. "The light" is that he has conceived the reality of independence from others, and that belongs to the attributes of God's majesty, and it is one of the attributes of light. "The darkness" is that he believes that this attribute is found in these bodies, although that attribute does not befit them, and this is darkness. Thus it is established that this is a veil mixed of light and darkness. Then the varieties of this kind are many. Among people there are those who believe that the possible is independent of an Agent; and among them are those who grant that, but say that the agent of these things is their natures, or their motions, or their combination and separation, or their relation to the motions of the spheres, or to the movers of these spheres. All of these belong to this kind.

The third kind: the purely luminous veils.
Know that there is no way to know the Truth, glorified is He, except through those negative and relational attributes (al-sifat al-salbiyyah wa-l-idafiyyah). There is no end to these attributes or to their degrees. So the servant is always ascending in them. If he reaches one level and remains in it, his absorption in contemplating that level becomes a veil for him from ascending to what is above it. And since these levels have no end, the servant is forever in motion and transition. As for His particular reality, it is veiled from all. We have pointed to the manner of the degrees of veiling. You know that he (ﷺ) only limited them to seventy thousand approximately, not precisely, for in reality they have no end.

* * *

The third section: on the explanation of how the parable is constructed.

Know that in a comparison (tashbih) there must be two things: the one compared (al-mushabbah) and that to which it is compared (al-mushabbah bihi). People have differed here about what the one compared is, and they have mentioned several views:

One of them, which is the view of the majority of the mutakallimun (theologians of kalam) and which al-Qadi supported, is that what is meant by the guidance (al-huda), which are the clear signs (al-ayat al-bayyinat), and the meaning is that God's guidance has reached the utmost limits of manifestation and clarity, and in this it is like the niche (mishkah) in which there is a clear glass, and in the glass a lamp kindled with oil that has reached the utmost purity. If it is said: why did He compare it to that when we know that the light of the sun is far more powerful than that? We say: He, glorified is He, intended to describe the perfect light that shines in the midst of darkness, because what predominates over people's imaginations and fancies are doubts, which are like darknesses, and God's guidance among them is like the perfect light that appears among the darknesses. This aim is not achieved by the light of the sun, because when its light appears the world is filled with pure light, and when it sets the world is filled with pure darkness. Therefore that example is more fitting and more appropriate here.

Know that the matters which God, exalted is He, has taken into account in this example are those that necessitate the perfection of light:

The first of them is the lamp (al-misbah), because when the lamp is not in the niche, its rays scatter; but when it is placed in the niche its rays are gathered together, and so they give more illumination. What confirms this is that when a lamp is in a small house, more of its light appears than in a large house.

The second is that when the lamp is in a clear glass, the rays emanating from the lamp are reflected from some sides of the glass to others, because of the clearness and transparency of the glass, and by this means the light and radiance increase. What confirms this is that when a ray of the sun falls upon clear glass, the apparent light is multiplied, so that something opposite it appears with a similar light; and if those rays are reflected from each side of the glass to the other side, the lights and illuminations multiply and reach the maximum possible.

**Third:** The light of the lamp varies according to the substance that it burns. When that oil is pure and unmixed, its condition differs from its condition when it is murky. Among the oils that are burned, none shows purity as oil does. Olive oil can reach such clarity and fineness that it equals water, with added whiteness and a ray of light moving through its parts.

**Fourth:** This oil also varies according to the tree it comes from. If the tree is "neither of the east nor of the west," meaning that it is exposed to the sun in all its conditions, its olives ripen more fully, and so its oil is purer and more likely to separate its clear part from its murky part, because the increase of sunlight has an effect on this. When these four matters come together and cooperate, that light becomes pure and perfect, and so it is fit to be made a parable for the guidance of God, exalted is He.

**Second:** The light in the words ﴿the parable of His light﴾ is the Qur'an. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿There has certainly come to you from God a light﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:15]. This is the view of al-Hasan, Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and Zayd ibn Aslam.

**Third:** The light is the Messenger, because he is the guide, and because God, exalted is He, described him as ﴿a lamp giving light﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:46]. This is the view of 'Ata'.

These two views fall within the first view, because among the kinds of guidance are the sending down of Books and the sending of Messengers. God, exalted is He, said about the Books: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura 42:52]. And He said about the Messengers: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the Messengers﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:165].

**Fourth:** The light is what is in the hearts of the believers of knowledge of God, exalted is He, and knowledge of the laws. This is indicated by the fact that God described faith as light and disbelief as darkness. He said: ﴿So is one whose breast God has opened to Islam and who is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar 39:22]. And He said: ﴿That He may bring out those who believe and do righteous deeds from darkness into light﴾ [al-Talaq 65:11]. The essence of this is that it understood guidance as being guided, and the purpose of the parable is that the faith of the believer has reached such purity from doubts and such distinction from the darkness of misguidance, as the level of the lamp mentioned. This is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas. Ubayy said: "The parable of the light of the believer," and this is how he used to recite it. It is said that he used to recite: "The parable of the light of the one who believed in Him." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The parable of His light in the heart of the believer."

**Fifth:** This is what Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, mentioned. It is this: We have explained that the perceptive faculties are lights, and the levels of the human perceptive faculties are five:

One: The sensitive faculty, which receives what the five senses convey. It is like the root of the animal spirit, and its beginning, since by it the animal becomes an animal. It exists in the nursing infant.

Two: The imaginative faculty, which confirms what the senses have conveyed and keeps it stored with it, to present it to the intellectual faculty above it when there is need for it.

Three: The intellectual faculty, which perceives universal realities.

Four: The reflective faculty, which takes intellectual knowledge and arranges it in order, and from its arrangement it infers knowledge of an unknown.

Five: The holy faculty (al-quwwah al-qudsiyyah), which is peculiar to the Prophets, peace be upon them, and to some of the saints. In it appear the flashes of the unseen and the secrets of the divine realm. To it points His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ [al-Shura 42:52].

When you know these faculties, they are all together lights, since by them the kinds of existing things appear. These five levels can be compared with the five things God mentioned: the niche, the glass, the lamp, the tree and the oil.

As for the sensitive spirit: when you look at its property, you find that its lights come out through several openings, such as the two eyes, the two ears and the two nostrils. The most suitable example of it from the world of bodies is the niche.

As for the second, which is the imaginative spirit, we find for it three distinctive properties:

The first: It is of the nature of the lower, dense world, because the imagined thing has a quantity, a shape and a place, and it is the nature of bodily attachments to be veiled from pure intellectual lights, which are universal abstract conceptions.

The second: When this dense imagination becomes clear, fine and refined, it becomes balanced with intelligible meanings, conveys their lights and does not block the rising of their light. For this reason the interpreter of dreams infers intelligible meanings from imaginal forms, just as one infers the king from the sun, the vizier from the moon, and from one who seals the private parts and mouths of people, that he is a caller to prayer who calls before dawn.

The third: Imagination at the beginning of the matter is greatly needed, so that by it the intellectual knowledge is secured and does not waver. Imaginal likenesses that bring intellectual knowledge are excellent. You will find nothing among bodies that resembles imagination in these three qualities except the glass. It is in origin of a dense substance, but it became clear and fine until it no longer blocks the light of the lamp, but conveys it as it is. Then it protects it from being extinguished by violent winds.

As for the third, which is the intellectual faculty, it is the one able to perceive universal quiddities and divine knowledge. The representation of it by the lamp is not hidden from you. You know this from what we explained, that the Prophets are shining lamps.

As for the fourth, which is the reflective faculty, one of its properties is that it takes one quiddity, then divides it into two parts, as when we say: "The existent is either necessary or possible." Then it makes each part again into two, and so on, until the branches multiply through rational divisions. Then at last it leads to its results, which are its fruits. Then it returns and makes those fruits into seeds for their like, until they reach fruits without end. So it is fitting that its likeness in this world be the tree. When its fruits are a material for the increase of the lights of knowledge and its growth, it is fitting that it not be likened to a quince tree or an apple tree, but specifically to the olive tree. This is because the essence of its fruit is the oil, which is the material of lamps, and which has, among all other oils, the property of greater brightness and less smoke. And if the livestock whose milk and offspring are abundant, and the tree whose fruit is abundant, are called blessed, then that which does not end at any limited point is more fitting to be called a blessed tree. And if the branches of purely intellectual thoughts are abstracted from the attributes of bodies, then it is fitting that it be "neither of the east nor of the west."

As for the fifth, which is the holy prophetic faculty, it is at the highest point of nobility and purity. The reflective faculty divides into what needs teaching and alerting and what does not need it. There must be the existence of this last kind, decisively, to prevent an infinite regress. So it is fitting that this kind be described, in its perfection, its purity and the intensity of its readiness, as one whose oil "would almost glow even if no fire touched it." This example agrees with this kind. Since these lights are arranged one upon another, sense is the first, and it is like the prelude to imagination, and imagination is like the prelude to intellect. So it is fitting that the niche be like the container for the glass, which is like the container for the lamp.

**Sixth:** This is what Abu 'Ali ibn Sina mentioned. He applied these five examples to the levels of the perceptions of the human soul. He said: There is no doubt that the human soul is receptive to universal knowledge and abstract perceptions. Then at the beginning of the matter it is empty of all this knowledge. There it is called the material intellect (al-'aql al-haylani), and it is the niche.

At the second level, there come into it the self-evident sciences, through whose combinations one can attain the acquisition of theoretical sciences. Then, if the capacity for transition is weak, it is the tree. If it is stronger than that, it is the oil. If it is very intense, it is the glass, which is as if it were a brilliant star. If it is at the ultimate extreme, which is the holy soul of the Prophets, it is the one whose oil "would almost glow even if no fire touched it."

At the third level: From the innate, necessary sciences there are acquired the theoretical sciences, except that they are not present in actuality. Rather, they are such that whenever their possessor wills to summon them, he is able to do so. This is called the actual intellect (al-'aql bi-l-fi'l), and this is the lamp.

At the fourth level: Those necessary and theoretical knowledges are present in actuality, and their possessor is as if he looks at them. This is called the acquired intellect (al-'aql al-mustafad), and it is "light upon light," because the disposition is a light, and the attainment of what the disposition is over is another light. Then he claimed that these sciences that come into human spirits come only from a spiritual substance called the active intellect (al-'aql al-fa''al), which is the governor of what is beneath the sphere of the moon, and it is the fire.

**Seventh:** This is the view of some Sufis: God, exalted is He, likened the breast to the niche, the heart to the glass and the knowledge to the lamp. This lamp was kindled from a blessed tree, which is the inspirations of the angels, because of His saying: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ [al-Nahl 16:2], and His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:193-194]. He likened the angels to the blessed tree because of the abundance of their benefits. He described it as "neither of the east nor of the west" because they are spiritual. He described them with His saying: ﴿whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾ because of the abundance of their knowledge and the intensity of their awareness of the secrets of the divine realm, exalted is God. The apparent point here is that the thing likened is not the thing to which it is likened.

**Eighth:** Muqatil said: "The parable of His light," that is, the parable of the light of faith in the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), is like a niche in which is a lamp. The niche corresponds to the loins of 'Abd Allah, the glass corresponds to the body of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the lamp corresponds to faith in the heart of Muhammad, or corresponds to prophethood in his heart.

**Ninth:** Some people said: The niche corresponds to Ibrahim, peace be upon him; the glass corresponds to Isma'il, peace be upon him; the lamp corresponds to the body of Muhammad (ﷺ); and the tree is prophethood and messengership.

**Tenth:** The statement "His light" refers to the believer. This is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who used to recite it as "the parable of the light of the believer." It is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

Know that the first view is the one preferred, because God mentioned before this verse: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs﴾. If by His words ﴿the parable of His light﴾ is meant "the parable of His guidance and His clarification," this agrees with what came before. Also, when we interpreted His saying ﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ as meaning that He is the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth, then if we interpret His saying ﴿the parable of His light﴾ as meaning the parable of His guidance, this agrees with what came before.

* * *

**Section Four: On the remaining issues related to this verse**

It contains issues:

**First issue:** The niche (mishkah) is the recess in a wall that does not go through. This is the well-known view, but they mentioned other views about it:

One: Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: the mishkah is the upright post in the middle of the lamp into which the wick is inserted. This is also the view of Mujahid and al-Qurazi.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: here it is the stem of the lamp, made of glass, in which the wick is placed.

The third: al-Dahhak said: it is the ring from which the lamp is hung. The first is the most correct.

**Question 2:** They claimed that *al-mishkāh* (the niche) is *al-kūwah* (the opening) in the language of Abyssinia. Al-Zajjāj said: *al-mishkāh* is from the speech of the Arabs, and its counterpart is *al-mishkāh*, which is a small fine flour.

**Question 3:** Some said: this verse is of the *maqlūb* (inverted construction), and the intended meaning is "the likeness of His light is like a lamp in a niche," because the thing compared to is what is the source and origin of the light, and that is the lamp, not the niche.

**Question 4:** *Al-miṣbāḥ* is the lamp (*sirāj*), and its root is from light (*ḍawʾ*), and from it comes *al-ṣubḥ* (the dawn).

**Question 5:** *Zujājah* ("glass") was read with *ḍamm*, *fatḥ* and *kasr* (on the first letter). As for *durriyyun*, it was read with *ḍamm*, *kasr* and *fatḥ* on the *dāl*. As for the *ḍamm*, it has three aspects:

First: *ḍamm* on the *dāl*, with the *rāʾ* and *yāʾ* doubled, without *hamz* (glottal stop). This is the well-known reading. Its meaning is that it resembles a pearl (*durr*) in its purity and sheen. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you see the people of the high ranks just as you see the bright star in the horizon of the sky."

Second: the same as the first, except that it has the lengthening (*madd*) and the *hamz*. This is the reading of Ḥamzah and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Abū Bakr.
[p. 206]
Some grammarians held that it is a *laḥn* (grammatical error). Sībawayh said: "This is the weakest of the dialects, and it is derived from light and gleaming, and it is not attributed to *durr* (pearl)." Abū ʿAlī said: the basis of this reading is that it is *faʿīl* from *al-darʾ*, meaning "pushing away," and that it is an adjective, and that as an adjective it is like *al-marīʾ* as a noun.

Third: *ḍamm* on the *dāl*, with the *rāʾ* and *yāʾ* lightened, without lengthening or *hamz*. As for the *kasr*, it has two aspects:

First: *durriʾa* with *kasr* on the *dāl*, the *rāʾ* doubled, with lengthening and *hamz*. This is the reading of Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is *faʿīl* from *al-darʾ*, which is pushing, like *al-sikkīr* and *al-fisīq*, so its light pushes parts of itself away from one another because of its sheen.

Second: with *kasr* on the *dāl* and the *rāʾ* doubled, without *hamz* or lengthening. This is the reading of Ibn Khulayd and ʿUtbah ibn Ḥammād from Nāfiʿ. As for the *fatḥ*, it has four aspects:

First: *fatḥ* on the *dāl*, the *rāʾ* doubled, with lengthening and *hamz*, from al-Aʿmash.

Second: *fatḥ* on the *dāl*, the *rāʾ* doubled, without lengthening or *hamz*, from al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and Qatādah.

Third: *fatḥ* on the *dāl*, the *rāʾ* lightened, with *hamz*, without lengthening or *yāʾ*, from ʿĀṣim.

Fourth: the same, except that it is without *hamz*, with a light *yāʾ* in place of the *hamz*.

As for His words ﴿yūqadu﴾ (is kindled), the well-known reading is *tawaqqada* with the four vowels (*fatḥāt*) and the doubled *qāf*, in the pattern *tafaʿʿala*. From al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and Qatādah it is the same, except that they put *ḍamm* on the *dāl*. The author of *al-Kashshāf* mentioned *yawaqqadu* with *fatḥ* on the *yāʾ* (marked with two dots below), the *wāw* and the *qāf* doubled, and the *dāl* with *rafʿ* (nominative). He said: the omission of the *tāʾ* because two extra letters come together is strange. From Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: with *ḍamm* on the *yāʾ*, sukūn on the *wāw*, *fatḥ* on the *qāf* lightened, and *rafʿ* on the *dāl*. From Nāfiʿ and Ḥafṣ it is the same, except that it is with *tāʾ*. From ʿĀṣim: with *ḍamm* on the *yāʾ*, *fatḥ* on the *wāw*, the *qāf* doubled and *fatḥ*. From Abū ʿAmr it is the same, except that it is with *tāʾ*. From Ṭalḥah: *tūqidu* with *ḍamm* on the *tāʾ*, a sukūn *wāw*, *kasr* on the *qāf* and lightened.

**Question 6:** His words ﴿ka-annahā kawkabun durriyyun﴾ ("as if it were a brilliant star"): that is, large and shining. *Durārī al-nujūm* are its great ones. They agreed that what is meant is a star among the shining stars, such as Venus, Jupiter, and the fixed stars of the first magnitude.

**Question 7:** His words ﴿min shajaratin mubārakah﴾ ("from a blessed tree"): that is, from the oil of a blessed tree, meaning one of abundant blessing and benefit. It was said: it is the first tree that grew after the Flood, and seventy prophets blessed it, among them the Friend (al-Khalīl, Abraham). It was said: what is meant is the olive of Syria, because it is the blessed land, so God made this a blessed tree.

* * *

**Question 8:** They differed concerning the meaning of describing the tree as ﴿lā sharqiyyatin wa-lā gharbiyyah﴾ ("neither of the east nor of the west"), in several aspects:

One: al-Ḥasan said: it is the olive tree of Paradise, for if it were of the trees of this world it would be either eastern or western. This is weak, because God only struck the parable with what they had witnessed, and they had not witnessed the tree of Paradise.

Second: that what is meant is the olive tree in Syria, because Syria is the middle of the world, so its trees are not described as eastern or western. This is also weak, because whoever says the earth is a sphere does not establish the east and west as two specific places; rather, every land has its own east and west. Also, the parable is struck for everyone who knows olive oil, and it is found outside Syria just as it is found there.

Third: that it is a tree around which other trees intertwine, so the sun does not reach it in east or west. Some said: it is a tree whose foliage intertwines tightly, so the sun does not reach it, whether the sun is in the east or the west. There is no tree whose branch bears fruit from its beginning to its end like the olive and the pomegranate. This too is weak, because the purpose is the purity of the oil, and that is not achieved except by the complete ripening of the olive, and that in custom comes about by the sun's effect reaching it, not by its not reaching it.

Fourth: Ibn ʿAbbās said: what is meant is the tree that stands out upon a high mountain or a wide plain, so the sun shines upon it at the times of rising and setting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatādah, and it is chosen by al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. They said: its meaning is that it is neither eastern alone nor western alone, but it is both eastern and western. This is like saying "So-and-so is neither a traveler nor a resident," when he both travels and resides. This view is the preferred one, because when the tree is like this, its oil is at the utmost purity, and then the purpose of the parable is more complete and perfect.

Fifth: the niche is the breast (*ṣadr*) of Muḥammad (ﷺ), the glass is his heart, and the lamp is what is in his heart (ﷺ) of the religion, kindled from a blessed tree, meaning ﴿the creed of your father Abraham﴾ (Qur'an 22:78), upon him be the blessings of God. So the tree is Abraham (peace be upon him). Then He described Abraham, saying: "neither eastern nor western," that is, he did not pray towards the east nor towards the west, like the Jews and the Christians, but he (peace be upon him) prayed towards the Kaʿbah.

* * *

**Question 9:** God described its oil as ﴿yakādu yuḍī'u wa-law lam tamsaskhu nār﴾ ("its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it"), because pure, clear oil, when seen from afar, appears as if it has a ray of light. When fire touches it, it increases in light upon light. Likewise, the heart of the believer almost acts upon guidance before knowledge comes to it, and when knowledge comes to it, it increases in light upon light and guidance upon guidance. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām said: the heart of the believer recognizes the truth before it is explained to it, because it agrees with it. This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by the light of God." Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: what is meant by the oil is the light of Muḥammad (ﷺ), meaning that his light almost makes things clear to people before he speaks. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Muḥammad (ﷺ) almost speaks with wisdom before the revelation. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah said:

*"Even if there were no clear signs in him,*
*his very nature would inform you of the news."*

* * *

**Question 10:** His words, exalted is He, ﴿nūrun ʿalā nūr﴾ ("light upon light"): what is meant is the successive coming of these lights and their gathering together. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: the believer is between four qualities: if he is given, he is thankful; if he is tested, he is patient; if he speaks, he is truthful; and if he judges, he is just. So he, among the rest of people, is like the living man who walks among the dead, moving about in five lights: his speech is light, his action is light, his entering is light, his exiting is light, and his destination is toward the light on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Rabīʿ said: I asked Abū al-ʿĀliyah about his entering and his exiting, and he said: his secret and his public conduct.

* * *

**Question 11:** Al-Jubbāʾī said: the verse indicates that everyone who is ignorant, the ignorance comes from himself; otherwise the proofs are clear, and if they had looked into them they would have known. Our companions (the Ashʿarīs) said: this verse is the explicit statement of our school, for He, glorified is He, after making clear that these proofs have reached such a degree of manifestness and clarity that no more can be added to it, said: ﴿God guides to His light whomever He wills﴾. That is, the clarity of these proofs is not sufficient and does not benefit unless God creates faith. It is not possible that what is meant by His words ﴿God guides﴾ is the clarification of the proofs and the evidences, because if we take the light to mean the clarifying of the proofs, it is not permissible to take the guidance in it to mean that as well, otherwise the speech would fall out of purpose. So nothing remains but to take the guidance here to mean the creation of knowledge.

Abū Muslim ibn Baḥr answered this in two ways:

First: that His words ﴿God guides to His light whomever He wills﴾ are to be understood as increases of guidance, which is like the opposite of the abandonment (*khidhlān*) that befalls the astray.

Second: that He, glorified is He, guides by His light, which is the path to Paradise, whomever He wills, and He compared it to His words: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right; [good news for you today: gardens]﴾ (Qur'an 57:12).

Al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār rejected these two answers. As for the first, because the preceding speech is about the revealed verses, so if we take it to mean guidance, it includes everyone, and if we take it to mean increase, only some are included, and if it is taken to mean the path to Paradise, it is not included in it at all except in meaning, not in wording. When he rejected these two answers, he said: it is better to say that He, exalted is He, guided by that some and not others, namely those who have reached the limit of responsibility.
[p. 208]
Know that this answer is weaker than the first two, because His words ﴿God guides to His light whomever He wills﴾ imply that these verses, despite their clarity, are not sufficient. This does not include the child or the insane, so what they said falls away.

**Question 12:** His words, exalted is He, ﴿wa-yaḍribu Allāhu al-amthāla li-l-nās﴾ ("And God sets forth parables for people"): what is meant by "people" is the responsible people, that is, the Prophet and those sent to him. He, glorified is He, mentioned this in the context of a great blessing. The Muʿtazilah used this as evidence and said: it would only be a great blessing if they were able to benefit from it, and if everything were created by God, they would not be able to benefit from it. The answer to this is what has passed. Then He made clear that He, glorified is He, is ﴿knower of all things﴾ (*bi-kulli shay'in ʿalīm*), and that is like a warning to whoever does not take heed, does not reflect upon His parables, and does not look into His proofs, so that he would know their clarity and their distance from doubts.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein He is glorified morning and evening﴾ ﴿by men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾ ﴿so that Allah may reward them for the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty. Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾.

Know that there are several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah) in this verse.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿in houses Allah has permitted﴾, requires an omitted element (mahdhuf) such that it means "therein" (fiha). The commentators have mentioned several views on this.

One of them: the intended meaning is, "like a niche in which there is a lamp, in houses Allah has permitted." This is the choice of many of the muhaqqiqun (careful scholars). Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani objected to it on two grounds.

The first: the purpose of mentioning the lamp is the comparison (mathal), and the lamp being in houses Allah has permitted adds nothing to this purpose, because that does not make the lamp any brighter or more luminous.

The second: what was mentioned earlier contains features which require that it be one (singular), such as His saying, ﴿like a niche﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:35), His saying, ﴿in it is a lamp﴾ (24:35), His saying, ﴿in a glass﴾ (24:35), and His saying, ﴿as if it were a glittering star﴾ (24:35). The word "houses" is plural, and it is not valid for this one (object) to be in all the houses.

The answer to the first objection: a lamp placed in a clear glass, when it is in the mosques, is greater and more magnificent, and therefore brighter, so the comparison with it is more complete and perfect.

The answer to the second: since the purpose of the comparison is the one that has this description, everything falls under it, such as a niche in which there is a lamp in a glass, blazing with oil. The benefit of this is that its light appears in these houses at night when there is need to worship Allah, the Exalted. If a man said, "The one suitable for my service is a man who is known for knowledge, sufficiency and contentment, and who keeps to his house," that would be acceptable. And if he mentions it in the singular form, the meaning is the category (naw'), and so likewise is what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in this verse.

The second view: the estimate is, "it is kindled from a blessed tree, in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

The third view, which is the opinion of Abu Muslim, is that it refers back to His saying, ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:34). That is: "and an example from those who passed away before you, in houses Allah has permitted to be raised." The ones who passed away are meant to be the prophets and the believers, and the houses are the mosques. Allah related the accounts of the prophets, peace be upon them, and mentioned their places, calling them mihrabs (prayer niches), by His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the mihrab﴾ (Surah Sad, 38:21), and ﴿whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 3:37). So He says, ﴿And We have sent down to you clear verses﴾ (24:34), and "We have sent down the stories of those who were raised before you among the prophets and the believers," ﴿in houses Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ (24:36).

The fourth view: al-Jubba'i's view that it is a new, independent statement (kalam mustaani') with no connection to what precedes it. The estimate is: "Pray in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

The fifth view, which is the opinion of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj: there is no omission in the verse, but rather there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). It is as if He said, "Men whose description is such-and-such glorify Him in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

As for Abu Muslim's view, al-Qadi objected to it on two grounds.

The first: His saying, ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾, is meant to refer to those among the deniers of the messengers who passed away, because it is connected to what came before about compulsion to fornication for the sake of worldly gain. So that does not fit the description of these houses, since they are houses in which Allah has permitted His name to be mentioned.

The second: this verse has become disconnected from that verse by what intervened between them, namely His saying, ﴿Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (24:35).

As for al-Jubba'i's view, it has been said that a supposed omission (idmar) is not to be resorted to except in cases of necessity, and with the interpretation mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj there is no need for it, so it is not permissible to resort to it.

If it is said that the view of al-Zajjaj also faces a problem, because according to his view the meaning becomes "in houses Allah has permitted, He is glorified in them," so His saying "in them" (fiha) would be a repetition without benefit, then why do you say that bearing this extra addition is better than bearing that deficiency? We say: additions for the sake of emphasis are numerous, so resorting to them is better.

The second issue: most of the exegetes (mufassirin) said that what is meant by His saying, ﴿in houses﴾, is the mosques. From 'Ikrimah it is reported that he said regarding ﴿in houses﴾ that it means all houses. The first view is better for two reasons.

The first: there are houses that cannot be described as those which Allah, exalted is He, has permitted to be raised.

The second: He, exalted is He, described them with remembrance, glorification and prayer, and that is only fitting for mosques. Then, for those who say that what is meant is the mosques, there are two opinions.

One of them: what is meant is four mosques: the Ka'bah, which Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, built; the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, built; the mosque of Madinah, which the Prophet (ﷺ) built; and the mosque of Quba, which was founded on piety (Surah al-Tawbah, 9:108), and which the Prophet (ﷺ) built. From al-Hasan it is reported that it is the Bayt al-Maqdis, in which ten thousand lamps are lit.

The second: what is meant is all the mosques. The first opinion is weak, because it is a specification without evidence. So it is better to take the word as referring to all the mosques. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The mosques are the houses of Allah on earth, and they shine for the people of the heavens just as the stars shine for the people of the earth."

* * *

The third issue: they differed regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿to be raised﴾ (an turfa'), in several views.

One of them: what is meant by raising them is building them, as in His saying, ﴿He raised its height and made it level﴾ (Surah al-Nazi'at, 79:28), and His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:127). From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported: they are the mosques, which Allah commanded to be built.

The second: they are raised, that is, they are exalted, purified from impurities and from idle speech. This is from al-Zajjaj.

The third: what is meant is both matters together.

The second view is better, because His saying, ﴿in houses Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, its apparent meaning is that they were houses before being raised, and then Allah permitted that they be raised.

* * *

The fourth issue: they differed regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿and in which His name is mentioned﴾.

The first view: it is general, covering every kind of remembrance.

The second: that His Book be recited in them, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that nothing unbecoming be spoken in them. The first view is better because of the generality of the wording.

The fifth issue: Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited yusabbaḥu (with a fatḥah on the ba') (يُسَبَّحُ), and the rest recited it with a kasrah. According to the first reading, the statement extends to the end of the three adverbial expressions, namely, "to Him therein in the mornings and the evenings." Then al-Zajjaj said: "rijal (men)" is in the nominative case, because when He said, ﴿He is glorified to Him therein﴾, it was as if it were said, "Who glorifies?" and the answer was, "men glorify."

* * *

The sixth issue: they differed regarding this glorification. Most of them took it to mean prayer itself. Then they differed: some took it to mean all five daily prayers, and some took it to mean the dawn and afternoon prayers, saying that these two were obligatory at the beginning of the matter and then more were added to them. Others took it to mean glorification in the sense of declaring Allah, exalted is He, free of whatever is unbecoming to Him in His essence and His actions. It was argued against this by the fact that He joined prayer and zakat to it, when He said, ﴿from the remembrance of Allah and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat﴾. This latter view is more apparent.

* * *

The seventh issue: al-asal is the plural of asil, and al-usul is the plural of asil, which means the late afternoon (al-'ashiy). The word al-ghuduww (morning) is used because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) which is not pluralized, and asil is a collective noun (ism jam'). The author of al-Kashshaf said: "bil-ghuduww" means "at the times of the morning," that is, "in the mornings." It has been read wal-iṣal (والإيصال), which is entering the time of asil; it is said āṣala, like a'tama and aẓhara.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah have mercy on both of them, said: "The Duha prayer is mentioned in the Book of Allah, the Exalted," and he recited this verse. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no one who goes out in the morning and returns in the evening to the mosque, preferring it over anything else, except that he has from Allah a provision in Paradise equal to it." In the narration of Sahl ibn Sa'd, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever goes to the mosque in the morning and returns in the evening to teach good or to learn it, is like the one who fights in the cause of Allah and returns with spoils."

* * *

The eighth issue: they differed regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾. Some said that He negated that they were merchants and sellers at all. Others said rather that He affirmed them to be merchants and sellers, and He explained that, despite that, no distraction from the various benefits of trade preoccupies them. This is the view of most. al-Hasan said: "By Allah, they did indeed trade, but when the obligations of Allah came, nothing distracted them from them, so they stood to perform prayer and zakat." From Salim: he saw a group of people from the market who had left their dealings and gone to prayer, and he said: "These are the ones about whom Allah, exalted is He, said, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾." The same is reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Know that this view is better than the first, because one does not say that so-and-so is not distracted by trade from such-and-such unless he is a merchant, although the first view is possible.

Here there are questions.

The first question: since He said, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾, the sale (bay') is already included in it, so why did He mention the sale again? We say the answer to this is from several aspects.

The first: trade is a genus under which fall the kinds of buying and selling, but He, glorified is He, specified sale by mention because it is more likely to distract, since the profit gained in sale is a certain and immediate gain, while the profit gained in buying is an uncertain future one.

The second: sale entails exchanging goods for cash, while buying is the reverse, and the desire to obtain cash is greater than the reverse.

The third: al-Farra' said: "trade" (tijarah) is for those who import goods. It is said: "so-and-so traded in such-and-such" if he brought it from another land, and "sale" is what he sold by his own hands.

The second question: why did He specify men by mention? The answer: because women are not among the people of trade or of gatherings.

* * *

The ninth issue: they differed regarding what is meant by the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. Some people said that what is meant is praise of Allah and supplications. Others said that what is meant is the prayers. If it is said, what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾? We say there are two answers to this.

One of them: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: what is meant by the establishment of prayer is performing it at its appointed times.

The second: it is permissible that His saying, ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾, be an explanation of the remembrance of Allah, so they remember Allah before prayer and during prayer.

The tenth issue: we have mentioned at the beginning of the tafsir of Surah al-Baqarah, in His saying, ﴿and they establish prayer﴾, that iqamat al-salah is performing it fully in accordance with its conditions. The reason for dropping the ha' (in iqamah) is what al-Zajjaj said: one says aqamtu al-salah iqamatan, and the original was iqwaman, but the waw was changed to an alif, so two alifs came together and one was deleted because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters, so it remained aqamtu al-salah iqaman, and then a ha' was added as a substitute for the deleted element, and the idafah (genitive construction) here stands in for the deleted ha' in the substitution. He said: "This is a consensus (ijma') of the grammarians."

The eleventh issue: they differed regarding prayer. Some said it refers to the obligatory prayers, and some included voluntary prayers in it, according to what we related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the Duha prayer. The first is closer, because it is closer to the definite (ta'rif). Likewise regarding zakat, the meaning is the prescribed zakat, because it is the known term in the Sharia called by that name. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: what is meant by zakat is obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and sincerity. Similarly in His saying, ﴿and he used to command his family to prayer and zakat﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:55), and His saying, ﴿none of you would have been purified﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:21), and His saying, ﴿you purify them and cleanse them thereby﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah, 9:103). This view is weak because of what preceded, and also because He linked zakat with giving (iitaa'), and this can only be understood as what is given from the rights of wealth.

Issue 12: He, glorified is He, made clear that these men, although they devote themselves to the remembrance of Allah and acts of obedience, are nevertheless described as fearful and apprehensive. So He said: ﴿They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾. That fear arises only from their knowledge that they did not worship Allah with the worship due to Him. Scholars differed about the meaning of the turning of hearts and eyes, and gave several opinions:

The first opinion: hearts will be agitated from terror and dread, and eyes will be fixed in a stare, based on His saying: ﴿And when the eyes shall be dazed, and the hearts reach the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10].

The second: their states will change, so that hearts that were sealed and could not comprehend will comprehend, and eyes that could not see will see. It is as if they pass from doubt to conjecture, from conjecture to certainty, and from certainty to direct witnessing, based on His saying: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ [az-Zumar: 47], and His saying: ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering﴾ [Qaf: 22].

The third: hearts turn about on that day, hoping for salvation and fearing destruction, and eyes turn toward whatever direction they are commanded: from the right side or from the left? And from which direction will their books be given to them: from the right hands or from the left hands? The Mu'tazilah do not accept this interpretation, for they say that the people of reward have no fear whatsoever on that day, and the people of punishment do not hope for pardon. But we have demonstrated the falsity of this doctrine more than once.

The fourth: hearts leave their places and reach the throats, and eyes turn bluish. Ad-Dahhak said: The disbeliever will be gathered with sharp sight, his eyes will turn blue, and then he will become blind. The heart turns from fear, not finding any escape, until it lodges in the throat. This is His saying: ﴿When the hearts are at the throats, suppressing grief﴾ [Ghafir: 18].

The fifth: al-Jubba'i said: The meaning of the turning of hearts and eyes is the change of their forms because of the punishment that befalls them, so that at one time they are in the form of something cooked in fire, and at another time in the form of something burnt. He said: It is also possible that He means their being turned over on the embers of Hell, which is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 110].

* * *

Issue 13: His saying: ﴿that Allah may reward them the best of what they did﴾ means: they perform these acts of devotion so that Allah may reward them and recompense them for the best of what they did. On this there are several aspects:

The first: by "the best" is meant all good deeds, namely acts of obedience, both obligatory and voluntary. Muqatil said: He mentioned "the best" only to indicate that He does not requite them for the evil of their deeds, but rather forgives them.

The second: He, glorified is He, rewards them with a recompense for the best of what they did, multiplied from ten up to seven hundred for each one.

The third: al-Qadi said: The meaning of this is that their acts of obedience expiate their sins, and Allah, exalted is He, rewards them only with the best of deeds. This is consistent with his doctrine of abortion (of deeds) and weighing.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and increase them of His bounty﴾, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, rewards them with the best of deeds and does not limit Himself to the measure of what they deserve, but increases them of His bounty beyond what He mentioned in other verses of multiplication. If it is said: This indicates that performing obedience has an effect on the entitlement to reward, for He distinguished the recompense from the bounty, and you do not say this, since according to you the servant does not deserve anything from his Lord. We reply: We affirm entitlement, but through the promise; that measure is what is deserved, and what exceeds it is the bounty. Then He said: ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. By this He indicates His perfect power, His perfect generosity, the execution of His will, and the vastness of His beneficence. Thus, since He described them as diligent and striving in obedience while being in the utmost fear, Allah, glorified is He, gives them the great reward for their acts of obedience and increases for them the boundless bounty in return for their fear.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein He is glorified morning and evening﴾ ﴿by men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾ ﴿so that Allah may reward them for the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty. Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾.

Know that there are several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah) in this verse.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿in houses Allah has permitted﴾, requires an omitted element (mahdhuf) such that it means "therein" (fiha). The commentators have mentioned several views on this.

One of them: the intended meaning is, "like a niche in which there is a lamp, in houses Allah has permitted." This is the choice of many of the muhaqqiqun (careful scholars). Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani objected to it on two grounds.

The first: the purpose of mentioning the lamp is the comparison (mathal), and the lamp being in houses Allah has permitted adds nothing to this purpose, because that does not make the lamp any brighter or more luminous.

The second: what was mentioned earlier contains features which require that it be one (singular), such as His saying, ﴿like a niche﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:35), His saying, ﴿in it is a lamp﴾ (24:35), His saying, ﴿in a glass﴾ (24:35), and His saying, ﴿as if it were a glittering star﴾ (24:35). The word "houses" is plural, and it is not valid for this one (object) to be in all the houses.

The answer to the first objection: a lamp placed in a clear glass, when it is in the mosques, is greater and more magnificent, and therefore brighter, so the comparison with it is more complete and perfect.

The answer to the second: since the purpose of the comparison is the one that has this description, everything falls under it, such as a niche in which there is a lamp in a glass, blazing with oil. The benefit of this is that its light appears in these houses at night when there is need to worship Allah, the Exalted. If a man said, "The one suitable for my service is a man who is known for knowledge, sufficiency and contentment, and who keeps to his house," that would be acceptable. And if he mentions it in the singular form, the meaning is the category (naw'), and so likewise is what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in this verse.

The second view: the estimate is, "it is kindled from a blessed tree, in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

The third view, which is the opinion of Abu Muslim, is that it refers back to His saying, ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:34). That is: "and an example from those who passed away before you, in houses Allah has permitted to be raised." The ones who passed away are meant to be the prophets and the believers, and the houses are the mosques. Allah related the accounts of the prophets, peace be upon them, and mentioned their places, calling them mihrabs (prayer niches), by His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the mihrab﴾ (Surah Sad, 38:21), and ﴿whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 3:37). So He says, ﴿And We have sent down to you clear verses﴾ (24:34), and "We have sent down the stories of those who were raised before you among the prophets and the believers," ﴿in houses Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ (24:36).

The fourth view: al-Jubba'i's view that it is a new, independent statement (kalam mustaani') with no connection to what precedes it. The estimate is: "Pray in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

The fifth view, which is the opinion of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj: there is no omission in the verse, but rather there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). It is as if He said, "Men whose description is such-and-such glorify Him in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

As for Abu Muslim's view, al-Qadi objected to it on two grounds.

The first: His saying, ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾, is meant to refer to those among the deniers of the messengers who passed away, because it is connected to what came before about compulsion to fornication for the sake of worldly gain. So that does not fit the description of these houses, since they are houses in which Allah has permitted His name to be mentioned.

The second: this verse has become disconnected from that verse by what intervened between them, namely His saying, ﴿Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (24:35).

As for al-Jubba'i's view, it has been said that a supposed omission (idmar) is not to be resorted to except in cases of necessity, and with the interpretation mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj there is no need for it, so it is not permissible to resort to it.

If it is said that the view of al-Zajjaj also faces a problem, because according to his view the meaning becomes "in houses Allah has permitted, He is glorified in them," so His saying "in them" (fiha) would be a repetition without benefit, then why do you say that bearing this extra addition is better than bearing that deficiency? We say: additions for the sake of emphasis are numerous, so resorting to them is better.

The second issue: most of the exegetes (mufassirin) said that what is meant by His saying, ﴿in houses﴾, is the mosques. From 'Ikrimah it is reported that he said regarding ﴿in houses﴾ that it means all houses. The first view is better for two reasons.

The first: there are houses that cannot be described as those which Allah, exalted is He, has permitted to be raised.

The second: He, exalted is He, described them with remembrance, glorification and prayer, and that is only fitting for mosques. Then, for those who say that what is meant is the mosques, there are two opinions.
