One of them: what is meant is four mosques: the Ka'bah, which Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, built; the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, built; the mosque of Madinah, which the Prophet (ﷺ) built; and the mosque of Quba, which was founded on piety (Surah al-Tawbah, 9:108), and which the Prophet (ﷺ) built. From al-Hasan it is reported that it is the Bayt al-Maqdis, in which ten thousand lamps are lit.

The second: what is meant is all the mosques. The first opinion is weak, because it is a specification without evidence. So it is better to take the word as referring to all the mosques. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The mosques are the houses of Allah on earth, and they shine for the people of the heavens just as the stars shine for the people of the earth."

* * *

The third issue: they differed regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿to be raised﴾ (an turfa'), in several views.

One of them: what is meant by raising them is building them, as in His saying, ﴿He raised its height and made it level﴾ (Surah al-Nazi'at, 79:28), and His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:127). From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported: they are the mosques, which Allah commanded to be built.

The second: they are raised, that is, they are exalted, purified from impurities and from idle speech. This is from al-Zajjaj.

The third: what is meant is both matters together.

The second view is better, because His saying, ﴿in houses Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, its apparent meaning is that they were houses before being raised, and then Allah permitted that they be raised.

* * *

The fourth issue: they differed regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿and in which His name is mentioned﴾.

The first view: it is general, covering every kind of remembrance.

The second: that His Book be recited in them, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that nothing unbecoming be spoken in them. The first view is better because of the generality of the wording.

The fifth issue: Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited yusabbaḥu (with a fatḥah on the ba') (يُسَبَّحُ), and the rest recited it with a kasrah. According to the first reading, the statement extends to the end of the three adverbial expressions, namely, "to Him therein in the mornings and the evenings." Then al-Zajjaj said: "rijal (men)" is in the nominative case, because when He said, ﴿He is glorified to Him therein﴾, it was as if it were said, "Who glorifies?" and the answer was, "men glorify."

* * *

The sixth issue: they differed regarding this glorification. Most of them took it to mean prayer itself. Then they differed: some took it to mean all five daily prayers, and some took it to mean the dawn and afternoon prayers, saying that these two were obligatory at the beginning of the matter and then more were added to them. Others took it to mean glorification in the sense of declaring Allah, exalted is He, free of whatever is unbecoming to Him in His essence and His actions. It was argued against this by the fact that He joined prayer and zakat to it, when He said, ﴿from the remembrance of Allah and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat﴾. This latter view is more apparent.

* * *

The seventh issue: al-asal is the plural of asil, and al-usul is the plural of asil, which means the late afternoon (al-'ashiy). The word al-ghuduww (morning) is used because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) which is not pluralized, and asil is a collective noun (ism jam'). The author of al-Kashshaf said: "bil-ghuduww" means "at the times of the morning," that is, "in the mornings." It has been read wal-iṣal (والإيصال), which is entering the time of asil; it is said āṣala, like a'tama and aẓhara.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah have mercy on both of them, said: "The Duha prayer is mentioned in the Book of Allah, the Exalted," and he recited this verse. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no one who goes out in the morning and returns in the evening to the mosque, preferring it over anything else, except that he has from Allah a provision in Paradise equal to it." In the narration of Sahl ibn Sa'd, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever goes to the mosque in the morning and returns in the evening to teach good or to learn it, is like the one who fights in the cause of Allah and returns with spoils."

* * *

The eighth issue: they differed regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾. Some said that He negated that they were merchants and sellers at all. Others said rather that He affirmed them to be merchants and sellers, and He explained that, despite that, no distraction from the various benefits of trade preoccupies them. This is the view of most. al-Hasan said: "By Allah, they did indeed trade, but when the obligations of Allah came, nothing distracted them from them, so they stood to perform prayer and zakat." From Salim: he saw a group of people from the market who had left their dealings and gone to prayer, and he said: "These are the ones about whom Allah, exalted is He, said, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾." The same is reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Know that this view is better than the first, because one does not say that so-and-so is not distracted by trade from such-and-such unless he is a merchant, although the first view is possible.

Here there are questions.

The first question: since He said, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾, the sale (bay') is already included in it, so why did He mention the sale again? We say the answer to this is from several aspects.

The first: trade is a genus under which fall the kinds of buying and selling, but He, glorified is He, specified sale by mention because it is more likely to distract, since the profit gained in sale is a certain and immediate gain, while the profit gained in buying is an uncertain future one.

The second: sale entails exchanging goods for cash, while buying is the reverse, and the desire to obtain cash is greater than the reverse.

The third: al-Farra' said: "trade" (tijarah) is for those who import goods. It is said: "so-and-so traded in such-and-such" if he brought it from another land, and "sale" is what he sold by his own hands.

The second question: why did He specify men by mention? The answer: because women are not among the people of trade or of gatherings.

The ones who passed away are meant to be the prophets and the believers, and the houses are the mosques. Allah related the accounts of the prophets, peace be upon them, and mentioned their places, calling them mihrabs (prayer niches), by His saying, ﴿when they climbed over the mihrab﴾ (Surah Sad, 38:21), and ﴿whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 3:37). So He says, ﴿And We have sent down to you clear verses﴾ (24:34), and "We have sent down the stories of those who were raised before you among the prophets and the believers," ﴿in houses Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ (24:36).

The fourth view: al-Jubba'i's view that it is a new, independent statement (kalam mustaani') with no connection to what precedes it. The estimate is: "Pray in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

The fifth view, which is the opinion of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj: there is no omission in the verse, but rather there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). It is as if He said, "Men whose description is such-and-such glorify Him in houses Allah has permitted to be raised."

As for Abu Muslim's view, al-Qadi objected to it on two grounds.

The first: His saying, ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾, is meant to refer to those among the deniers of the messengers who passed away, because it is connected to what came before about compulsion to fornication for the sake of worldly gain. So that does not fit the description of these houses, since they are houses in which Allah has permitted His name to be mentioned.

The second: this verse has become disconnected from that verse by what intervened between them, namely His saying, ﴿Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (24:35).

As for al-Jubba'i's view, it has been said that a supposed omission (idmar) is not to be resorted to except in cases of necessity, and with the interpretation mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj there is no need for it, so it is not permissible to resort to it.

If it is said that the view of al-Zajjaj also faces a problem, because according to his view the meaning becomes "in houses Allah has permitted, He is glorified in them," so His saying "in them" (fiha) would be a repetition without benefit, then why do you say that bearing this extra addition is better than bearing that deficiency? We say: additions for the sake of emphasis are numerous, so resorting to them is better.

The second issue: most of the exegetes (mufassirin) said that what is meant by His saying, ﴿in houses﴾, is the mosques. From 'Ikrimah it is reported that he said regarding ﴿in houses﴾ that it means all houses. The first view is better for two reasons.

The first: there are houses that cannot be described as those which Allah, exalted is He, has permitted to be raised.

The second: He, exalted is He, described them with remembrance, glorification and prayer, and that is only fitting for mosques. Then, for those who say that what is meant is the mosques, there are two opinions.

One of them: what is meant is four mosques: the Ka'bah, which Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, built; the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, built; the mosque of Madinah, which the Prophet (ﷺ) built; and the mosque of Quba, which was founded on piety (Surah al-Tawbah, 9:108), and which the Prophet (ﷺ) built. From al-Hasan it is reported that it is the Bayt al-Maqdis, in which ten thousand lamps are lit.

The second: what is meant is all the mosques. The first opinion is weak, because it is a specification without evidence. So it is better to take the word as referring to all the mosques. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The mosques are the houses of Allah on earth, and they shine for the people of the heavens just as the stars shine for the people of the earth."

* * *

The third issue: they differed regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿to be raised﴾ (an turfa'), in several views.

One of them: what is meant by raising them is building them, as in His saying, ﴿He raised its height and made it level﴾ (Surah al-Nazi'at, 79:28), and His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:127). From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported: they are the mosques, which Allah commanded to be built.

The second: they are raised, that is, they are exalted, purified from impurities and from idle speech. This is from al-Zajjaj.

The third: what is meant is both matters together.

The second view is better, because His saying, ﴿in houses Allah has permitted to be raised﴾, its apparent meaning is that they were houses before being raised, and then Allah permitted that they be raised.

* * *

The fourth issue: they differed regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿and in which His name is mentioned﴾.

The first view: it is general, covering every kind of remembrance.

The second: that His Book be recited in them, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that nothing unbecoming be spoken in them. The first view is better because of the generality of the wording.

The fifth issue: Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited yusabbaḥu (with a fatḥah on the ba') (يُسَبَّحُ), and the rest recited it with a kasrah. According to the first reading, the statement extends to the end of the three adverbial expressions, namely, "to Him therein in the mornings and the evenings." Then al-Zajjaj said: "rijal (men)" is in the nominative case, because when He said, ﴿He is glorified to Him therein﴾, it was as if it were said, "Who glorifies?" and the answer was, "men glorify."

* * *

The sixth issue: they differed regarding this glorification. Most of them took it to mean prayer itself. Then they differed: some took it to mean all five daily prayers, and some took it to mean the dawn and afternoon prayers, saying that these two were obligatory at the beginning of the matter and then more were added to them. Others took it to mean glorification in the sense of declaring Allah, exalted is He, free of whatever is unbecoming to Him in His essence and His actions. It was argued against this by the fact that He joined prayer and zakat to it, when He said, ﴿from the remembrance of Allah and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat﴾. This latter view is more apparent.

* * *

The seventh issue: al-asal is the plural of asil, and al-usul is the plural of asil, which means the late afternoon (al-'ashiy). The word al-ghuduww (morning) is used because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) which is not pluralized, and asil is a collective noun (ism jam'). The author of al-Kashshaf said: "bil-ghuduww" means "at the times of the morning," that is, "in the mornings." It has been read wal-iṣal (والإيصال), which is entering the time of asil; it is said āṣala, like a'tama and aẓhara.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah have mercy on both of them, said: "The Duha prayer is mentioned in the Book of Allah, the Exalted," and he recited this verse. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no one who goes out in the morning and returns in the evening to the mosque, preferring it over anything else, except that he has from Allah a provision in Paradise equal to it." In the narration of Sahl ibn Sa'd, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever goes to the mosque in the morning and returns in the evening to teach good or to learn it, is like the one who fights in the cause of Allah and returns with spoils."

* * *

The eighth issue: they differed regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾. Some said that He negated that they were merchants and sellers at all. Others said rather that He affirmed them to be merchants and sellers, and He explained that, despite that, no distraction from the various benefits of trade preoccupies them. This is the view of most. al-Hasan said: "By Allah, they did indeed trade, but when the obligations of Allah came, nothing distracted them from them, so they stood to perform prayer and zakat." From Salim: he saw a group of people from the market who had left their dealings and gone to prayer, and he said: "These are the ones about whom Allah, exalted is He, said, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾." The same is reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Know that this view is better than the first, because one does not say that so-and-so is not distracted by trade from such-and-such unless he is a merchant, although the first view is possible.

Here there are questions.

The first question: since He said, ﴿trade does not distract them﴾, the sale (bay') is already included in it, so why did He mention the sale again? We say the answer to this is from several aspects.

The first: trade is a genus under which fall the kinds of buying and selling, but He, glorified is He, specified sale by mention because it is more likely to distract, since the profit gained in sale is a certain and immediate gain, while the profit gained in buying is an uncertain future one.

The second: sale entails exchanging goods for cash, while buying is the reverse, and the desire to obtain cash is greater than the reverse.

The third: al-Farra' said: "trade" (tijarah) is for those who import goods. It is said: "so-and-so traded in such-and-such" if he brought it from another land, and "sale" is what he sold by his own hands.

The second question: why did He specify men by mention? The answer: because women are not among the people of trade or of gatherings.

* * *

The ninth issue: they differed regarding what is meant by the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. Some people said that what is meant is praise of Allah and supplications. Others said that what is meant is the prayers. If it is said, what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾? We say there are two answers to this.

One of them: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: what is meant by the establishment of prayer is performing it at its appointed times.

The second: it is permissible that His saying, ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾, be an explanation of the remembrance of Allah, so they remember Allah before prayer and during prayer.

The tenth issue: we have mentioned at the beginning of the tafsir of Surah al-Baqarah, in His saying, ﴿and they establish prayer﴾, that iqamat al-salah is performing it fully in accordance with its conditions. The reason for dropping the ha' (in iqamah) is what al-Zajjaj said: one says aqamtu al-salah iqamatan, and the original was iqwaman, but the waw was changed to an alif, so two alifs came together and one was deleted because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters, so it remained aqamtu al-salah iqaman, and then a ha' was added as a substitute for the deleted element, and the idafah (genitive construction) here stands in for the deleted ha' in the substitution. He said: "This is a consensus (ijma') of the grammarians."

The eleventh issue: they differed regarding prayer. Some said it refers to the obligatory prayers, and some included voluntary prayers in it, according to what we related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the Duha prayer. The first is closer, because it is closer to the definite (ta'rif). Likewise regarding zakat, the meaning is the prescribed zakat, because it is the known term in the Sharia called by that name. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: what is meant by zakat is obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and sincerity. Similarly in His saying, ﴿and he used to command his family to prayer and zakat﴾ (Surah Maryam, 19:55), and His saying, ﴿none of you would have been purified﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:21), and His saying, ﴿you purify them and cleanse them thereby﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah, 9:103). This view is weak because of what preceded, and also because He linked zakat with giving (iitaa'), and this can only be understood as what is given from the rights of wealth.

Issue 12: He, glorified is He, made clear that these men, although they devote themselves to the remembrance of Allah and acts of obedience, are nevertheless described as fearful and apprehensive. So He said: ﴿They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾. That fear arises only from their knowledge that they did not worship Allah with the worship due to Him. Scholars differed about the meaning of the turning of hearts and eyes, and gave several opinions:

The first opinion: hearts will be agitated from terror and dread, and eyes will be fixed in a stare, based on His saying: ﴿And when the eyes shall be dazed, and the hearts reach the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10].

The second: their states will change, so that hearts that were sealed and could not comprehend will comprehend, and eyes that could not see will see. It is as if they pass from doubt to conjecture, from conjecture to certainty, and from certainty to direct witnessing, based on His saying: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ [az-Zumar: 47], and His saying: ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering﴾ [Qaf: 22].

The third: hearts turn about on that day, hoping for salvation and fearing destruction, and eyes turn toward whatever direction they are commanded: from the right side or from the left? And from which direction will their books be given to them: from the right hands or from the left hands? The Mu'tazilah do not accept this interpretation, for they say that the people of reward have no fear whatsoever on that day, and the people of punishment do not hope for pardon. But we have demonstrated the falsity of this doctrine more than once.

The fourth: hearts leave their places and reach the throats, and eyes turn bluish. Ad-Dahhak said: The disbeliever will be gathered with sharp sight, his eyes will turn blue, and then he will become blind. The heart turns from fear, not finding any escape, until it lodges in the throat. This is His saying: ﴿When the hearts are at the throats, suppressing grief﴾ [Ghafir: 18].

The fifth: al-Jubba'i said: The meaning of the turning of hearts and eyes is the change of their forms because of the punishment that befalls them, so that at one time they are in the form of something cooked in fire, and at another time in the form of something burnt. He said: It is also possible that He means their being turned over on the embers of Hell, which is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 110].

* * *

Issue 13: His saying: ﴿that Allah may reward them the best of what they did﴾ means: they perform these acts of devotion so that Allah may reward them and recompense them for the best of what they did. On this there are several aspects:

The first: by "the best" is meant all good deeds, namely acts of obedience, both obligatory and voluntary. Muqatil said: He mentioned "the best" only to indicate that He does not requite them for the evil of their deeds, but rather forgives them.

The second: He, glorified is He, rewards them with a recompense for the best of what they did, multiplied from ten up to seven hundred for each one.

The third: al-Qadi said: The meaning of this is that their acts of obedience expiate their sins, and Allah, exalted is He, rewards them only with the best of deeds. This is consistent with his doctrine of abortion (of deeds) and weighing.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and increase them of His bounty﴾, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, rewards them with the best of deeds and does not limit Himself to the measure of what they deserve, but increases them of His bounty beyond what He mentioned in other verses of multiplication. If it is said: This indicates that performing obedience has an effect on the entitlement to reward, for He distinguished the recompense from the bounty, and you do not say this, since according to you the servant does not deserve anything from his Lord. We reply: We affirm entitlement, but through the promise; that measure is what is deserved, and what exceeds it is the bounty. Then He said: ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. By this He indicates His perfect power, His perfect generosity, the execution of His will, and the vastness of His beneficence. Thus, since He described them as diligent and striving in obedience while being in the utmost fear, Allah, glorified is He, gives them the great reward for their acts of obedience and increases for them the boundless bounty in return for their fear.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 39–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain. The thirsty one thinks it is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full. And God is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿Or [they are] like darknesses in a vast deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds: darknesses, one above another. If he extends his hand, he can barely see it. And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, had described the state of the believer, that in this world he is in light and by means of it he holds fast to righteous deeds, and then described that in the Hereafter he will be successful with lasting bliss and great reward, He followed this by describing that the disbeliever will be in the greatest loss in the Hereafter and in the greatest kinds of darkness in this world. He coined a parable for each of the two. As for the parable indicating his failure in the Hereafter, it is His saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain.﴾ Al-Azhari said: "al-sarab (mirage) is what appears to the eye at the time of the great forenoon in the deserts, resembling flowing water, but it is not water; rather, the one who looks at it from afar supposes it to be flowing water. It is said: sariba al-ma' yaslurbu surubban, when it flows, so it is sarib (flowing)." As for al-al (the shimmer), it is what appears to the eye at the beginning of the day, so that the observer sees the small as large. The apparent sense of al-Khalil's words is that al-al and al-sarab are one and the same. As for qi'ah (level plain), al-Farra' said: it is the plural of qa'in, like jar and jirah, and al-qa' is the flat, level part of the earth. The author of al-Kashshaf said: qi'ah has the meaning of qa'. al-Zajjaj said: al-zam'an (the thirsty one) may have its hamza lightened, and it is the one of extreme thirst.

Then the aspect of the comparison: whatever the disbeliever does, if it is among the deeds of righteousness, he does not deserve a reward for it, although he believes that he has a reward for it; and if it is among the deeds of sin, he deserves punishment for it, although he believes he deserves a reward for it. In any case, he believes that he has a reward with God, the exalted. When he arrives at the plains of the Resurrection and does not find the reward, but finds the great punishment, his regret becomes great and his grief extreme. So his state resembles the state of the thirsty one whose need for water is intense; when he sees the mirage, his heart clings to it, he hopes for salvation through it, and his expectation grows strong. Then when he reaches it and despairs of what he had hoped for, that becomes grievous to him. This example is extremely fine. Mujahid said: "the mirage is the deed of the disbeliever, and his coming to it is his death and departure from the world."

If it is said: His saying ﴿until, when he comes to it﴾ indicates that it is something, and His saying ﴿he finds it to be nothing﴾ contradicts it? We say: the answer to this is in three respects.

The first: its meaning is that he does not find it to be anything beneficial, as one says: "So-and-so did nothing, even though he strove."

The second: ﴿until, when he comes to it﴾ means he came to the place of the mirage, and did not find the mirage to be anything; he was content with mentioning the mirage instead of mentioning its place.

The third: the pronoun refers to the mirage, because the mirage is seen from afar due to its density, as if it were fog and dust, and when one comes near it, it thins out, scatters, and becomes like air.

As for His saying: ﴿and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full﴾, meaning: he finds at that time the punishment of God with which He threatened the disbeliever, so what he had been in, of the supposition of great benefit, changes into certainty of great harm. Or it means he finds the angels of God with him, seizing him and taking him toward Hell, and they give him to drink of the boiling water and the ghassaq (the dark, foul liquid). They are the ones about whom God, exalted, said: ﴿laboring, weary﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 3], ﴿and they suppose that they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 104], ﴿and We shall turn to the deeds they did and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. It has been said: it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a ibn Umayya, who had devoted himself to worship, wore woolen garments, and sought religion in the Jahiliyyah, then disbelieved in Islam.

As for His saying: ﴿and God is swift in reckoning﴾, that is because He, glorified is He, knows all knowables, so reckoning is not burdensome to Him. Some of the theologians said: its meaning is that the reckoning of one does not preoccupy Him from another, unlike us. If He were speaking by an instrument, as the anthropomorphists say, that would not be valid.

As for the second parable, it is His saying: ﴿Or [they are] like darknesses in a vast deep sea﴾. Concerning the particle "aw" (or) here there are several aspects:

One: know that God, exalted, has made clear that if the deeds of the disbelievers are good, their likeness is the mirage, and if they are ugly, they are the darknesses.

Two: the meaning of the sentence is that their deeds are either like a mirage in a level plain, which is in the Hereafter, or like darknesses in a sea, which is in this world.

Three: the first verse is about their deeds, and that they gain nothing from them; the second verse is about their beliefs, for they resemble darknesses, as He said: ﴿and He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16], meaning from disbelief to faith. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾

As for al-bahr al-lujji (the vast deep sea), it is the one possessing al-lujjah, which is the greatest part of the abundant water, deep at the bottom. Concerning al-lujji there are two dialectal forms: with the lam kasra and with the lam damma.

As for the depiction of the likeness: the bottom of the vast deep sea is extremely dark because of the depth of the water. When waves follow one upon another, the darkness increases. If clouds are above the waves, the darkness reaches its utmost limit. So the one who falls to the bottom of this vast deep sea is in the extreme of intense darkness. Since it is customary that the hand is among the nearest things one sees, and among the farthest things one supposes one does not see, He said: ﴿he can barely see it﴾, and by this, glorified is He, He showed that the darkness reached its furthest extremity. Then He compared the disbeliever to it in his belief, which is the opposite of the believer in His saying: ﴿Light upon light﴾ [al-Nur: 35], and in His saying: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Hadid: 12]. For this reason Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "The disbeliever turns about in five kinds of darkness: his speech, his deed, his entrance, his exit, and his final destination, the Fire."

Concerning the manner of this comparison there are other aspects:

One: God, exalted, mentioned three kinds of darkness: the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the waves, and the darkness of the clouds. Likewise the disbeliever has three darknesses: the darkness of belief, the darkness of speech, and the darkness of action. This is from al-Hasan.

Two: they likened his heart, his sight, and his hearing to these three darknesses. This is from Ibn Abbas.

Three: the disbeliever does not know, and does not know that he does not know, and believes that he knows. These three levels resemble those darknesses.

Four: these darknesses are piled up, and likewise the disbeliever, because of the intensity of his persistence in his disbelief, misguidance has piled up upon him, to the extent that the most evident proofs, when mentioned in his presence, he does not understand.

Five: a dark heart in a dark breast.

As for His saying: ﴿darknesses, one above another﴾: it is related from Ibn Kathir that he read "sahab" and read "zulumat" in the genitive, as a substitution for His saying ﴿or like darknesses﴾. Also from him, he read "sahabu zulumat" as one says "sahabu rahmah" and "sahabu 'adhab" in the idafah construction. The reading of the rest is "sahabun zulumatun," both in the nominative with tanwin. The complete sentence ends at His saying ﴿sahab﴾, then He began ﴿zulumat﴾, meaning: what was previously mentioned is ﴿darknesses, one above another﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿he can barely see it﴾, there are two opinions:

One: that kad (barely) in negation is affirmation, and in affirmation is negation. So His saying ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71] is a negation in wording but an affirmation in meaning, because they did it. And his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Poverty almost becomes disbelief" is an affirmation in wording but a negation in meaning, because he did not disbelieve. Likewise here, His saying ﴿he can barely see it﴾ means that he saw it.

The second: that kad means approximation, so His saying ﴿he can barely see it﴾ means he did not come close to seeing it. It is known that one who did not come close to occurring did not occur either. This second opinion is the chosen one, and the first is weak for two reasons:

The first: whatever is less than these darknesses is not seen in them, so how could it be seen with these darknesses?

The second: the purpose of this parable is to exaggerate the ignorance of the disbelievers, and that is only achieved when sight is not found at all amid these darknesses.

As for His saying: ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾ Our companions said: when He, glorified is He, described the guidance of the believer as being in the utmost clarity and evidence, He followed it by saying: ﴿God guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35]; and when He described the misguidance of the disbeliever as being in the utmost darkness, He followed it by His saying: ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾ The purpose of this is that a person should know that the appearance of proofs does not benefit faith, and the darkness of the path does not prevent it, for everything is bound to God's creation, His guidance, and His determination. The qadi said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light﴾ is: in this world, through His subtle favors; ﴿for him there is no light﴾ means he is not guided and so is bewildered. It is also possible that ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light﴾ means: no deliverance in the Hereafter and no success with reward; ﴿for him there is no light.﴾ The discussion of this, by way of refutation and affirmation, is well known.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 39–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain. The thirsty one thinks it is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full. And God is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿Or [they are] like darknesses in a vast deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds: darknesses, one above another. If he extends his hand, he can barely see it. And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, had described the state of the believer, that in this world he is in light and by means of it he holds fast to righteous deeds, and then described that in the Hereafter he will be successful with lasting bliss and great reward, He followed this by describing that the disbeliever will be in the greatest loss in the Hereafter and in the greatest kinds of darkness in this world. He coined a parable for each of the two. As for the parable indicating his failure in the Hereafter, it is His saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain.﴾ Al-Azhari said: "al-sarab (mirage) is what appears to the eye at the time of the great forenoon in the deserts, resembling flowing water, but it is not water; rather, the one who looks at it from afar supposes it to be flowing water. It is said: sariba al-ma' yaslurbu surubban, when it flows, so it is sarib (flowing)." As for al-al (the shimmer), it is what appears to the eye at the beginning of the day, so that the observer sees the small as large. The apparent sense of al-Khalil's words is that al-al and al-sarab are one and the same. As for qi'ah (level plain), al-Farra' said: it is the plural of qa'in, like jar and jirah, and al-qa' is the flat, level part of the earth. The author of al-Kashshaf said: qi'ah has the meaning of qa'. al-Zajjaj said: al-zam'an (the thirsty one) may have its hamza lightened, and it is the one of extreme thirst.

Then the aspect of the comparison: whatever the disbeliever does, if it is among the deeds of righteousness, he does not deserve a reward for it, although he believes that he has a reward for it; and if it is among the deeds of sin, he deserves punishment for it, although he believes he deserves a reward for it. In any case, he believes that he has a reward with God, the exalted. When he arrives at the plains of the Resurrection and does not find the reward, but finds the great punishment, his regret becomes great and his grief extreme. So his state resembles the state of the thirsty one whose need for water is intense; when he sees the mirage, his heart clings to it, he hopes for salvation through it, and his expectation grows strong. Then when he reaches it and despairs of what he had hoped for, that becomes grievous to him. This example is extremely fine. Mujahid said: "the mirage is the deed of the disbeliever, and his coming to it is his death and departure from the world."

If it is said: His saying ﴿until, when he comes to it﴾ indicates that it is something, and His saying ﴿he finds it to be nothing﴾ contradicts it? We say: the answer to this is in three respects.

The first: its meaning is that he does not find it to be anything beneficial, as one says: "So-and-so did nothing, even though he strove."

The second: ﴿until, when he comes to it﴾ means he came to the place of the mirage, and did not find the mirage to be anything; he was content with mentioning the mirage instead of mentioning its place.

The third: the pronoun refers to the mirage, because the mirage is seen from afar due to its density, as if it were fog and dust, and when one comes near it, it thins out, scatters, and becomes like air.

As for His saying: ﴿and he finds God with him, and He pays him his account in full﴾, meaning: he finds at that time the punishment of God with which He threatened the disbeliever, so what he had been in, of the supposition of great benefit, changes into certainty of great harm. Or it means he finds the angels of God with him, seizing him and taking him toward Hell, and they give him to drink of the boiling water and the ghassaq (the dark, foul liquid). They are the ones about whom God, exalted, said: ﴿laboring, weary﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 3], ﴿and they suppose that they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 104], ﴿and We shall turn to the deeds they did and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. It has been said: it was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a ibn Umayya, who had devoted himself to worship, wore woolen garments, and sought religion in the Jahiliyyah, then disbelieved in Islam.

As for His saying: ﴿and God is swift in reckoning﴾, that is because He, glorified is He, knows all knowables, so reckoning is not burdensome to Him. Some of the theologians said: its meaning is that the reckoning of one does not preoccupy Him from another, unlike us. If He were speaking by an instrument, as the anthropomorphists say, that would not be valid.

As for the second parable, it is His saying: ﴿Or [they are] like darknesses in a vast deep sea﴾. Concerning the particle "aw" (or) here there are several aspects:

One: know that God, exalted, has made clear that if the deeds of the disbelievers are good, their likeness is the mirage, and if they are ugly, they are the darknesses.

Two: the meaning of the sentence is that their deeds are either like a mirage in a level plain, which is in the Hereafter, or like darknesses in a sea, which is in this world.

Three: the first verse is about their deeds, and that they gain nothing from them; the second verse is about their beliefs, for they resemble darknesses, as He said: ﴿and He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16], meaning from disbelief to faith. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾

As for al-bahr al-lujji (the vast deep sea), it is the one possessing al-lujjah, which is the greatest part of the abundant water, deep at the bottom. Concerning al-lujji there are two dialectal forms: with the lam kasra and with the lam damma.

As for the depiction of the likeness: the bottom of the vast deep sea is extremely dark because of the depth of the water. When waves follow one upon another, the darkness increases. If clouds are above the waves, the darkness reaches its utmost limit. So the one who falls to the bottom of this vast deep sea is in the extreme of intense darkness. Since it is customary that the hand is among the nearest things one sees, and among the farthest things one supposes one does not see, He said: ﴿he can barely see it﴾, and by this, glorified is He, He showed that the darkness reached its furthest extremity. Then He compared the disbeliever to it in his belief, which is the opposite of the believer in His saying: ﴿Light upon light﴾ [al-Nur: 35], and in His saying: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Hadid: 12]. For this reason Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "The disbeliever turns about in five kinds of darkness: his speech, his deed, his entrance, his exit, and his final destination, the Fire."

Concerning the manner of this comparison there are other aspects:

One: God, exalted, mentioned three kinds of darkness: the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the waves, and the darkness of the clouds. Likewise the disbeliever has three darknesses: the darkness of belief, the darkness of speech, and the darkness of action. This is from al-Hasan.

Two: they likened his heart, his sight, and his hearing to these three darknesses. This is from Ibn Abbas.

Three: the disbeliever does not know, and does not know that he does not know, and believes that he knows. These three levels resemble those darknesses.

Four: these darknesses are piled up, and likewise the disbeliever, because of the intensity of his persistence in his disbelief, misguidance has piled up upon him, to the extent that the most evident proofs, when mentioned in his presence, he does not understand.

Five: a dark heart in a dark breast.

As for His saying: ﴿darknesses, one above another﴾: it is related from Ibn Kathir that he read "sahab" and read "zulumat" in the genitive, as a substitution for His saying ﴿or like darknesses﴾. Also from him, he read "sahabu zulumat" as one says "sahabu rahmah" and "sahabu 'adhab" in the idafah construction. The reading of the rest is "sahabun zulumatun," both in the nominative with tanwin. The complete sentence ends at His saying ﴿sahab﴾, then He began ﴿zulumat﴾, meaning: what was previously mentioned is ﴿darknesses, one above another﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿he can barely see it﴾, there are two opinions:

One: that kad (barely) in negation is affirmation, and in affirmation is negation. So His saying ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71] is a negation in wording but an affirmation in meaning, because they did it. And his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Poverty almost becomes disbelief" is an affirmation in wording but a negation in meaning, because he did not disbelieve. Likewise here, His saying ﴿he can barely see it﴾ means that he saw it.

The second: that kad means approximation, so His saying ﴿he can barely see it﴾ means he did not come close to seeing it. It is known that one who did not come close to occurring did not occur either. This second opinion is the chosen one, and the first is weak for two reasons:

The first: whatever is less than these darknesses is not seen in them, so how could it be seen with these darknesses?

The second: the purpose of this parable is to exaggerate the ignorance of the disbelievers, and that is only achieved when sight is not found at all amid these darknesses.

As for His saying: ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾ Our companions said: when He, glorified is He, described the guidance of the believer as being in the utmost clarity and evidence, He followed it by saying: ﴿God guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35]; and when He described the misguidance of the disbeliever as being in the utmost darkness, He followed it by His saying: ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light, for him there is no light.﴾ The purpose of this is that a person should know that the appearance of proofs does not benefit faith, and the darkness of the path does not prevent it, for everything is bound to God's creation, His guidance, and His determination. The qadi said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light﴾ is: in this world, through His subtle favors; ﴿for him there is no light﴾ means he is not guided and so is bewildered. It is also possible that ﴿And he for whom God has not made a light﴾ means: no deliverance in the Hereafter and no success with reward; ﴿for him there is no light.﴾ The discussion of this, by way of refutation and affirmation, is well known.

[p. 10]

The Exalted says: ﴿Do you not see that to Allah glorify all who are in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight? Each knows its prayer and its glorification. And Allah knows well what they do.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, described the lights of the hearts of the believers and the darkness of the hearts of the ignorant, He followed this with proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness).

The first type is what He mentions in this verse. There is no doubt that the intended meaning is "Do you not know," because seeing with the eye does not reach glorification, whereas knowledge of the heart does. Although the apparent form of this statement is a question, its purpose is affirmation and clarification. Thus He draws attention to what follows from His exaltation: whoever is in the heavens glorifies Him, and likewise whoever is on the earth.

Know that the meaning of glorification (tasbih) may be one of three things. It may be that these things indicate that Allah is exalted above deficiencies and characterized by the attributes of majesty. Or it may be that they speak and utter glorification. Or it may be that for some it means indicating His transcendence, and for the rest it means speaking with the tongue. The first option is closest, because the second is impossible: on earth there are those who are not morally accountable (mukallaf) and who do not glorify in this sense, and among the accountable there are also those who do not glorify in this sense, such as the disbelievers.

As for the third option, that those in the heavens, who are the angels, glorify with the tongue, while those on earth glorify some by tongue and some by indication, this requires using a single word in both its literal and figurative senses at once, which is not permissible. So only the first option remains. The reason is that these things share in the fact that their bodies and attributes indicate Allah's transcendence, glorified and exalted is He, and His power, divinity, oneness, and justice. This is called transcendence in a broadened sense.

If it is said: then glorification in this sense is present in all created things, so what is the reason for restricting it here to rational beings? We answer: because the creation of rational beings is a stronger indication of the existence of the Creator, glorified is He, since the wonders and marvels in their creation are greater, namely reason, speech, and understanding.

As for His saying, ﴿and the birds in flight﴾, one may ask: what is the connection of this with what precedes? The answer: when He, glorified is He, mentioned that the inhabitants of the heavens and the inhabitants of the earth glorify Him, He mentioned that those who are suspended in the air between heaven and earth, which are the birds, also glorify Him. This is because giving a heavy body the strength by which it can stand in the atmosphere of the sky, spreading its wings in flight with their gripping and extending, is one of the greatest proofs of the power of the Creator who governs, glorified is He, and making their flight a prostration to Him, glorified is He. This confirms what we have mentioned, that the intended meaning of glorification is that these states indicate transcendence, not verbal speech.

As for His saying, ﴿Each knows its prayer and its glorification﴾, there are three possible readings:

The first: the meaning is "Allah knows each one's prayer and glorification." They said that His saying, ﴿And Allah knows well what they do﴾, supports this, and it is the choice of the majority of the mutakallimun (theologians).

The second: the pronoun in "prayer" and "glorification" refers back to the word ﴿each﴾, meaning that they know what is obligatory upon them of prayer and glorification.

The third: the pronoun refers to the mention of Allah, meaning that every glorifier and every worshipper knows the prayer of Allah which He has imposed upon him. On these two interpretations, His saying ﴿And Allah knows well﴾ is a new, independent statement.

It is narrated from Abu Thabit, who said: "I was sitting with Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said to me: 'Do you know what these sparrows say at sunrise and after sunrise?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'They sanctify their Lord and ask Him for the sustenance of their day.'"

The theologians found this improbable and said: if birds knew Allah, they would be like rational beings who understand our speech and gestures. But they are not like that, for we know by necessity that they are far more deficient than a child who does not know these matters. So it is even more impossible for them to have such knowledge. And if it is established that they do not know Allah, it is impossible that they glorify Him by speech. Thus it is established that they glorify Allah only by the language of state (lisan al-hal), as was explained earlier.

[p. 11]

Some scholars said: we observe that Allah, the Exalted, inspired birds and all insects with subtle works which most rational beings are unable to perform. If this is so, why is it not permissible that He inspire them with knowledge of Him, with supplication to Him, and with glorifying Him? The demonstration that He, glorified is He, inspired them with subtle works is in several respects:

The first: their cunning in the manner of hunting. Consider the spider, how it devises subtle stratagems for catching flies. It is said that the bear lies down in the path of the bull, and when the bull lowers its horns to gore, it grips its horns with its two forelegs and keeps biting between its forelegs until it weakens it. It is also said that it throws stones, takes up a stick, and strikes a man until he imagines he is dead, and then leaves him; sometimes it returns to sniff him and feel his breath. It climbs trees with the lightest of ascents, and it cracks a walnut between its two paws, striking one side with one and hitting with the other, then blows into it, so the shell falls away and it licks out the kernel. Strange things are also related about the mouse in its stealing.

The second: the matter of the bee, its leadership, and its building of hexagonal hives, which the most accomplished engineers cannot build.

The third: the migration of cranes from one end of the world to the other end, seeking climates that suit them. It is also said that among the peculiarities of horses is that each one recognizes the voice of the horse that once met it at some time. Dogs bark with the well-known call of their kind. When a leopard is given, or drinks, the known medicine called "leopard-strangler," it goes to human dung and eats it. Crocodiles open their mouths for a bird that alights upon them, like the magpie, which cleans between their teeth; on the bird's head there is something like a thorn, and when the crocodile intends to snap at the bird, it is hurt by that thorn and opens its mouth, and the bird flies out. The tortoise, after eating a snake, takes a mountain thyme (sa'tar), and then returns and is healed from it. A reliable experienced hunter reported that he saw a houbara bustard fighting a viper and fleeing from it to a plant, from which it ate, then returning, and this was its habit continually. That old hunter was sitting in a deep hiding place, performing the hunt, and the plant was near his hiding place. When the houbara was occupied with the viper, he uprooted the plant. The houbara returned to its place of growth and did not find it, and began circling around the spot continuously until it fell dead. The old man understood that the houbara had been using it to treat itself from the bite. That plant was wild cress (jirjir). As for the weasel, in fighting a snake it relies on eating rue (sadhab), for the rue's scent is among the things that repel vipers. When dogs have worms in their bellies, they eat ears of wheat. When lizards injure one another, they heal their wounds with mountain thyme.

The fourth: hedgehogs can sense the north and south winds before they blow, so they change the entrance to their burrows. In Constantinople there was a man who grew rich because he used to forecast the winds before they blew, and people benefited from his warnings. The cause of this was a hedgehog in his house which did this, and he used it as a guide. The swallow is an excellent builder in making its nest from mud and pieces of wood. If mud is scarce, it gets wet and rolls in the dirt so that its wings carry a quantity of mud. When it has hatched its young, it takes great care of the chicks, picks up their droppings with its beak, and throws them away from the nest. Then it teaches them to drop their dung toward the edge of the nest. When a hunter approaches the place of the partridge's chicks, the partridge appears to him and comes close, enticing him to follow it, and then goes off to another side away from its young. The woodpecker rarely lands on the ground, but rather on trees, and pecks at the spot where it knows there is a worm. Cranes rise very high in the air when flying, and if fog or cloud hides some of them from others, they make a clearly audible rustling with their wings by which they keep track of one another. When they sleep on a mountain, they place their heads under their wings, except the leader, who sleeps with his head uncovered, so that he wakes quickly, and when he hears a sentry he cries out. The movement of ants going to their places in a straight line, each preserving the others, is a wondrous matter. Know that a full account of this subject is mentioned in the book Tabai' al-Hayawan (The Natures of Animals). The point is that the shrewdest of rational beings are unable to match such stratagems. If this is possible, why is it not possible to say that they are inspired by Allah, the Exalted, with knowledge of Him and with praise of Him, even if they do not know the other matters which people know? And how excellent is the saying of Shihab al-Islam al-Sam'ani: "The majesty of the Majestic is too exalted to be weighed by the scale of i'tizal (Mu'tazilite rationalism)."

As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return﴾, despite its brevity, it contains an indication of the complete knowledge of the origin (mabda') and the return (ma'ad). His saying ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ alerts that everything is from Him, because everything other than Him is contingent (mumkin) and originated, and the contingent and the originated exist only when traced back to the eternal, necessarily existent (wajib al-wujud). Thus all bodies and accidents, the deeds, words, and thoughts of servants are included in this statement.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾, it is a complete expression concerning knowledge of the return (ma'ad), namely that all things must return to Him, glorified is He. It also has another aspect: existence begins from the most noble to the most base, descending, and then rises from the most base to the most noble, ascending, for He makes it a body, then makes it characterized by vegetative life, then animal life, then human life, then angelic nature, and then it reaches the Necessary Existent in Himself.

So the first consideration is His saying ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and the second is His saying ﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 43–44:

﴿Have you not considered that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, and you see the rain coming out from within them? And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail, and strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾ ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have sight.﴾

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Of them are some that walk on their bellies, some that walk on two legs, and some that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ Indeed, We have sent down clear signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Of them are some that walk on their bellies, some that walk on two legs, and some that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent down clear signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

Know that this is the third type of proof for the Divine Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah). Having first argued from the conditions of the heavens and the earth, and second from the celestial phenomena (al-athar al-ulwiyyah), He now argues, third, from the conditions of animals. Know that this verse raises several questions.

**The first question:** Why did Allah say ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾ when many animals were not created from water? The angels are the most numerous of the animals, and they were created from light. The jinn were created from fire. Allah created Adam from dust, as in His words: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ (Al ʿImran 59), and He created ʿIsa from the wind, as in His words: ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ (al-Tahrim 12). Moreover, we see that many animals are generated without a drop of semen. The answer has several aspects:

First, and the best of them, is what al-Qaffal said: that the words ﴿from water﴾ are a complement of ﴿every creature﴾ and not a complement of ﴿created﴾. The meaning is that every creature is generated from water, and therefore it is created by Allah the Most High.

Second, the origin of all created things is water, according to what is related: "The first thing Allah the Most High created was a jewel, and He looked at it with the eye of awe, and it became water. Then from that water He created fire, air and light." Since the purpose of this verse is to explain the origin of creation, and the first origin is water, he mentioned it in this manner.

Third, the intended meaning of "creature" (dabbah) is that which crawls upon the face of the earth, and their dwelling is there. This excludes the angels and the jinn. Since the overwhelming majority of these animals were created from water, either because they are generated from a drop of semen, or because they cannot live except with water, he used the general term "every" to treat the majority as if it were the whole.

**The second question:** Why is "water" indefinite in ﴿from water﴾, while it comes definite in ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ (al-Anbiya 30)? [p. 16] The answer: It came indefinite here because the meaning is that He created every creature from a kind of water that is specific to that creature. It came definite in ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ because the purpose there is that they were created from this substance, whereas here the point is that this substance is divided into many kinds.

**The third question:** The pronoun in ﴿Of them﴾ (minhum) is used for rational beings, and likewise the word ﴿some﴾ (man). Why then is it used for non-rational beings? The answer: Allah mentioned non-rational beings together with rational ones, namely the angels, humans and jinn, so the form suited to the rational was given precedence, because making the nobler the principal and the baser the subsidiary is preferable to the reverse. And in common speech one says, "Who are the two approaching?" referring to a man and a camel.

**The fourth question:** Why did he call crawling on the belly "walking" (mashy)? This question is confirmed by the fact that a child may be described as crawling (yahbu) and one does not say that he walks (yamshi), even if he crawls in the manner that a snake crawls. The answer: This is by way of metaphor (istiʿarah), as they say of a continuing matter, "This matter has walked," and one says, "No matter goes smoothly for him" (la yatamashsha lahu amr). Or it is by way of harmonization (mushakalah) with that crawler together with those who walk.

**The fifth question:** The division is incomplete, because we find creatures that walk on more than four legs, such as spiders, scorpions and centipedes, and even an animal that has forty-four legs, called the ear-borer (dakhhal al-udhn). The answer: The category you mention is like the rare, and so it is regarded as non-existent. Moreover, the philosophers acknowledge that a creature with many legs, when it walks, relies only on four directions, so it is as if it walks on four. And also, the words of the Most High ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾ serve as an indication of the remaining categories.

**The sixth question:** Why do the three kinds come in this order? The answer: He mentioned first what is more wondrous, namely that which walks without an instrument of walking such as legs or feet, then that which walks on two legs, then that which walks on four. Know that the words ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾ are a reminder that just as animals differ according to the manner of walking, so they differ according to other matters. Here, then, let us mention some of the divisions:

**The first division:** Animals may share certain organs, and they may differ in other organs. As for sharing, it is like the sharing of a human and a horse in having flesh, sinews and bone. As for difference, it is either in the organ itself or in its attribute. As for difference in the organ itself, it is of two kinds:

The first: the organ is not present in the other, even though its constituent parts are present in the second, such as the horse and the human. The horse has a tail, and the human does not have a tail, but the parts of the tail are nothing but bone, sinew, flesh, skin and hair, and all of these are present in the human.

The second: that organ is not present in the second at all, neither in itself nor in its parts, such as the tortoise, which has a shell (sadaf) that encloses it, whereas the human does not have that. Likewise the fish has scales (fulus) and the hedgehog has quills (shawk), and none of these is found in the human.

As for difference in the attribute of an organ, it is either in quantity, quality, position, action, or passivity. As for that which is in quantity, it either relates to magnitude, such as the eye of the owl being large and the eye of the eagle being small, or to number, such as the legs of one kind of spider being six, while the legs of another kind are eight or ten. As for that which is in quality, it is like their differences in colour, shape, hardness and softness. As for that which is in position, it is like the difference in the position of the elephant's breast, which is near the chest, and the horse's breast, which is near the navel. As for that which is in action, it is like the elephant's ear being fit for swatting flies while also being an organ of hearing, which is not the case in the human, and like its nose being an instrument for grasping, unlike the nose of other creatures. As for that which is in passivity, [p. 17] it is like the eye of the bat being quickly bewildered by light, while the eye of the swallow is not.

**The second division:** An animal is either aquatic, meaning its original dwelling is water, or terrestrial, or it is aquatic and then becomes terrestrial. As for aquatic animals, their conditions vary in several respects:

First: Their place, their food and their breathing are all aquatic. Instead of breathing air, such an animal takes in water through a kind of aquatic inhalation; it draws water into its interior and then expels it, and it does not live if it is separated from water. All fish are like this. Among them are those whose place and food are aquatic but which breathe air, like the aquatic tortoise. Among them are those whose place and food are aquatic and which do not breathe or inhale at all, like certain kinds of shellfish that do not come out into the air and do not draw water into their interiors.

Second: Aquatic animals inhabit different waters: some dwell in the waters of flowing rivers, some in the waters of marshes, like frogs, and some dwell in the waters of the sea.

Third: Among them are those of the deep, and among them those of the shore, and among them those of the mud, and among them those of the rocks.

Fourth: Among animals that move in water, some propel themselves in diving by their heads and in swimming by their fins, like fish. Some rely on their legs for swimming, like the frog. Some walk on the floor of the water, like the crab. Some crawl, like a kind of fish that has no fin, and like the worm. As for terrestrial animals, their conditions also vary in two respects:

First: Some breathe through one channel, such as the mouth and the nostril, and some do not breathe in this way but in another manner through their pores, like the wasp and the bee.

Second: Terrestrial animals are of different kinds. Some have a known dwelling, and some have a dwelling wherever they happen to be, except when they give birth, and then they settle for the sake of nursing. Those that have a dwelling vary: some have a crevice as their dwelling, some have holes, some have a high-lying jar-like hollow, and some have the surface of the earth.

Third: Every terrestrial flying creature with wings walks on its two legs. Among them are those whose walking is difficult, like the large black swallow and the bat. As for those whose wings are skin or membrane, some may be without legs, like a kind of Ethiopian serpent that flies.

Fourth: Birds differ. Some live together in company, like the cranes; some prefer solitude, like the eagle and all the predatory birds that compete for prey because they need to devise tricks to hunt and because they compete for it. Some live in pairs and remain together, like the sand grouse. Some gather at times and are solitary at other times. Solitary animals may be civil, may be purely wild, or may be domesticated in gardens. Among animals, the human is the one who cannot live alone, because the means of his life and livelihood are fulfilled only through civil cooperation. The bee, the ant and certain cranes share this with the human, but the bee and the crane obey one leader, whereas the ant has a society but no leader.

Fifth: Among birds there are flesh-eaters, grain-pickers and grass-eaters. Some birds have a particular food, such as the bee, whose food is flowers, and the spider, whose food is flies; and some birds share the same food.

As for the third category, namely the animal that is at times aquatic and at other times terrestrial, it is said to be an animal that lives in the sea and dwells there, and then emerges onto the land and remains there.

**The third division:** Some animals are naturally tame, like the human; some are tame by birth, like the cat and the horse; some are tamed by force, like the leopard; and some are never tamed, like the panther. Of those that are tamed by force, some become tame quickly and remain tame, like the elephant, and some are slow, like the lion. It is likely that in every species there is a tame kind and a wild kind, even among humans.

**The fourth division:** Among animals, some make a sound and some make no sound. Every sound-making animal becomes louder when it is aroused and when the urge to mate moves it, except the human. Also, some animals have an intense lust that is constant at all times, like the rooster, and some are chaste, having a specific time for mating.

**The fifth division:** According to character: Some animals are calm of temperament and little given to anger, like the cow. Some are extremely ignorant and sharply angry, like the wild boar. Some are gentle yet deceptive, like the camel. Some are ill-behaved and treacherous, like the snake. Some are brave, strong, noble, great of spirit and generous of nature, like the lion. Some are strong yet treacherous and savage, like the wolf. Some are cunning, crafty and ill-behaved, like the fox. Some are irascible, extremely angry and foolish, yet fawning and seeking to be liked, like the dog. Some are extremely clever and tame, like the elephant and the monkey. Some are envious and vain of their beauty, like the peacock. Some are extremely cautious, like the camel and the donkey.

**The sixth division:** Among animals, there are those whose reproduction is by the female bearing a live young animal. Others reproduce by the female giving birth to a worm, as with the bee and the spider, whose young are worms, and whose organs are completed afterwards. Others reproduce by the female laying eggs.

Know that minds are too limited to comprehend fully the states of even the smallest animals. The way to infer the Creator from them is clear. For if the matter were simply the composition of the four natures, that would apply equally to all of them. Therefore the specialization of each one of these animals with its organs, faculties, body sizes, lifespans and dispositions must be by the planning of a dominant, wise Planner, exalted is He above what the deniers say. The best statement on this point is His, glorified is He: ﴿Allah creates what He wills. Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾, because He is the one capable of all and knowing of all. He is the one who knows the states of these animals; so what mind can grasp them, and what thought can reach an atom of their secrets? Rather, He is the one who creates what He wills, and no one prevents Him or repels Him.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, our companions' (the Ash'aris') argument by it is as previously mentioned. The response: al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) answered it by saying that the intended meaning is that He guides whoever has reached the limit of legal obligation (taklif), and not others; or the intended meaning is whoever obeys Him and merits reward, so He guides him to Paradise, as mentioned previously in its parallels. Our response to this response is also as mentioned previously in its parallels. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Of them are some that walk on their bellies, some that walk on two legs, and some that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ Indeed, We have sent down clear signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Of them are some that walk on their bellies, some that walk on two legs, and some that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent down clear signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

Know that this is the third type of proof for the Divine Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah). Having first argued from the conditions of the heavens and the earth, and second from the celestial phenomena (al-athar al-ulwiyyah), He now argues, third, from the conditions of animals. Know that this verse raises several questions.

**The first question:** Why did Allah say ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾ when many animals were not created from water? The angels are the most numerous of the animals, and they were created from light. The jinn were created from fire. Allah created Adam from dust, as in His words: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ (Al ʿImran 59), and He created ʿIsa from the wind, as in His words: ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ (al-Tahrim 12). Moreover, we see that many animals are generated without a drop of semen. The answer has several aspects:

First, and the best of them, is what al-Qaffal said: that the words ﴿from water﴾ are a complement of ﴿every creature﴾ and not a complement of ﴿created﴾. The meaning is that every creature is generated from water, and therefore it is created by Allah the Most High.

Second, the origin of all created things is water, according to what is related: "The first thing Allah the Most High created was a jewel, and He looked at it with the eye of awe, and it became water. Then from that water He created fire, air and light." Since the purpose of this verse is to explain the origin of creation, and the first origin is water, he mentioned it in this manner.

Third, the intended meaning of "creature" (dabbah) is that which crawls upon the face of the earth, and their dwelling is there. This excludes the angels and the jinn. Since the overwhelming majority of these animals were created from water, either because they are generated from a drop of semen, or because they cannot live except with water, he used the general term "every" to treat the majority as if it were the whole.

**The second question:** Why is "water" indefinite in ﴿from water﴾, while it comes definite in ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ (al-Anbiya 30)? [p. 16] The answer: It came indefinite here because the meaning is that He created every creature from a kind of water that is specific to that creature. It came definite in ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ because the purpose there is that they were created from this substance, whereas here the point is that this substance is divided into many kinds.

**The third question:** The pronoun in ﴿Of them﴾ (minhum) is used for rational beings, and likewise the word ﴿some﴾ (man). Why then is it used for non-rational beings? The answer: Allah mentioned non-rational beings together with rational ones, namely the angels, humans and jinn, so the form suited to the rational was given precedence, because making the nobler the principal and the baser the subsidiary is preferable to the reverse. And in common speech one says, "Who are the two approaching?" referring to a man and a camel.

**The fourth question:** Why did he call crawling on the belly "walking" (mashy)? This question is confirmed by the fact that a child may be described as crawling (yahbu) and one does not say that he walks (yamshi), even if he crawls in the manner that a snake crawls. The answer: This is by way of metaphor (istiʿarah), as they say of a continuing matter, "This matter has walked," and one says, "No matter goes smoothly for him" (la yatamashsha lahu amr).
