The Exalted said: ﴿They say, "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey," then after that a faction of them turn away. Those are not believers.﴾ ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a faction of them turn away.﴾ ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly.﴾ ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them? Rather, they are the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), He followed them with a condemnation of a people who professed the religion with their tongues but did not accept it in their hearts. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Muqatil said: This verse was revealed concerning Bishr, the hypocrite, who had a dispute with a Jew over a piece of land. The Jew wanted to take him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to judge between them, but the hypocrite kept pulling him toward Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, saying that Muhammad (ﷺ) was unjust toward us. Their story has already passed in Surat an-Nisa'.

al-Dahhak said: It was revealed concerning al-Mughira ibn Wa'il, who had land shared between him and Ali ibn Abi Talib. They divided it, and Ali's portion was such that water could reach it only with great difficulty. Al-Mughira said, "Sell me your land," and he sold it to him, and they exchanged. Then it was said to al-Mughira, "You took a salt flat that water cannot reach." So he said to Ali, "Take back your land, for I bought it only if I was satisfied with it, and I am not satisfied with it, since water cannot reach it." Ali said, "No, you bought it, you were satisfied with it, you took possession of it, and you knew its condition. I will not accept it from you." He invited him to bring the matter before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Mughira said, "As for Muhammad, I will not come to him or submit to his judgment, for he hates me, and I fear he will be unjust to me." So this verse was revealed.

al-Hasan said: This verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites who displayed faith and concealed disbelief.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿They say, "We believe"﴾ up to His saying, ﴿Those are not believers﴾, indicates that faith does not consist in speech alone, for if it did, it would not be correct to deny that they are believers, when they had done what is in reality faith. If it is said that He related of all of them that they say "We believe," and then related of a faction of them that they turned away, how is it correct to say of all of them, ﴿Those are not believers﴾, when the ones who turned away are only some of them? We answer: His saying, ﴿Those are not believers﴾, refers to those who turned away, not to the whole group mentioned first. Moreover, if it refers to the first group, it is also correct, and the meaning of His saying, ﴿then after that a faction of them turn away﴾, is that this faction turns back to the rest of them, so some of them show to others their retraction of what they had professed. Then He, glory be to Him, explained that when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that he may judge between them, a faction of them turn away. This is a rejection of contentment with the judgment of the Messenger. By His saying, ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly﴾, He pointed out that they turn away only when they know the truth is against them, or when they doubt. But when they know that the truth is in their favor, they abandon turning away and hasten to the judgment, submitting with a readiness to accept it. In this there is evidence that they do not follow the truth; rather, they seek immediate benefit. That too is hypocrisy.

As for His saying, ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them?﴾, there are questions concerning it:

The first question: The word "am" (or) is used for interrogation, and interrogation is not permissible with respect to Allah, the Exalted. The answer: The form is interrogative, but its meaning is declarative, as Jarir said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts [and the most generous of all peoples in filling the wine-jars' bellies]?"

The second question: If they feared that Allah would wrong them, then they had doubted the religion, and if they doubted, then there is a disease in their hearts. Thus they are one thing, so what is the benefit of enumerating them? The answer: His saying, ﴿Is there a disease in their hearts﴾, points to hypocrisy. His saying, ﴿or have they doubted﴾, points to the fact that this doubt and suspicion arose after Islam had been established in the heart. His saying, ﴿or do they fear that Allah will wrong them﴾, points to the fact that they had reached such love of this world that they would abandon the religion for its sake.

The third question: Suppose these three are distinct but mutually connected; how then is the word "am" applied to them? The answer:

[p. 20]

The closest answer is that He condemned them for each of these attributes. In their hearts was a disease, which is hypocrisy; in them was doubt and suspicion; and they feared injustice from the Messenger, peace be upon him. Each of these is disbelief and hypocrisy. Then He, the Exalted, explained by His saying, ﴿Rather, they are the wrongdoers﴾, the falsehood of what they were upon, because wrongdoing (zulm) encompasses every disobedience, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a tremendous wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], since a person is either a wrongdoer to himself or a wrongdoer to others. It may also be said that when the Exalted mentioned among the possibilities that they feared injustice, He refuted that by His saying, ﴿Rather, they are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: they do not fear that the Messenger, peace be upon him, will be unjust to them, because they know of his trustworthiness and integrity. Rather, they are wrongdoers who want to wrong the one who has a right over them, while they deny it. That is something they cannot do in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and yet they refuse to be judged by him.

Say: "Do not swear; reasonable obedience [is what is wanted]. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do."﴾ ﴿Say: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon him is only that with which he has been charged, and upon you is that with which you have been charged. And if you obey him, you will be guided. And there is not upon the Messenger except the clear notification."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related the saying of the hypocrites and what they said and did, He followed it with mention of what the believers ought to do and how they ought to conduct themselves. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The only saying of the believers﴾ and in this are several issues:

The first issue: al-Hasan recited "qawlu al-mu'minin" (with the nominative). The accusative (qawla) is stronger, because the more definite of the two nouns is the one that should be the subject (ism of kana), and "an yaqulu" (that they say) is more definite, since it cannot be made indefinite, unlike "qawla al-mu'minin."

The second issue: His saying ﴿The only saying of the believers﴾ means: thus it must be that their saying and conduct, when they are called to the judgment of the Book of Allah and His Messenger, is that they say: "We hear and we obey," so that their coming to him and their submission to him is by hearing and obedience. The meaning of ﴿We hear﴾ is "we respond," according to the interpretation of the Muslims' saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him," i.e., accepts and answers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾, i.e., in what is difficult for him and what is pleasing to him, ﴿and fears Allah﴾ regarding what has proceeded from him of sins in the past, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾ regarding what remains of his life. ﴿Those are the attainers of success.﴾ This verse, despite its brevity, comprises everything the believers ought to do.

As for His saying: ﴿And they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if you command them, they will surely go forth﴾, Muqatil said: whoever swears by Allah has exerted himself in the oath. Then he said: When Allah explained the hypocrites' aversion to the judgment of the Messenger of Allah, they said: "By Allah, if you command us to leave our homes, our wealth, and our women, we would leave, and if you command us to fight, we would fight." Then He, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to forbid them from this oath by His saying: ﴿Say: Do not swear﴾. Had their oath been as it should be, forbidding it would not have been permissible, because one who swears to carry out righteousness and what is obligatory must not be forbidden from it. When this is established, it is established that their oath was due to their hypocrisy, and that their inner state was contrary to their outward state, and whoever intends betrayal and not fulfillment, his oath can only be ugly.

As for His saying: ﴿reasonable obedience﴾, it is either the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., what is required of you is reasonable obedience, not false oaths; or a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., reasonable obedience is better than your oath about what you do not truthfully uphold. It was said its meaning is: leave the oath and do not be deceived by it, and upon you is reasonable obedience, so hold fast to it. Al-Yazidi recited "ta'atan ma'rufatan" with the accusative, meaning: obey the obedience of Allah. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, i.e., He is All-Seeing, nothing of your inner secrets is hidden from Him, and He will surely expose you and requite you for your hypocrisy.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon him is only that with which he has been charged, and upon you is that with which you have been charged﴾, know that He, exalted is He, turned the speech from the third person to the second person in the manner of iltifat, and this is more eloquent in rebuking them. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ means: if you turn away from the obedience of Allah and the obedience of His Messenger, then upon the Messenger is what he was charged with of conveying the message, and upon you is what you were charged with of obedience. ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾, i.e., you will attain the truth. And if you disobey him, then there is not upon the Messenger except the clear notification. "Al-balagh" means the conveying, and "al-mubin" means the clear, the one who makes clear what you need. It is related from Nafi' that he recited "fa-innama 'alayhi ma hamala" with a fatha on the ha' and light pronunciation, meaning: upon him is the sin of what he carried of disobedience.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 55:

﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, as He made successors those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely change their state after their fear into security. They worship Me, not associating anything with Me. And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that the implied construction of the verse is: "Convey (the message), O Messenger, and obey Him, O believers, for Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds," meaning those who combined faith with righteous action, "that He will make them successors upon the earth, making them the successors (khulafa'), the dominant ones, and the possessors (of it), just as He made successors upon it those before them, in the time of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and others." And that He will establish for them their religion. This establishment means that He will support them with victory and honor. And He will change their state after their fear of the enemy into security, by granting them victory over them so that they kill them and are secure from their evil. So they worship Me in security, not associating anything with Me, and they do not fear. ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ means after this promise and apostatizes, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that this verse contains an explanation of most of the fundamental religious issues (al-masa'il al-usuliyya). Let us point to their core:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾, indicates that He, glory be to Him, is a speaker (mutakallim), because promising is a kind of speech, and whoever is described by a kind is described by the genus. Also, He, glory be to Him, is an obeyed King, and an obeyed King must be in a position where he can promise his allies and threaten his enemies. Thus it is established that He, glory be to Him, is a speaker.

* * *

**The second issue:** The verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, knows things before they occur, contrary to Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who said that He does not know them before they occur. The way of deriving proof from it is that He, glory be to Him, informed of the occurrence of a matter in the future with a detailed informing, and the informed matter occurred in agreement with the information, and such information cannot be valid except with knowledge.

* * *

**The third issue:** The verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, is Living and Powerful over all possibilities, because He said: ﴿They will surely make them successors upon the earth as He made successors those before them, and will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and will surely change their state after their fear into security﴾. He did all of that, and the occurrence of these things is valid only from the One Who is Powerful over all that is within the scope of power.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, is the One deserving of worship, because He said ﴿They worship Me﴾. The Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist theological school) said: the verse indicates that the act of Allah, exalted is He, is causally motivated by a purpose, because the meaning is "in order that they worship Me." They also said: the verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, wills worship from all, because whoever does an act for a purpose must necessarily will that purpose.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is free from partners, by His saying ﴿not associating anything with Me﴾. This indicates the negation of a second god, and that it is not permissible to worship other than Allah, exalted is He, whether it is a star, as the Sabians (al-Sabi'a) claim, or an idol, as the idol-worshippers claim.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** The verse indicates the validity of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because He informed of the unseen in His saying: ﴿They will surely make them successors upon the earth as He made successors those before them, and will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and will surely change their state after their fear into security﴾. This informed matter has been found to agree with the information, and such information is a miracle (mu'jiz), and a miracle is proof of truthfulness. So it indicates the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ).

* * *

**The seventh issue:** The verse indicates that righteous action is outside the definition of faith, contrary to the Mu'tazila, because He conjoined righteous action to faith, and the conjoined is outside of that to which it is conjoined.

* * *

**The eighth issue:** The verse indicates the imamate (imamah) of the four Imams, and that is because He, exalted is He, promised those who believed and did righteous deeds from among those present in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿They will surely make them successors upon the earth as He made successors those before them﴾, and that He will establish for them their approved religion, and that He will change their state after fear into security. It is known that what is meant by this promise after the Messenger are these people, because the succession of others can only occur after him. And it is known that there is no prophet after him, because he is the Seal of the Prophets. So what is meant by this succession is the path of the imamate. And it is known that after the Messenger, the succession with this description occurred only in the days of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, because in their days there were great conquests, establishment (of the religion) occurred, and religion and security became manifest. This did not occur in the days of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, because he did not devote himself to fighting the disbelievers, being occupied with fighting those among the People of the Prayer who opposed him. Thus, by this, the verse's indication of the validity of the succession of these people is established.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of the verse is abandoned, because it requires that succession be granted to everyone who believes and does righteous deeds, and the matter is not like that. We set that aside. But why should it not be permissible that what is meant by His saying ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ is that He will settle them in the earth and empower them to act freely, not that what is meant is the caliphate of Allah, exalted is He? Among what indicates this is His saying: ﴿as He made successors those before them﴾, and the succession of those who came before them was not by way of the imamate, so the matter concerning them must also be like that. We set that aside. But here there is what indicates that it is not permissible to interpret it as the caliphate of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because among your school's doctrine is that he, peace be upon him, did not appoint anyone as successor, and it is narrated from Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: "I leave you as the Messenger of Allah left you." We set that aside. But why should it not be permissible that what is meant by it is Ali, peace be upon him, and the singular may be expressed with the plural form as a form of honor, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], and He said concerning Ali, peace be upon him: ﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakat while bowing﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 55]. We set that aside, but we interpret it as referring to the Twelve Imams.

As for the answer to the first: the word "min" (among) is for partitive meaning, so His saying ﴿among you﴾ indicates that what is meant by this address is some of them.

As for the answer to the second: the succession in the sense you have mentioned is attained by all creation, so what is mentioned here in the context of glad tidings must necessarily be different from it.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as He made successors those before them﴾, those who were before them were successors at times by means of prophethood and at other times by means of the imamate, and the succession is attained in both cases.

As for the answer to the third: although it is among our doctrine that he, peace be upon him, did not appoint anyone as successor by designation, he did appoint successors by description and by directing (the choice) to selection. So there is nothing preventing that, concerning these four Imams, Allah, exalted is He, appointed them and the Messenger appointed them. On this basis they said of Abu Bakr: "O successor of the Messenger of Allah." So what is said, that he, peace be upon him, did not appoint a successor, is meant in the sense of designation by name, and when it is said that he appointed a successor, what is meant is by way of description and direction.

As for the answer to the fourth: interpreting a plural form as referring to a singular is metaphorical (majaz), and it contradicts the original usage.

As for the answer to the fifth: it is invalid for two reasons:

The first: His saying ﴿among you﴾ indicates that this address was with those present, and these Imams were not present.

The second: He, exalted is He, promised them strength, power, and effective authority in the world, and that was not found in him (Ali). Thus it is established by this the validity of the imamate of the four Imams, and the claim of the Rafida (Rafidah, a Shi'i group) who criticize Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman is refuted, and so is the claim of the Khawarij who criticize Uthman and Ali. Let us return to the exegesis.

As for His saying: ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾, one may ask: where is the oath introduced by the lam and nun in ﴿la-yastakhlifannahum﴾? We say: it is omitted, its estimate being: "Allah promised them that He will surely make them successors," or the promise of Allah, in its realization, was made equivalent to an oath, so it is introduced by what an oath is introduced by, as if He had said: "Allah swore that He will surely make them successors."

As for His saying: ﴿as He made successors those before them﴾, meaning, as He made Harun, Yusha', Dawud, and Sulayman successors. The estimate of the construction is: "He will surely make them successors with a succession like the succession of those prophets before them, peace be upon them." And it was recited as "kama istukhlifa" (with a passive verb, the taa' with a damma and the lam with a kasra), and it was also recited with a fatha.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them﴾, the meaning is that He will firmly establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and it is Islam. Ibn Kathir, Asim, and Ya'qub recited "wa-la-yubdilannahum" (with the form from ibdal, with lightening of the middle letter), and the rest recited it with tashdid (the doubled form, from tabdil). We have already mentioned the difference between them in His saying: ﴿We will exchange them for other skins﴾ [al-Nisa': 56].

As for His saying: ﴿They worship Me, not associating anything with Me﴾, it contains an indication that those He means do not turn away from the worship of Allah, exalted is He, to association. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ in the state of their worship and sincerity to Allah, that He will surely do such and such to them; and it is permissible that it be a new, independent clause, in the manner of praising them.

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that﴾, meaning, denies the rightful claim of these blessings, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning, the disobedient.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 56–57:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish the prayer and give zakat and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve will cause failure [to Allah] within the earth; their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the destination.﴾

As for the explanation of establishing the prayer and giving zakat, and the word la'alla (perhaps, so that) and the word mercy, all of these have been discussed repeatedly before.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve will cause failure [to Allah] within the earth﴾, the meaning is: Do not think, O Muhammad, that those who disbelieve are outstripping and escaping [Us], to the point that they could frustrate Me from overtaking them. It has been recited as "lā yaḥsabanna" with the letter yā' (ya) dotted from below, and in this there are several possibilities:
The first: that "muʿjizīna fil-arḍ" ("causing failure within the earth") are the two objects, and the meaning is: Let not those who disbelieve think that anyone can frustrate Allah within the earth, so that they would hope for the like of that themselves.

The second: that the pronoun referring to the Messenger ﷺ is in it, due to his mention having preceded in His saying: ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾. The meaning is: Let not those who disbelieve think [themselves] causing failure.

The third: that the original is "wa lā yaḥsabannahumu alladhīna kafarū muʿjizīn," and then the pronoun that is the first object was omitted.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿And their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the destination﴾, the author of [al-Kashshaf] said: The structure does not allow it to be connected to His saying "lā taḥsabanna," because that is a negation and this is an affirmation. Therefore it is coordinated with the conjunction "wa" (and) upon a pronoun preceding it, its estimate being: "Do not think that those who disbelieve will cause failure [to Allah] within the earth; rather they are subdued, and their refuge is the Fire."
