Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 58–59 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those of you who have not reached puberty ask permission of you at three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you put off your clothing at midday, and after the night prayer. Those are three times of nakedness (ʿawrah) for you. There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they move about among you, some of you upon others. Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame upon them for putting off their clothing without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

Know that in the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. Although its apparent meaning is men, what is intended is men and women, because the masculine is given precedence over the feminine. When it is not differentiated, everyone enters under His saying ﴿O you who have believed, let them ask permission of you﴾. And what clarifies this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾, because that is said of men and women. In my view, however, the ruling is established for women by a clear analogy (qiyas jali), because women are in a stricter position than men regarding the guarding of nakedness. So when this ruling is established for men, its establishment for women is by way of greater priority (al-awla), just as we establish the prohibition of striking by clear analogy with the prohibition of saying "uff" (to parents).

* * *

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ includes both adults and children. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that what is meant is the children. They argued that an adult slave is not permitted to look at his master's household except at what a free person is permitted to look at. Ibn al-Musayyib said: Let not His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ deceive you; it is not fitting for a woman that her slave look at her earring, her hair, or anything of her beauty. Others said: rather, an adult male slave is permitted to look at the hair of his female master and what is similar to it. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the restriction, to the slaves of the believers and to free children, of the permission to do what Allah, may He be exalted, had earlier forbidden to the community of believers in His saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. For He permitted them, except at the three times, and permitted their entering among those who have not reached puberty without permission, and the entering of the attendants upon them, by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they move about among you﴾, that is, some of you move about upon others, at times other than the three. He confirmed this by obligating those who have reached puberty to follow the practice of those before them among the adults in asking permission at all other times, and He joined them to those who fall under His saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants﴾.

* * *

The third issue: His saying: ﴿let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. If what is meant is the male and female slaves when they are adults, it is not impossible that it is a command to them in reality. But if what is meant is ﴿and those who have not reached puberty﴾, it is not permissible that it be a command to them, and it must be a command to us, that we order them to do so and send them to it, just as we are commanded to order the child. And he who has understood prayer may perform it, not in the manner of an obligation upon them, but it is an obligation upon us because of the benefit in it for us and for them after puberty. It is not far-fetched that the wording of the command, although in appearance directed at them, is in reality directed at the master, like your saying to a man: "Let your family and your child fear you." The apparent address is to them, and the real address is to him, by doing that which they fear in his presence.

* * *

The fourth issue: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent a boy from the Ansar to ʿUmar to call him, and he found him asleep in the house. He pushed the door and greeted, but ʿUmar did not awaken. He returned, pushed the door again, stood behind him and shook him, but he did not awaken. The boy said: O Allah, wake him for me. He pushed the door again, then called out to him, and he awoke and sat up, and the boy entered. Something of ʿUmar was uncovered, and ʿUmar realized that the boy had seen that from him. He said: I wish that Allah had forbidden our sons, our women and our servants from entering upon us at these hours without permission." Then he went with him to the Messenger ﷺ, and found that there had been revealed to him: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. At that, ʿUmar praised Allah, may He be exalted. The Messenger, upon him be peace, said: "What is that, O ʿUmar?" He informed him of what the boy had done. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ marveled at his action, asked his name and praised him, and said: "Indeed Allah loves the forbearing, the modest, the chaste who refrains, and He dislikes the vulgar, the bold, the one who begs insistently." This verse is one of the verses revealed on account of ʿUmar. Some said: it was revealed concerning Asma' bint Abi Marthad. She said: "We enter upon a man and a woman, and perhaps they are under one blanket." It was also said: "A large boy of hers entered upon her at a time she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: Our servants and our boys enter upon us in a state we dislike, so the verse was revealed."

The fifth issue: Ibn ʿUmar and Mujahid said that His saying ﴿let them ask permission of you﴾ refers to males only, not females, because His saying ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is in the masculine form, not the feminine. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it applies to men and women, who should ask permission at all times, by night and by day. The correct view is that this ruling must be established for women, because just as a person dislikes males seeing his circumstances, he may also dislike females seeing them. But the ruling is established for women by analogy, not by the apparent wording, as we have previously stated.

The sixth issue: Some scholars said: the command in His saying ﴿let them ask permission of you﴾ is for recommendation (nadb) and desirability (istihbab). Others said: it is for obligation (ijab), and this is more correct, because it is established that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and those of you who have not reached puberty﴾, there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: Ibn ʿUmar recited "al-hulm" (الحُلْم) with a sukun.

The second issue: The jurists agreed that wet dreams (al-ihtilam) are a sign of puberty (bulugh). They differed when a boy reaches fifteen years and has not had a wet dream. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The boy is not an adult until he reaches eighteen years and completes them; for a girl, seventeen years. Al-Shafiʿi, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them, said for both boy and girl: fifteen years. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and those of you who have not reached puberty﴾ indicates the invalidity of the view of one who makes the limit of puberty fifteen years when one has not had a wet dream; for Allah, may He be exalted, did not differentiate between one who has reached it and one who falls short of it, provided he has not reached the wet dream. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ through many channels: "The pen is lifted from three: from the sleeper until he awakens, from the insane until he recovers, and from the child until he has a wet dream." And he did not differentiate between one who has reached fifteen years and one who has not. If it is said: this statement also invalidates the determination of eighteen years. He answered: We know that the customary age of puberty is fifteen years, and everything based on customary practice may admit excess or deficiency. We have found one who reached puberty at twelve years. We have explained that exceeding the usual is permissible just as falling short of it is. So Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, treated the excess like the deficiency, which is three years. It has been related from Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, nineteen years for a boy, and this is to be understood as completing eighteen years and entering the nineteenth.

The proof of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, is what Ibn ʿUmar related: that he was presented to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Uhud when he was fourteen years old, and he did not permit him; and he was presented to him on the day of the Trench when he was fifteen years old, and he permitted him. Abu Bakr al-Razi objected to this, saying: This report is inconsistent, because Uhud was in the third year and the Trench in the fifth year, so how can there be a single year between them? Moreover, permission to fight has no connection with puberty, for he may reject one who has reached puberty because of his weakness, and permit one who has not reached puberty because of his strength and his capacity to bear arms. A proof of this is that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, did not ask him about the wet dream or the age.

The second investigation: They differed as to whether the growth of hair (al-inbat) is a sign of puberty. Abu Hanifa and his companions did not treat it as puberty, while al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, treated it as puberty. Abu Bakr al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and those of you who have not reached puberty﴾ negates that growth of hair is puberty if one has not had a wet dream, just as it negated that fifteen years is puberty. Likewise is His saying, upon him be peace: "and from the child until he has a wet dream."

The proof of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah, may He be exalted, have mercy on him, is what ʿAtiyya al-Qurazi related: that the Prophet ﷺ ordered that those of Qurayza who had grown hair be killed and that those who had not grown hair be spared. He said: "They looked at me, and I had not grown hair, so they spared me."

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: This hadith cannot be used to establish the Shariʿa, by it or by its like, for several reasons:
One: ʿAtiyya is unknown, and is known only from this report, especially since he objects to the verse; and the report negates puberty except by wet dream.
Two: Its wordings differ. In some of them, he ordered the killing of whoever had the pubic hair grown, and in some, whoever's cheek had turned green (the first down). It is known that one does not reach this state except after having already reached puberty, and the growth of pubic hair does not occur except to a man who is grown. So the growth of hair and the appearance of pubic hair are a metaphor for reaching the measure of age we mentioned, which is eighteen years or more.
Three: Growth of hair indicates physical strength, so the order to kill was for that reason, not for puberty.

Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These possibilities are refuted by what is related: that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about a boy, and he said: "Has his cheek turned green?" This indicates that this was like a matter agreed upon among the Companions.

The third investigation: It is related from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they considered, for puberty, that a person reach five spans (ashbar) in height. It is related from ʿAli, upon him be peace, that he said: "When the boy reaches five spans, the prescribed penalties apply to him, and retaliation is taken for him and from him." And from Ibn Sirin, from Anas, who said: "Abu Bakr was brought a boy who had stolen, so he ordered that he be measured, and he fell short by a joint of a finger, so he released him." This view was adopted by al-Farazdaq in his saying:

He has not ceased since his hands tied his waistwrap, and he grew tall and reached five spans.

Most jurists do not hold this view, because a person may be below the age of puberty and yet be tall, and above the age of puberty and yet be short, so it carries no weight.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Some people said that His words, ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur: 27], indicate that seeking permission is obligatory in every situation, and that this was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by this verse in other than these three times. Others said: the first verse is addressed to the mukallaf (one who is legally responsible), since it is addressed to those who have believed, while what Allah mentions in this verse concerns those who are not mukallaf. Regarding this, it was said that in some circumstances such a person may not enter except with permission, and in others without permission. So there is no basis for interpreting this as abrogation, because whatever the first verse covers among those addressed, the second verse does not cover at all. If it is said that, on the supposition that His words ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ include those who have reached puberty, then abrogation is necessary, we reply: that is not necessary either, because His words ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses﴾ apply only to those who own the houses, by virtue of this attribution (of ownership). Given this, it does not include slaves and female slaves, so abrogation is not necessary on this view either. As for if the statement is understood to refer to young slaves, the matter is clearer.

**The sixth issue:** Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: No scholar has held that the command to seek permission has been abrogated. ʿAtaʾ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "There are three verses of the Book of Allah that people have abandoned, and I do not see anyone acting upon them." ʿAtaʾ said: "I memorised two and forgot one." He then recited this verse, and His words ﴿O mankind, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. Saʿid ibn Jubayr mentioned that the third verse is His words ﴿And when the division is witnessed by relatives...﴾ [al-Nisa: 8], and so on.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿It is not upon you nor upon them any sin, beyond these times, that they go about among you, some of you attending upon others﴾, there are several questions:

**The first question:** Do you say that His words ﴿It is not upon you nor upon them any sin﴾ imply permissibility in every situation? **Answer:** We have already explained that this applies only to children, so it is permissible for them to enter for service without permission outside the three times, and it is permissible for us to allow them to do so and to enter upon them as well.

**The second question:** Does this imply permissibility for them to see the nakedness (ʿawrah) of the household? **Answer:** No. Allah only permitted this because it was customary that nakedness is not exposed at other times. Therefore, if a woman exposes her nakedness while suspecting that servants may enter upon her, this is forbidden for her. If the servant is one who is subject to legal responsibility, it is also forbidden for him to enter if he suspects that there is exposure of nakedness. If it is said: Is there not among the people one who permitted a mature male slave to look at the hair of his mistress? We reply: whoever permitted that removed the hair from being ʿawrah on account of the right of ownership, just as it is removed from being ʿawrah on account of the right of kinship, since ʿawrah is divided: there is that which is ʿawrah in every situation, and there is that whose status varies according to relation, so that it is ʿawrah with a stranger but not ʿawrah with others, as previously mentioned.

**The third question:** Do you say that this permission is restricted to servants and not to others? **Answer:** Yes. His words ﴿It is not upon you nor upon them any sin, beyond these times﴾ indicate that this ruling is specific to children and not to adults, as previously mentioned. Allah has explicitly stated this afterwards when He said: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission as those before them sought permission﴾ [al-Nur: 59]. What is meant is that whoever reaches puberty later should be in the same position as those who reached it earlier with regard to the obligation to seek permission. This is the meaning of His words ﴿as those before them sought permission﴾. It may be thought that one who served during childhood, once he reaches puberty, may no longer seek permission, and that his situation differs from one who did not serve and was not owned. So Allah made clear that just as He forbade adults to enter without permission, the same applies to these (former children) once they reach puberty, even if they previously served or ownership of them was established for them.

* * *

**The fourth question:** Is the command to seek permission specific to slaves and those who have not reached puberty, or does it encompass all relatives? And if a slave is a relative, is it obligatory for a stranger too to seek permission? **Answer:** As for the first case, yes, either because of the general wording of His words ﴿Do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission﴾, or by analogy with the slave, and one who has not reached puberty is included even more so. As for the second case, it is obligatory to seek permission because of the generality of the verse.

**The fifth question:** What is the grammatical position of ﴿It is not upon you﴾ (laysa ʿalaykum)? **Answer:** If ﴿three times of nakedness﴾ is read in the nominative (*thalathu ʿawrat*), then it is in the position of a description, and the meaning is: they are three times of nakedness specified for seeking permission. If it is read in the accusative (*thalatha*), then it has no grammatical position, and it is a statement affirming the command to seek permission during those specific times.

**The sixth question:** What is the meaning of His words ﴿going about among you﴾ (ṭawwafūna ʿalaykum)? **Answer:** Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj said: it is a new sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*), like your saying in speech: "They are only your servants and those who go about among you." The ṭawwafūn are those who frequently enter, leave and move about, and the root is from ṭawaf (circling/going around). The meaning is: some of you go around among others without permission.

**The seventh question:** What is the case of *baʿḍukum* (some of you)? **Answer:** It is in the nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate is ʿalā baʿḍin (upon some), with the meaning "one of you goes about upon another." The predicate was omitted because ṭawwafūna indicates it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verses 58–59 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those of you who have not reached puberty ask permission of you at three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you put off your clothing at midday, and after the night prayer. Those are three times of nakedness (ʿawrah) for you. There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they move about among you, some of you upon others. Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame upon them for putting off their clothing without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

Know that in the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. Although its apparent meaning is men, what is intended is men and women, because the masculine is given precedence over the feminine. When it is not differentiated, everyone enters under His saying ﴿O you who have believed, let them ask permission of you﴾. And what clarifies this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾, because that is said of men and women. In my view, however, the ruling is established for women by a clear analogy (qiyas jali), because women are in a stricter position than men regarding the guarding of nakedness. So when this ruling is established for men, its establishment for women is by way of greater priority (al-awla), just as we establish the prohibition of striking by clear analogy with the prohibition of saying "uff" (to parents).

* * *

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ includes both adults and children. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that what is meant is the children. They argued that an adult slave is not permitted to look at his master's household except at what a free person is permitted to look at. Ibn al-Musayyib said: Let not His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ deceive you; it is not fitting for a woman that her slave look at her earring, her hair, or anything of her beauty. Others said: rather, an adult male slave is permitted to look at the hair of his female master and what is similar to it. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the restriction, to the slaves of the believers and to free children, of the permission to do what Allah, may He be exalted, had earlier forbidden to the community of believers in His saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. For He permitted them, except at the three times, and permitted their entering among those who have not reached puberty without permission, and the entering of the attendants upon them, by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they move about among you﴾, that is, some of you move about upon others, at times other than the three. He confirmed this by obligating those who have reached puberty to follow the practice of those before them among the adults in asking permission at all other times, and He joined them to those who fall under His saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought familiarity and greeted their occupants﴾.

* * *

The third issue: His saying: ﴿let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. If what is meant is the male and female slaves when they are adults, it is not impossible that it is a command to them in reality. But if what is meant is ﴿and those who have not reached puberty﴾, it is not permissible that it be a command to them, and it must be a command to us, that we order them to do so and send them to it, just as we are commanded to order the child. And he who has understood prayer may perform it, not in the manner of an obligation upon them, but it is an obligation upon us because of the benefit in it for us and for them after puberty. It is not far-fetched that the wording of the command, although in appearance directed at them, is in reality directed at the master, like your saying to a man: "Let your family and your child fear you." The apparent address is to them, and the real address is to him, by doing that which they fear in his presence.

* * *

The fourth issue: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent a boy from the Ansar to ʿUmar to call him, and he found him asleep in the house. He pushed the door and greeted, but ʿUmar did not awaken. He returned, pushed the door again, stood behind him and shook him, but he did not awaken. The boy said: O Allah, wake him for me. He pushed the door again, then called out to him, and he awoke and sat up, and the boy entered. Something of ʿUmar was uncovered, and ʿUmar realized that the boy had seen that from him. He said: I wish that Allah had forbidden our sons, our women and our servants from entering upon us at these hours without permission." Then he went with him to the Messenger ﷺ, and found that there had been revealed to him: ﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾. At that, ʿUmar praised Allah, may He be exalted. The Messenger, upon him be peace, said: "What is that, O ʿUmar?" He informed him of what the boy had done. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ marveled at his action, asked his name and praised him, and said: "Indeed Allah loves the forbearing, the modest, the chaste who refrains, and He dislikes the vulgar, the bold, the one who begs insistently." This verse is one of the verses revealed on account of ʿUmar. Some said: it was revealed concerning Asma' bint Abi Marthad. She said: "We enter upon a man and a woman, and perhaps they are under one blanket." It was also said: "A large boy of hers entered upon her at a time she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: Our servants and our boys enter upon us in a state we dislike, so the verse was revealed."

The fifth issue: Ibn ʿUmar and Mujahid said that His saying ﴿let them ask permission of you﴾ refers to males only, not females, because His saying ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is in the masculine form, not the feminine. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it applies to men and women, who should ask permission at all times, by night and by day. The correct view is that this ruling must be established for women, because just as a person dislikes males seeing his circumstances, he may also dislike females seeing them. But the ruling is established for women by analogy, not by the apparent wording, as we have previously stated.

The sixth issue: Some scholars said: the command in His saying ﴿let them ask permission of you﴾ is for recommendation (nadb) and desirability (istihbab). Others said: it is for obligation (ijab), and this is more correct, because it is established that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and those of you who have not reached puberty﴾, there are issues concerning it.

The first issue: Ibn ʿUmar recited "al-hulm" (الحُلْم) with a sukun.

The second issue: The jurists agreed that wet dreams (al-ihtilam) are a sign of puberty (bulugh). They differed when a boy reaches fifteen years and has not had a wet dream. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The boy is not an adult until he reaches eighteen years and completes them; for a girl, seventeen years. Al-Shafiʿi, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them, said for both boy and girl: fifteen years. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and those of you who have not reached puberty﴾ indicates the invalidity of the view of one who makes the limit of puberty fifteen years when one has not had a wet dream; for Allah, may He be exalted, did not differentiate between one who has reached it and one who falls short of it, provided he has not reached the wet dream. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ through many channels: "The pen is lifted from three: from the sleeper until he awakens, from the insane until he recovers, and from the child until he has a wet dream." And he did not differentiate between one who has reached fifteen years and one who has not. If it is said: this statement also invalidates the determination of eighteen years. He answered: We know that the customary age of puberty is fifteen years, and everything based on customary practice may admit excess or deficiency. We have found one who reached puberty at twelve years. We have explained that exceeding the usual is permissible just as falling short of it is. So Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, treated the excess like the deficiency, which is three years. It has been related from Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, nineteen years for a boy, and this is to be understood as completing eighteen years and entering the nineteenth.

The proof of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, is what Ibn ʿUmar related: that he was presented to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Uhud when he was fourteen years old, and he did not permit him; and he was presented to him on the day of the Trench when he was fifteen years old, and he permitted him. Abu Bakr al-Razi objected to this, saying: This report is inconsistent, because Uhud was in the third year and the Trench in the fifth year, so how can there be a single year between them? Moreover, permission to fight has no connection with puberty, for he may reject one who has reached puberty because of his weakness, and permit one who has not reached puberty because of his strength and his capacity to bear arms. A proof of this is that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, did not ask him about the wet dream or the age.

The second investigation: They differed as to whether the growth of hair (al-inbat) is a sign of puberty. Abu Hanifa and his companions did not treat it as puberty, while al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, treated it as puberty. Abu Bakr al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and those of you who have not reached puberty﴾ negates that growth of hair is puberty if one has not had a wet dream, just as it negated that fifteen years is puberty. Likewise is His saying, upon him be peace: "and from the child until he has a wet dream."

The proof of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah, may He be exalted, have mercy on him, is what ʿAtiyya al-Qurazi related: that the Prophet ﷺ ordered that those of Qurayza who had grown hair be killed and that those who had not grown hair be spared. He said: "They looked at me, and I had not grown hair, so they spared me."

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: This hadith cannot be used to establish the Shariʿa, by it or by its like, for several reasons:
One: ʿAtiyya is unknown, and is known only from this report, especially since he objects to the verse; and the report negates puberty except by wet dream.
Two: Its wordings differ. In some of them, he ordered the killing of whoever had the pubic hair grown, and in some, whoever's cheek had turned green (the first down). It is known that one does not reach this state except after having already reached puberty, and the growth of pubic hair does not occur except to a man who is grown. So the growth of hair and the appearance of pubic hair are a metaphor for reaching the measure of age we mentioned, which is eighteen years or more.
Three: Growth of hair indicates physical strength, so the order to kill was for that reason, not for puberty.

Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These possibilities are refuted by what is related: that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about a boy, and he said: "Has his cheek turned green?" This indicates that this was like a matter agreed upon among the Companions.

The third investigation: It is related from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they considered, for puberty, that a person reach five spans (ashbar) in height. It is related from ʿAli, upon him be peace, that he said: "When the boy reaches five spans, the prescribed penalties apply to him, and retaliation is taken for him and from him." And from Ibn Sirin, from Anas, who said: "Abu Bakr was brought a boy who had stolen, so he ordered that he be measured, and he fell short by a joint of a finger, so he released him." This view was adopted by al-Farazdaq in his saying:

He has not ceased since his hands tied his waistwrap, and he grew tall and reached five spans.

Most jurists do not hold this view, because a person may be below the age of puberty and yet be tall, and above the age of puberty and yet be short, so it carries no weight.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Some people said that His words, ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur: 27], indicate that seeking permission is obligatory in every situation, and that this was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by this verse in other than these three times. Others said: the first verse is addressed to the mukallaf (one who is legally responsible), since it is addressed to those who have believed, while what Allah mentions in this verse concerns those who are not mukallaf. Regarding this, it was said that in some circumstances such a person may not enter except with permission, and in others without permission. So there is no basis for interpreting this as abrogation, because whatever the first verse covers among those addressed, the second verse does not cover at all. If it is said that, on the supposition that His words ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ include those who have reached puberty, then abrogation is necessary, we reply: that is not necessary either, because His words ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses﴾ apply only to those who own the houses, by virtue of this attribution (of ownership). Given this, it does not include slaves and female slaves, so abrogation is not necessary on this view either. As for if the statement is understood to refer to young slaves, the matter is clearer.

**The sixth issue:** Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: No scholar has held that the command to seek permission has been abrogated. ʿAtaʾ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "There are three verses of the Book of Allah that people have abandoned, and I do not see anyone acting upon them." ʿAtaʾ said: "I memorised two and forgot one." He then recited this verse, and His words ﴿O mankind, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. Saʿid ibn Jubayr mentioned that the third verse is His words ﴿And when the division is witnessed by relatives...﴾ [al-Nisa: 8], and so on.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿It is not upon you nor upon them any sin, beyond these times, that they go about among you, some of you attending upon others﴾, there are several questions:

**The first question:** Do you say that His words ﴿It is not upon you nor upon them any sin﴾ imply permissibility in every situation? **Answer:** We have already explained that this applies only to children, so it is permissible for them to enter for service without permission outside the three times, and it is permissible for us to allow them to do so and to enter upon them as well.

**The second question:** Does this imply permissibility for them to see the nakedness (ʿawrah) of the household? **Answer:** No. Allah only permitted this because it was customary that nakedness is not exposed at other times. Therefore, if a woman exposes her nakedness while suspecting that servants may enter upon her, this is forbidden for her. If the servant is one who is subject to legal responsibility, it is also forbidden for him to enter if he suspects that there is exposure of nakedness. If it is said: Is there not among the people one who permitted a mature male slave to look at the hair of his mistress? We reply: whoever permitted that removed the hair from being ʿawrah on account of the right of ownership, just as it is removed from being ʿawrah on account of the right of kinship, since ʿawrah is divided: there is that which is ʿawrah in every situation, and there is that whose status varies according to relation, so that it is ʿawrah with a stranger but not ʿawrah with others, as previously mentioned.

**The third question:** Do you say that this permission is restricted to servants and not to others? **Answer:** Yes. His words ﴿It is not upon you nor upon them any sin, beyond these times﴾ indicate that this ruling is specific to children and not to adults, as previously mentioned. Allah has explicitly stated this afterwards when He said: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission as those before them sought permission﴾ [al-Nur: 59]. What is meant is that whoever reaches puberty later should be in the same position as those who reached it earlier with regard to the obligation to seek permission. This is the meaning of His words ﴿as those before them sought permission﴾. It may be thought that one who served during childhood, once he reaches puberty, may no longer seek permission, and that his situation differs from one who did not serve and was not owned. So Allah made clear that just as He forbade adults to enter without permission, the same applies to these (former children) once they reach puberty, even if they previously served or ownership of them was established for them.

* * *

**The fourth question:** Is the command to seek permission specific to slaves and those who have not reached puberty, or does it encompass all relatives? And if a slave is a relative, is it obligatory for a stranger too to seek permission? **Answer:** As for the first case, yes, either because of the general wording of His words ﴿Do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission﴾, or by analogy with the slave, and one who has not reached puberty is included even more so. As for the second case, it is obligatory to seek permission because of the generality of the verse.

**The fifth question:** What is the grammatical position of ﴿It is not upon you﴾ (laysa ʿalaykum)? **Answer:** If ﴿three times of nakedness﴾ is read in the nominative (*thalathu ʿawrat*), then it is in the position of a description, and the meaning is: they are three times of nakedness specified for seeking permission. If it is read in the accusative (*thalatha*), then it has no grammatical position, and it is a statement affirming the command to seek permission during those specific times.

**The sixth question:** What is the meaning of His words ﴿going about among you﴾ (ṭawwafūna ʿalaykum)? **Answer:** Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj said: it is a new sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*), like your saying in speech: "They are only your servants and those who go about among you." The ṭawwafūn are those who frequently enter, leave and move about, and the root is from ṭawaf (circling/going around). The meaning is: some of you go around among others without permission.

**The seventh question:** What is the case of *baʿḍukum* (some of you)? **Answer:** It is in the nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate is ʿalā baʿḍin (upon some), with the meaning "one of you goes about upon another." The predicate was omitted because ṭawwafūna indicates it.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 60:

As for His saying, ﴿And as for women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn al-Sikkit said: "A woman is qā'id (past child-bearing) when she has ceased menstruating, and the plural is qawā'id. When you want to describe the act of sitting, you say qā'ida." The exegetes said: "The qawā'id are those who have ceased menstruating and bearing children due to old age, and there is no hope of marriage for them." The better view is that their cessation of menstruation is not taken into account, because that ends while the desire for them remains. What is meant is their cessation from being sought in marriage, and this only happens when they reach an age at which men no longer desire them.

The second issue: His saying, Most High, about women, ﴿who have no hope﴾ is like His saying: ﴿unless they forgo﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237].

The third issue: There is no doubt that He, Most High, did not permit them to lay aside all their garments, since that would expose every nakedness. Therefore the exegetes said: what is meant by "garments" here is the outer cloak (jilbab), the wrap (burd), and the veil that is over the khimar. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that he recited "that they lay aside their jalabib (outer cloaks)". And from al-Suddi, from his shaykhs: "that they lay aside their khumur over their heads". And from some of them that he recited "that they lay aside some of their garments". Allah, Most High, specified them with this ruling because suspicion is removed from them, and since they have reached this stage, if it were dominant in their estimation that the opposite were the case, it would not be lawful for them to lay aside their garments. For this reason He said: ﴿and that they refrain is better for them﴾. He made that more excellent only because it is further from suspicion, and this implies that where suspicion exists it is obligatory for them not to lay these aside, just as the like is obligatory for a young woman.

The fourth issue: The true meaning of tabarruj is the affectation of displaying what must be concealed, from the expression "a ship bārij", meaning one with no covering over it. Tabarruj is also the breadth of the eye in which its whiteness surrounds all its blackness, with nothing of it hidden. However, it is specifically applied to a woman uncovering herself to men by displaying her adornment and showing her attractions.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your houses or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or from that whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately.﴾ Then, when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus Allah makes the signs clear to you, that you may reason.

Know that in this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They differed concerning the meaning of the lifting of blame (ḥaraj) from the blind, the lame, and the sick. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that there is no blame or sin upon them for abandoning jihad. Al-Hasan said: the verse was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, whom Allah relieved of jihad, and he was blind. This view is weak, because Allah joined to it His words ﴿that you eat﴾, thereby indicating that the lifting of blame concerns only this matter. Most scholars said: the meaning is that the people used to avoid eating with these three categories and in these houses, so Allah the Exalted lifted that prohibition and removed it. They differed concerning the reason for which they held that prohibition. As for the blind, the lame, and the sick, they mentioned several explanations:

The first: They did not eat with the blind because he cannot see the good food, so he does not take it; nor with the lame, because he cannot sit comfortably, so that by the time he eats one morsel, the others eat two; and likewise the sick, because he is not able to eat as the healthy person eats. Al-Farra' said: according to this interpretation, ﴿ʿalā﴾ (upon) is in the sense of ﴿fī﴾ (in), meaning: there is no blame upon you in eating with these people.

The second: The blind, the lame, and the sick abstained from eating with the healthy. As for the blind, he said: "I do not see anything, so perhaps I would take the better and leave the worse." As for the lame and the sick, they feared that they would spoil the food for the healthy, due to matters that afflict the sick, and because the healthy would find them repulsive; and because the sick person might, out of greed, have his gaze and heart fixed on another's morsel, which the other would dislike. For these reasons they guarded themselves against eating with the healthy, so Allah the Exalted permitted this for them.

The third: al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah concerning this verse that when the Muslims went out to fight, they left the disabled behind, and they would hand over to them the keys of their doors, saying: "We have permitted you to eat from what is in our houses." But they were scrupulous about this and said: "We will not enter them while they are absent." So this verse was revealed as a concession for them. This is also the view of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. According to this, the meaning of the verse is the removal of blame from the disabled for eating from the house of one who hands them the key when he goes out to fight.

The fourth: It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān that this verse was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr, because he went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a campaign and left Ibn Mālik ibn Zayd in charge of his family. When he returned he found him weakened by hunger, and asked him about his condition. He said: "I was scrupulous about eating from your food without your permission."

As for the rest of the people, they mentioned two views:

The first: The believers used to take the weak and those with disabilities to the houses of their spouses, children, relatives, and friends, and they would feed them from them. When the words of Allah the Exalted were revealed: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly, except that it be a trade﴾ [an-Nisa': 29], meaning by sale, people then refrained from eating from one another's food, and this verse was revealed.

The second: Qatada said: the Ansar had within themselves a certain reserve, and they would not eat from these houses when they were rich. al-Suddi said: a man would enter the house of his father, or the house of his brother, or his sister, and the woman would offer him some food, and he would be scrupulous, because the master of the house was not there. So Allah the Exalted revealed this concession.

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: ḥaraj in language means constriction, and its meaning in religion is sin.

The third issue: Glorified is He, permitted people to eat from these places, and the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that permission to eat does not depend on seeking leave. The scholars differed on this. It is reported from Qatada that eating is permitted but not commendable. The majority of scholars rejected this, and then differed in several ways:

The first: That was in the early period of Islam, and then it was abrogated by his words, peace be upon him: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with the good pleasure of his soul." Among the things that indicate this abrogation is His words: ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given you for a meal, without waiting for its preparation﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. Among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ were some who had fathers, brothers, and sisters, so He generalized the prohibition against entering their houses except after permission to enter and to eat. If it is said that Allah permitted this only because the Muslims did not prevent these relatives from eating from their houses whether they were present or absent, so it was permissible to grant a concession in this matter, we say: if the matter were so, there would be no meaning in specifying these relatives by mention, because others are like them in this.

The second: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: the intended meaning of these relatives is when they are not believers. This is because Allah had earlier forbidden associating with them, by His words: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22]. Then He, glorified is He, permitted in this verse what He had forbidden there. He said: and what indicates this is that in this surah there is a command to greet the people of the houses: ﴿until you seek permission and greet its people﴾; but in the houses of these mentioned persons He did not command this, rather He commanded that they greet themselves. The summary is that the purpose of this verse is to establish permission in general, not permission at all times.

The third: Since it is known by custom that these people's hearts are content with the eating of those who come to them, and custom is like permission in this, it is possible to say that Allah specified them by mention because this custom is found among them for the most part; and for this reason He joined the friend to them. And since we know that this permission arose in this situation only because of the contentment present in it, there is no need to say that it was abrogated.

* * *

The fourth issue: Allah the Exalted mentioned eleven places in this verse:

The first of them: His words: ﴿nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your houses﴾. There is a question here: what is the benefit of permitting a person to eat his food in his own house? The answer: the intended meaning is the houses of your wives and your dependants; He attributed them to them, because a wife's house is like the husband's house. This is the view of al-Farra'. Ibn Qutayba said: He meant the houses of their children, and He attributed the houses of the children to the fathers, because the child is the earnings of his father and his property is like his property. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best thing a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings." The evidence for this is that He, glorified and exalted is He, enumerated the relatives and did not mention the children; because if the cause of the concession is kinship, then the one who is closest among them is more deserving.

The second: The houses of the fathers.
The third: The houses of the mothers.
The fourth: The houses of the brothers.
The fifth: The houses of the sisters.
The sixth: The houses of the paternal uncles.
The seventh: The houses of the paternal aunts.
The eighth: The houses of the maternal uncles.
The ninth: The houses of the maternal aunts.
The tenth: His words, the Exalted: ﴿or from that whose keys you possess﴾. It is read as ﴿miftāḥahu﴾ (singular), and in it there are several views:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: it is the agent and steward of a man over his estate and his livestock; there is no harm in his eating from the fruit of his estate and drinking from the milk of his livestock. Ownership of the keys means that they are in his hand and under his protection.

The second: al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means the disabled who used to guard for the warriors.

The third: The intended meaning is the houses of the slaves, because the property of the slave belongs to his master. al-Faḍl said: "al-mafātīḥ" has as its singular "mafতaḥ" with a fatḥa on the mīm, and the singular of "al-mafātīḥ" is "miftaḥ" with a kasra.

The eleventh: His words: ﴿or your friend﴾, and the meaning is: or the houses of your friends. The word "ṣadīq" may be singular or plural, and likewise "khalīṭ," "qaṭīn," and "ʿadd." It is related of al-Ḥasan that he entered his house and found a circle of his friends who had brought out baskets from beneath his bed containing khabīṣ and choice foods, and they were bent over eating them. His face's creases brightened with joy, and he laughed and said: "Thus we found them," meaning the senior Companions. And from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them: the friend is more than the two parents, because when the people of Paradise seek relief, they do not seek it from fathers and mothers but from friends, saying: "So we have no intercessors, nor a sincere friend" [ash-Shu'ara': 100–101]. It is also related that a brother of al-Rabiʿ ibn Khaythum in Allah entered his home in his absence, and he made himself at ease with his maidservant until she served him what he ate. When he returned, she informed him of this, and out of his delight at that he said: "If you are truthful, you are free."

* * *

The fifth issue: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, cited this verse as evidence that one who steals from a close kin within the prohibited degrees is not to have his hand cut off, because Allah permits by this verse eating from their houses and entering them without their permission, so their property is not guarded from them. If it is said: then it would follow that he is not to be cut off if he steals from the property of his friend, we say: whoever intends to steal his property is not a friend to him.

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately﴾, most of the exegetes said: the verse was revealed concerning the Banu Layth ibn ʿAmr, who are a tribe of Kinana. A man among them would not eat alone; he would remain all day, and if he did not find someone to eat with him he would eat nothing; and sometimes he had milking camels, and he would not drink from their milk until he found someone to drink with him. So Allah the Exalted informed them that when a man eats alone there is no blame upon him. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them. ʿIkrima and Abu Ṣāliḥ, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: when a guest came to one of the Ansar, he would not eat unless his guest ate with him; so Allah permitted them to eat however they wished, together or separately. al-Kalbi said: when they gathered to eat food, they would set aside food separately for the blind, and likewise for the disabled and the sick; so Allah made clear to them that this was not obligatory. Others said: they used to eat alone out of fear that in a gathering something would arise that would repel or harm; so Allah the Exalted made clear that this was not obligatory. His words ﴿jamīʿan﴾ (together) are in the accusative as a circumstantial state. ﴿Or ashtāt﴾ (separately) is the plural of ʿshatt,ʾ and shattā is the plural of shatīt, and shattān is the dual of shatt, as al-Mufaḍḍal said. It was also said: shatt is a verbal noun meaning dispersion, and then it is used as an adjective and made plural.

[p. 34]

As for His saying, ﴿So when you enter houses, greet your own selves﴾, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, made the souls of the Muslims like a single soul, following the pattern of His saying, ﴿And do not kill your selves﴾ [al-Nisa: 29]. Ibn Abbas said: If there is no one in the house, then one should say upon himself: "Peace be upon us from our Lord." And if he enters a mosque, he should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah, and upon us from our Lord." Qatadah said: We have been told that the angels return the greeting to him. Al-Qaffal said: If there are people of the dhimma (protected non-Muslim subjects) in the house, he should say: "Peace be upon those who follow the guidance."

His saying ﴿as a greeting﴾ is in the accusative as a masdar (verbal noun), as if He had said: "So greet with a greeting from Allah," meaning, with what Allah has commanded you. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Whoever says "as-salamu alaykum," its meaning is "the name of Allah is upon you." As for His saying ﴿blessed and good﴾, al-Dahhak said: The meaning of the blessing in it is the multiplication of reward. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah, glorified is He, informed that the greeting is blessed and established, because of the reward and recompense in it, and that if one obeys Allah in it, He increases its good and magnifies its reward. ﴿Thus Allah makes clear the verses to you﴾, that is, Allah explains His laws to you, ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that you may comprehend from Allah His command and His prohibition.

Humayd narrated from Anas, who said: "I served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for ten years, and he never said to me about anything I had done, 'Why did you do it?' nor about anything I had left, 'Why did you leave it?' I was standing at the head of the Prophet (ﷺ) pouring water over his hands, and he raised his head to me and said: 'Shall I not teach you three qualities by which you will benefit?' I said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah, yes.' He said: 'Whoever of my community you meet, greet them with peace, and your life will be lengthened. And when you enter a house, greet its people, and the good of your house will increase. And pray the Duha prayer, for it is the prayer of the ones who turn back repeatedly (to Allah).'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter requiring gathering, they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will of them, and ask forgiveness for them from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like your calling of one another. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind others. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He already knows your condition, and on the Day they are returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did. And Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: it was recited as ʿalā amrin jamīʿin (ﻋَلى أمْرٍ جَمِيعٍ, "upon a matter all together"). Then they mentioned several interpretations of His saying ﴿ʿalā amrin jāmiʿin﴾ (ﻋَلى أمْرٍ جامِعٍ, "upon a matter of common concern"):

The first: the matter of common concern is the matter that requires people to gather over it. The matter is described as "gathering" figuratively, such as fighting an enemy, consulting on an important affair, or a matter whose harm and benefit are general. His saying ﴿and when they are with him on a matter of common concern﴾ indicates that it is a grave affair, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) needs people of experience and opinion to seek help from their experience. Therefore, departing from one of them in this situation is something that is difficult for his heart.

The second: according to al-Dahhak, "a matter of common concern" refers to Friday (al-Jumuʿa) and the festivals, and everything in which a sermon is given.

The third: according to Mujahid, it refers to war and other matters.

The second issue: they differed regarding the occasion of its revelation. al-Kalbi said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would allude in his sermon to the hypocrites and criticize them, so the hypocrites would look right and left, and if no one saw them, they would slip away and leave without praying. If anyone saw them, they would stay and pray out of fear. So this verse was revealed. After its revelation, a believer would not leave for his needs until he had asked permission from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hypocrites would leave without permission.

The third issue: al-Jubbaʾi (al-Jubbāʾī, the Muʿtazili theologian) said: This indicates that their asking permission from the Messenger is from their faith. Otherwise, it would be possible for them to be perfect in faith while abandoning asking permission. This indicates that every obligation from Allah the Exalted and every avoidance of what is forbidden is part of faith.

The response: This is based on the premise that the word ʾinnamā (ﺇِنَّما, "only") is restrictive. Furthermore, the hypocrites abandoned asking permission only out of contempt, and there is no dispute that this is disbelief.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 63 (part 1 of 2):

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission﴾ means, out of honor for you and observance of etiquette, ﴿those are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, i.e., they act in accordance with what faith requires and entails. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the intended person is Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). That is because he asked permission during the expedition of Tabuk to return to his family, and he was granted permission, and it was said to him: "Go, for by Allah you are not a hypocrite." He intended to make the hypocrites hear that statement. When they heard it, they said: "What is wrong with Muhammad? When his companions ask his permission, he grants it to them, but when we ask his permission, he does not grant it to us. By Allah, we do not see him being just."

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Umar asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to perform the lesser pilgrimage (umrah), and he granted it to him, then said: 'O Abu Hafs, do not forget us from your righteous supplication.'"

Regarding His saying, ﴿and seek forgiveness for them from Allah﴾, there are two possibilities:

The first: He may seek forgiveness for them, as a reminder that it is preferable that asking permission not occur from them even if it is granted, because seeking forgiveness indicates a sin, and it may be mentioned in the case of some concessions.

The second: It is possible that He, exalted is He, commanded him to seek forgiveness for them in return for their adherence to the etiquette of Allah, exalted is He, in asking permission.

Second issue: Qatadah said: this verse abrogated His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. (Here "abrogated" translates the technical term naskh, meaning the supersession of one ruling by a later one.)

Third issue: The verse indicates that He, glorified is He, delegated to His Messenger some matter of the religion so that he might exercise independent reasoning (ijtihad) in it according to his own judgment.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others﴾, there are several interpretations:

One of them, which is the choice of al-Mubarrad and al-Qaffal, is: Do not treat his command to you and his summoning of you as you treat one another's, since his command is an obligatory duty that must be fulfilled. What indicates this is His saying immediately after this: ﴿So let those who oppose his order beware﴾.

The second: Do not address him as one of you addresses another, saying "O Muhammad," but say "O Messenger of Allah" or "O Prophet of Allah." This is from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: Do not raise your voices in calling him. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3]. This is from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: Beware of his supplication against you if you anger him, for his supplication is binding and is not like the supplication of anyone else. The first interpretation is closer to the structure of the verse.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, concealing themselves behind others﴾, the meaning is that they slip away little by little. The counterpart of tasallala (to slip away) is tadarraja and tadakhkhala (to move gradually or slip in). Al-liwadh (لِواذًا) means mutual concealment, which is that one takes cover behind another and that other behind him. The meaning is that they slip away from the congregation secretly, with some concealing themselves behind others. Liwadhan (لِواذًا) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "concealing themselves behind one another." It was also said: some of them would take cover behind a man when he asked permission, and when he was granted permission, the one who had not been granted permission would leave with him. The word لَواذًا is also recited with a fatha (لَواذًا), as a variant reading. Then they differed in several interpretations:

One of them: Muqatil said: the hypocrites found the Prophet's (ﷺ) sermon on Friday burdensome, so they would take cover behind some of his companions and leave without asking permission.

The second: Mujahid said: they would slip away from the row during battle.

The third: Ibn Qutaybah said: this was at the time of digging the trench.

The fourth: they would slip away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from his book, and from his remembrance. His saying: ﴿Allah already knows﴾ means a threat of retribution.

* * *

[Page 36]

As for His saying: ﴿So let those who oppose his order beware﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: Al-Akhfash said: ʿan (عَنْ) is superfluous (silah), and the meaning is "those who oppose his order." Others said: its meaning is "those who turn away from his order and deviate from his sunnah." So ʿan (عَنْ) was used to imply in opposing (mukhalafah) the meaning of turning away (i'rad).

Second issue: Just as the Messenger has been mentioned before, so Allah, exalted is He, has been mentioned before. But the intended one is the Messenger, so the pronoun refers to him. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: it is more apparent that it refers to Allah, exalted is He, because He is the closer one, and the rule for a pronoun is that it refers to what immediately precedes it, not to what came earlier.

Third issue: The verse indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation (wujub). The argument from it is that we say: one who abandons what is commanded opposes that command, and one who opposes a command deserves punishment, so one who abandons what is commanded deserves punishment, and there is no meaning to obligation except that. We said that one who abandons what is commanded opposes that command because conformity with a command is an expression of carrying out what it requires, and opposition is the opposite of conformity, so opposition to a command is an expression of failing to carry out what it requires. Thus it is established that one who abandons what is commanded is an opponent. We said that the opponent of a command deserves punishment because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let those who oppose his order beware lest a trial should befall them or a painful punishment should strike them﴾. He commanded the opponent of this command to beware of punishment, and commanding caution against punishment only happens after the cause for descending punishment has come into existence. Thus it is established that the opponent of the command of Allah, exalted is He, or of His Messenger has, in his case, something that requires the descent of punishment.

If it is said: We do not accept that one who abandons what is commanded opposes the command. Your statement that conformity with a command is an expression of carrying out what it requires and that opposition to it is an expression of failing to carry out what it requires, we answer: we do not accept that conformity with a command is an expression of carrying out what it requires. What is your evidence for this? Then we explain conformity with a command in two ways:

One: conformity with a command is an expression of carrying out what the command requires in the manner that the command requires it. For if the command required it as a recommendation (nadb), and you carried it out as an obligation, that would be opposition to the command.

Two: conformity with a command is an expression of acknowledging that this command is truth and must be accepted, so opposing it is an expression of denying that it is truth and must be accepted. Granting that what you mentioned indicates that opposition to a command is an expression of abandoning what it requires, it is nevertheless countered by other arguments. That is: if abandoning what is commanded were opposition to the command, then abandoning what is recommended would necessarily be opposition to the command of Allah, exalted is He, and that is false, for otherwise it would deserve punishment according to what you established in the second premise. Granting that one who abandons what is commanded opposes the command, why do you say that the opponent of a command deserves punishment because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let those who oppose his order beware﴾? We answer: we do not accept that this verse indicates the command of one who is an opponent of the command to beware, but rather it indicates a command to beware of opposing the command. Why should that not be the case? Granting that, it still indicates that the one who opposes the command is bound to beware, so why do you say that the opponent of a command is not bound to beware? If you say the word ʿan (عَنْ) is a superfluous extra particle, we say: the basic principle in speech, especially in the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is that nothing in it is superfluous. Granting that the verse indicates that the opponent of the command of Allah, exalted is He, is commanded to beware of punishment, why do you say that he is obligated to beware of punishment? At most, what is involved is that a command concerning it came, but why do you say that the command indicates obligation? This is the beginning of the issue. If you say: suppose it does not indicate the obligation of caution, it must still indicate that caution is good, and caution is good only after the cause for descending punishment exists. We answer: we do not accept that the goodness of caution is conditional upon the existence of the cause for descending punishment. Rather, caution is good when there is the possibility of punishment descending, which is why precaution (ihtiyat) is good. In our view, mere possibility exists, because this matter is one of probability and not certainty. Granting that the verse indicates the existence of what requires the descent of

[Page 37]

punishment, it is so not in every command but in one command, because His saying ﴿his order﴾ only conveys one command. For us, one command conveys obligation, so why do you say that every command is like that? Granting that every command is like that, the pronoun in His saying ﴿his order﴾ may refer back to Allah, exalted is He, or to the Messenger, and the verse indicates only that the command is obligatory with regard to one of them, so why do you say that it is so with regard to the other?

The answer: As for your saying, "Why do you say that conformity with a command is an expression of carrying out what it requires?" We answer: the evidence for this is that when a slave obeys his master's command, it is proper to say that this slave conforms to his master and acts according to his command. If he does not obey his command, it is said: he did not conform to him, rather he opposed him. The propriety of this usage is known necessarily by the people of the language. Thus it is established that conformity with a command is an expression of carrying out what it requires.

As for your saying: "Conformity is an expression of carrying out what the command requires in the manner the command requires it," we answer: since you have granted that conformity with a command is not achieved except by carrying out what the command requires, we say: there is no doubt that what the command requires is the act, because His saying "do" (ifʿal) only indicates the requirement of the act. When the act does not exist, what the command requires does not exist, so conformity does not exist, and it is necessary that opposition occur, because there is no intermediate position between conformity and opposition.

As for your saying: "Conformity is an expression of believing that this command is truth and must be accepted," we answer: this is not conformity with the command, but rather conformity with the evidence indicating that this command is true. The conformity of a thing is an expression of carrying out what requires the establishment of its requirement. When evidence indicates the truth of a thing, acknowledging its truth requires establishing what that evidence requires. As for the command, since it required the act to come into existence, conformity with it is an expression of establishing that act, and bringing it into existence requires establishing its existence. So conformity with the command is an expression of performing what it requires.

As for your saying: "If that were so, abandoning the recommended act would be opposition, and so it would be necessary to deserve punishment," we answer: this objection would only be valid if the recommended act were something commanded, and that is disputed.

As for your saying: "Why is it not possible that His saying ﴿so let them beware﴾ is a command to beware of the opponent, and not a command to the opponent to beware?" We answer: if that were so, the sentence would become "so let those who slip away concealing themselves behind others beware of those who oppose his order," and then His saying ﴿lest a trial should befall them or a painful punishment should strike them﴾ would be left without a clear function, because beware (hadhira) is not a verb that takes two objects.

As for your saying: "The word ʿan (عَنْ) is not superfluous," we answer: we have mentioned the disagreement of people concerning it in the first issue.

As for your saying: "Why do you say that His saying ﴿so let him beware﴾ indicates the obligation of caution against punishment?" We answer: we do not claim that caution is obligatory, but at least it is permissible, and that is conditional upon the existence of what requires the occurrence of punishment.

As for your saying: "Why do you say that the verse indicates that every opponent of a command deserves punishment?" We answer: because Allah, exalted is He, linked the descent of punishment to opposition, so it must be that opposition is the cause of it, and therefore its generality follows from the generality of the cause.

As for your saying: "Suppose the command of Allah or the command of His Messenger is for obligation, why do you say that the command is like that?" We answer: because there is no one who distinguishes between them, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Fourth issue: Some people said: the word amr (أمر) is shared between the verbal command and affair or manner, as one says: "the affair (amr) of so-and-so is upright." If that is established, then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿his order﴾ includes the Messenger's speech, his action, and his way, and that requires that everything he did, upon him be peace, is obligatory upon us. This issue is based on the premise that the pronoun in His saying ﴿his order﴾ refers back to the Prophet (ﷺ). As for if it refers back to Allah, exalted is He, the discussion falls away entirely. The full elaboration of this has been mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), and Allah knows best.

As for His saying, ﴿lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment strike them﴾, the meaning is that opposing the command necessitates one of these two matters. By "trial" (fitnah) is meant punishment in this world, and by "painful punishment" is meant the punishment of the Hereafter. God, exalted is He, mentioned the state of that opponent between these two matters in alternation only because that opponent may die without being punished in this world, and may also be afflicted with that in this world. For this reason He presented it in the form of alternation.

Then al-Hasan said: the trial is the manifestation of their hypocrisy. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it is killing. It has also been said: earthquakes and calamities. And from Ja'far ibn Muhammad: a cruel ruler will be set over them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 24, verse 64:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, this is like an indication of His power over them both, and over what is between them and what is within them, and His capability over the accountable being in what He deals with him concerning recompense, by reward or by punishment, and His knowledge of what he conceals and what he discloses. All of this serves as a deterrent from opposing His command.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He already knows what you are upon﴾, He only introduced ﴿qad﴾ to emphasize His knowledge of what they are upon of opposition in religion and hypocrisy. The emphasis on knowledge returns to the emphasis on the warning, because ﴿qad﴾, when it is placed before the present tense, carries the meaning of rubba (perhaps, "many a time"), so it agrees with rubba in its departure toward the sense of multiplication, as in the saying of the poet:

If the courtyard becomes deserted, then many a time there has stayed in it, after the departures of caravans, a caravan.

The address and the third person in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He already knows what you are upon, and the Day they are returned to Him﴾ may both be directed at the hypocrites by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and it is permissible that ﴿what you are upon﴾ is general while ﴿they are returned﴾ refers to the hypocrites. It has already been established in more than one place that the return to Him is the return to a place where no judgment belongs except to Him, so there is no point in repeating it, and Allah knows best.

And may Allah send blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
